title: Break my goals into weekly actions I can track
description: Converts quarterly or annual goals into specific weekly actions, milestones, and a simple tracker you review each Friday.
content:
Convert my goals into weekly actions.

**My goals:** [PASTE - e.g. "reduce invoice errors by 30% this quarter", "get certified in Power BI by June"]
**Time frame:** [e.g. "12 weeks starting July 1"]
**Hours per week I can give these goals:** [NUMBER]
**Existing commitments and busy weeks:** [e.g. "month-end close in weeks 1 and 5", "vacation in week 8"]
**How I'll be measured (if anyone measures):** [DETAILS]

Steps:
1. For each goal, define what done looks like and a leading indicator I can track weekly.
2. Break each goal into milestones, then into weekly actions small enough to finish that week.
3. Balance the load against my hours and busy weeks, and flag overloaded weeks.
4. Put dependencies and approvals early.

Return:
1. Goal summary: | Goal | Done looks like | Weekly indicator | Milestones |
2. Week-by-week plan: | Week | Actions | Goal | Hours | Milestone due |
3. A tracker I can paste into Excel or a to-do app, with columns for action, week, status, and notes.
4. A 10-minute Friday review checklist.
5. Warning signs that a goal is slipping, and what to cut first.

If a goal is too vague to plan, rewrite it as a measurable goal and mark it [CONFIRM] for me to approve. Don't invent targets or baselines.
variables: e.g. "month-end close in weeks 1 and 5", "vacation in week 8"

title: Build a bill calendar so nothing gets paid late
description: One calendar of every bill and renewal with due dates, payment method, and reminders, so you stop missing payments and late fees.
content:
Help me organize all my bills into one calendar so nothing is paid late.

**Bills and regular payments:** [LIST each - e.g. rent, utilities, phone, internet, insurance, credit card, loans, subscriptions, property tax, car registration - with amount, due date, and how I pay. No account numbers.]
**When my income arrives:** [e.g. paid on the 1st and 15th, monthly pension on the 3rd]
**Yearly or occasional bills:** [e.g. insurance renewal in March, license renewal]
**What goes wrong now:** [e.g. I forget, money's tight before payday, bills come by mail and get lost]
**How I like reminders:** [paper calendar / phone calendar / spreadsheet / someone checks with me]

Give me:
1. A month-at-a-glance table: Due date | Bill | Amount | Payment method | Autopay yes/no | Reminder date.
2. A check for timing problems: bills due before my income arrives, and suggestions such as asking a company to move a due date [CONFIRM WITH COMPANY].
3. Which bills are good candidates for autopay and which I may prefer to pay by hand, with the risks of each (e.g. overdraft if the account runs low).
4. A list of yearly and occasional bills with an amount to set aside each month.
5. A 10-minute weekly bill routine.
6. What to do if I can't pay a bill on time: who to call first and what to ask for.

Use only the amounts I give you. Mark anything missing as [ADD].
variables: e.g. paid on the 1st and 15th, monthly pension on the 3rd
e.g. insurance renewal in March, license renewal

title: Build a capacity plan comparing my workload to available hours
description: Calculates the hours your work needs versus the hours you or your team actually have, and shows where to cut or add help.
content:
Build a capacity plan for my workload.

**Whose capacity:** [just me / my team - list people and their working hours]
**Planning period:** [e.g. "next quarter, by month"]
**Work to fit in:** [PASTE PROJECTS, RECURRING WORK, AND EXPECTED REQUESTS - with estimated hours if known]
**Time already committed:** [meetings, admin, support duty, training, PTO, holidays]
**Known peaks:** [e.g. "year-end close in December", "product launch in week 6"]

Steps:
1. Calculate available hours: contracted hours minus PTO, holidays, meetings, and admin. Treat [e.g. 70%] of what remains as realistic project capacity unless I say otherwise.
2. Estimate demand hours for each item; mark estimates and give ranges for uncertain work.
3. Compare demand with capacity for each period and person.
4. Identify overloaded and underloaded periods and people.

Return:
1. Capacity table: | Period | Person | Available hours | Demand hours | Gap | Utilization % |
2. The main crunch points and what drives them.
3. Options to close each gap, with trade-offs: reschedule, cut scope, reassign, temporary help, overtime (last resort).
4. A recommended plan, and what I need to ask for or say no to.
5. An Excel-ready layout so I can update the numbers each month.

Show your math. Don't invent hours or headcount; ask if key numbers are missing. Treat planned utilization above 85% as a risk, not a target.
variables: just me / my team - list people and their working hours
meetings, admin, support duty, training, PTO, holidays
e.g. "year-end close in December", "product launch in week 6"

title: Build a certification study calendar that works back from exam day
description: A week-by-week plan that fits around work, schedules practice exams at checkpoints, and protects review time.
content:
Build a study calendar for my certification exam, working backward from the exam date.

**Certification:** [NAME]
**Exam date:** [DATE]
**Hours I can study by day of the week:** [e.g. "Mon-Thu 1 hr, Sat 3 hrs, Sun off"]
**Study priorities:** [PASTE THE READINESS CHECKLIST FROM STEP 1, or list weak and strong domains]
**Study materials:** [e.g. "official guide", "video course", "question bank", "labs"]
**Blackout dates:** [TRAVEL, WORK PEAKS, HOLIDAYS]

Rules:
- Reserve the final 7-10 days for review and full practice exams, not new material.
- Schedule a full practice exam around 40% of the way through and another around 75%.
- Spend most time on high-weight, low-confidence areas, but keep strong areas warm with short spaced reviews.
- Mix domains within a week rather than finishing one and never returning to it.
- Keep 10-15% of hours as buffer for missed sessions.
- Add hands-on practice for objectives that need it.

Return:
1. A week-by-week table: Week | Dates | Focus domains | Activities | Hours | Milestone.
2. A template for a single study session (warm-up review, new material, practice questions, error notes).
3. Checkpoint rules: the practice score I should be near at each checkpoint, and what to do if I'm below it, including whether to consider rescheduling (check the exam provider's rescheduling deadlines and fees).
4. How to adjust if I lose a full week.

This is step 2 of the "Pass a professional certification exam" pack. It works on its own, and can use the checklist from step 1.
variables: e.g. "Mon-Thu 1 hr, Sat 3 hrs, Sun off"

title: Build a habit that sticks
description: A practical plan to start a habit (or break one) using cues, tiny steps, and tracking.
content:
Help me build a habit that lasts.

**The habit:** [e.g. exercise 3x/week, read daily, stop doom-scrolling]
**Why it matters to me:** [REAL REASON]
**What's stopped me before:** [OBSTACLES]
**My daily routine:** [BRIEFLY]

Give me:
1. **The smallest version** I can do even on a bad day (2 minutes or less).
2. **Cue → routine → reward**: exactly when and where I'll do it, and what I'll attach it to.
3. **Friction plan**: make the good habit easier and the bad alternative harder.
4. **Tracking**: a simple way to track it and what counts as success.
5. **Relapse plan**: what to do after I miss a day (never miss twice).
6. **A 4-week ramp-up** from the tiny version to the target.

Check in with me: end by asking how I'll hold myself accountable.
variables: e.g. exercise 3x/week, read daily, stop doom-scrolling

title: Build a personal productivity system around my responsibilities
description: Designs a simple system for capturing, organizing, planning, and reviewing your work that fits your role, tools, and real week.
content:
Design a personal productivity system that fits my job.

**My role and main responsibilities:** [PASTE]
**Where work comes in:** [e.g. email, Teams or Slack, meetings, tickets, my manager]
**Tools I already use:** [e.g. Outlook, Microsoft To Do, Planner, OneNote, Notion, paper]
**What's going wrong now:** [e.g. "I forget follow-ups", "my to-do list has 80 items", "I never get to strategic work"]
**My typical week:** [meeting load, focus time, travel]
**How much setup I'll tolerate:** [e.g. "under 1 hour, nothing fancy"]

Build the system around five parts:
1. Capture: one place every task lands, and how it gets there from each channel.
2. Organize: a small set of lists or tags (e.g. by project, next action, waiting-for).
3. Plan: how I choose daily and weekly priorities.
4. Do: how I protect time for the work that matters.
5. Review: a short end-of-day close and a 30-minute weekly review.

Return:
- The system on one page, mapped to my tools.
- Exact setup steps for this week.
- A weekly review checklist.
- Rules for handling requests that arrive mid-day.
- The three habits that will make or break it, and how to restart after I fall off.

Keep it as simple as possible. Use only tools I already have unless a new one clearly solves a problem I described.
variables: e.g. email, Teams or Slack, meetings, tickets, my manager

title: Build a session timetable from everyone's availability
description: Turns messy availability notes into a filled weekly timetable with set group sizes, plus a backup option and a list of conflicts.
content:
Build a timetable that fits people into sessions based on their availability.

**Availability:** [PASTE as-is - messages, notes, or a list like "Sam: Mon/Wed after 4pm"]
**Session details:** [length, e.g. "45 minutes"; days and hours the venue or staff are available]
**People per session:** [e.g. "exactly 2", "3 to 6"]
**Sessions each person needs per week:** [e.g. "1", "2, not on consecutive days"]
**Other rules:** [e.g. "keep these two apart", "beginners together", "trainer needs a break after 3 sessions"]

Steps:
1. Convert the availability into a clean table: Person | Available days and times | Notes. List anything ambiguous (e.g. "evenings") with the assumption you made.
2. Build the primary timetable that fills each session to the target size, gives everyone their required sessions, and follows all rules.
3. Build an alternative timetable that trades off differently (e.g. fewer sessions but fuller, or more evenly spread days).
4. List anyone who could not be placed and why, plus the smallest change that would fix it (e.g. "if Priya can do Tue 5pm").

Return:
- Each timetable as a table: Day | Time | Attendees | Spots left.
- A per-person summary: Person | Session(s) assigned.
- The assumptions and conflicts list.

Do not place anyone outside their stated availability.

title: Build a weekly study schedule around my classes and job
description: A realistic recurring weekly schedule that fits classes, work, and commitments, with study blocks matched to each course.
content:
Build me a realistic weekly study schedule for this term.

**My classes:** [COURSE, meeting days and times, how hard it is for me, typical weekly workload]
**Work or other fixed commitments:** [JOB SHIFTS, SPORTS, CLUBS, COMMUTE, FAMILY RESPONSIBILITIES]
**When I focus best:** [morning / afternoon / night]
**Sleep I need:** [e.g. "in bed by 11:30, up at 7"]
**Big recurring deadlines:** [e.g. "weekly lab report due Mondays", "problem sets Thursdays"]
**What's gone wrong in past terms:** [e.g. "I cram on Sundays", "I skip readings"]

Rules:
- Use the common guideline of roughly 2 hours of study per credit hour in college (less in high school) as a starting point, then adjust to what's realistic for my load.
- Put harder subjects in my best-focus times.
- Keep study blocks 25-90 minutes with breaks; include a short review right after lectures where possible.
- Protect sleep, meals, and at least one real rest block.
- Leave flexible catch-up time each week.

Return:
1. A weekly table: Time block | Mon to Sun.
2. What each study block is for (e.g. "Bio: read chapter before Tuesday lecture").
3. A 10-minute Sunday planning routine to adjust for the coming week.
4. What to cut first in a heavy week.

If the total doesn't fit, tell me honestly and suggest options to discuss with my advisor or employer.
variables: JOB SHIFTS, SPORTS, CLUBS, COMMUTE, FAMILY RESPONSIBILITIES
e.g. "I cram on Sundays", "I skip readings"

title: Build a writing routine that gets my draft finished
description: A realistic weekly writing schedule, word targets, and a plan for bad weeks so you actually finish your draft.
content:
Help me build a writing routine that gets my first draft finished.

**Project:** [e.g. "a novel", "a poetry collection", "a memoir"]
**Where I am now:** [e.g. "12,000 words in", "just an outline"]
**Target length:** [e.g. "80,000 words", "30 poems"]
**Finish-by date, if any:** [DATE or "no deadline"]
**My week:** [work hours, family duties, when I have energy]
**What has derailed me before:** [e.g. "editing as I go", "skipping a day then a month", "phone"]

Give me:
1. A realistic daily or weekly target, with the math showing when I'd finish at that pace. If my deadline isn't realistic, say so and offer two options.
2. A weekly schedule: specific writing slots that fit my life, including a short "minimum day" version (e.g. 10 minutes or 100 words) for busy days.
3. A start-of-session ritual (under 5 minutes) and an end-of-session habit (e.g. leave a note for tomorrow mid-sentence).
4. Rules to protect drafting: when to edit, where to park ideas, how to handle a scene I can't figure out ([FIX LATER] notes).
5. A plan for missed days and bad weeks that doesn't involve guilt or "making up" all the words.
6. A simple progress tracker I can copy into a notebook or spreadsheet.

Keep it kind and practical; the aim is a finished messy draft, not a perfect one.
variables: work hours, family duties, when I have energy

title: Build my first-year compliance and admin calendar
description: A month-by-month calendar of filings, renewals, tax dates, and admin tasks so nothing gets missed in year one.
content:
Build a first-year compliance and admin calendar for my new business.

**Structure and location:** [e.g. "LLC in Florida, selling online to customers nationwide"]
**Date the business was formed:** [DATE]
**Tax year:** [calendar year or other]
**Registrations I have:** [tax IDs, sales tax permits, licenses, permits - with renewal dates if known]
**Do I have employees or contractors?** [DETAILS]
**Insurance policies and renewal dates:** [DETAILS]
**Other recurring tasks:** [domain renewal, software subscriptions, contract renewals]
**Previous step (optional):** [PASTE my co-founder agreement summary, so board or partner meetings it requires are scheduled]

Do this:
1. List the recurring obligation types that usually apply to a business like mine: annual reports, estimated tax payments, sales tax returns, payroll filings, contractor tax forms, license renewals, insurance renewals, and partner or board meetings.
2. Place them on a 12-month calendar, starting from my formation date. Where you don't know the exact date, write [CONFIRM DATE] and say where to find it - don't guess.
3. Add monthly and quarterly admin habits: bookkeeping close, invoice follow-up, cash review, backup of key files, password and access review.
4. Set reminders: how far ahead each one should alert me, and who is responsible.
5. Flag the items with the biggest penalties for missing them, so I give them extra buffer.

Output: a table (Month | Task | Type | Due date | Reminder date | Owner | Done), then a short list of the highest-risk items. This is general information; confirm all deadlines with my accountant and the relevant agencies.
variables: e.g. "LLC in Florida, selling online to customers nationwide"
domain renewal, software subscriptions, contract renewals

title: Change my address and set up utilities when I move
description: A complete list of who to notify and what to set up or cancel, with dates and a tracking sheet.
content:
Help me handle all the address changes and utilities for my move.

**Moving from and to:** [CITY/STATE or COUNTRY for each]
**Move-out and move-in dates:** [DATES]
**Renting or buying:** [at the old and new place]
**Current services:** [electricity, gas, water, trash, internet, streaming, phone, home security, gym, subscriptions]
**Accounts and people to update:** [e.g. "bank, employer, two credit cards, kids' school, vet, car registration"]

Give me:
1. A utilities plan: what to cancel or transfer at the old place and what to set up at the new one, with when to call (usually 2-3 weeks before) and service start and stop dates that overlap by a day so I'm never without power or water. Note that renters should ask the landlord which utilities they handle.
2. A complete address-change checklist grouped by: government (postal mail forwarding, driver's license, vehicle registration, voter registration, tax agency), money (bank, cards, loans, insurance, retirement accounts), work and school, health (doctors, pharmacy, insurance), and everything else.
3. Which changes have legal deadlines in my new location (e.g. driver's license transfer) - tell me to confirm on official government websites rather than relying on you.
4. A tracking table: Organization | Old/New | Action | Deadline | Done | Confirmation number.
5. Tips to avoid scams: only update addresses through official websites or numbers on your statements, and watch for fake "change of address" sites that charge fees.
variables: at the old and new place

title: Check passport, visa, and entry requirements before international travel
description: A checklist of documents, entry rules, and deadlines to verify before my executive travels abroad, with official sources to check.
content:
Help me check what my executive needs before an international trip.

**Traveler's nationality (passport country):** [COUNTRY]
**Other residency or visas held:** [if any]
**Route, including transits:** [e.g. "New York - Dubai (transit) - Mumbai"]
**Dates and length of stay:** [DATES]
**Purpose:** [business meetings / conference / site work / speaking]
**Passport expiry date:** [DATE]

Give me:
1. **What to verify for each country on the route** (including transit): visa or electronic travel authorization, passport validity rules, blank pages, business vs. work activity distinctions, and registration requirements. Present what is commonly required as a starting point and tell me to confirm on the official government or embassy website - entry rules change, and I must not rely on this alone.
2. **Timeline:** working back from departure, when to apply for anything that takes time.
3. **Document pack:** invitation letters, proof of onward travel, hotel bookings, company letter, insurance - with which ones are typically needed.
4. **Health and safety checks:** where to look for vaccination requirements and travel advisories.
5. **Red flags:** passport expiring within 6 months of return, tight transit with separate tickets, activities that might need a work permit.

Mark every requirement [VERIFY WITH OFFICIAL SOURCE]. Never state a rule as certain.
variables: business meetings / conference / site work / speaking

title: Create a chore chart that fits each of my kids' ages
description: Age-appropriate chores for each child, a fair weekly chart, and a simple system to keep everyone doing them.
content:
Help me set up household chores for my kids that actually get done.

**Kids and ages:** [e.g. "Maya 4, Leo 8, Sam 13"]
**Jobs I need help with:** [dishes, laundry, pets, tidying, trash, yard, etc.]
**Time each child realistically has on school days and weekends:** [DETAILS]
**Rewards approach:** [allowance tied to chores / no money / points / privileges / not sure]
**What's gone wrong before:** [e.g. "nagging", "arguments about fairness", "chart forgotten after a week"]

Give me:
1. A list of chores matched to each child's age and ability, with a one-line "done means" standard for each (e.g. "toys in bins, floor clear").
2. A weekly chart as a table: Chore | Who | Days | Done-means.
3. A fairness check so older kids don't feel dumped on and younger ones still contribute.
4. How to teach each new chore (show, do together, watch, solo).
5. A low-effort way to keep it going: reminders, check-in time, what happens when chores are skipped, and when to rotate jobs.

Keep tasks safe for each age (no sharp knives, hot stoves, or chemicals for young children) and the system simple enough to run in under 5 minutes a day.
variables: dishes, laundry, pets, tidying, trash, yard, etc.

title: Create a month-by-month wedding planning timeline
description: A planning calendar from today to the wedding with deadlines, owners, and payment due dates so nothing slips.
content:
Help us build our wedding planning timeline. This is step 4 of planning our wedding.

**Wedding date:** [DATE]
**Today's date:** [DATE]
**Already booked (from step 3, if we have it):** [venue, vendors, with deposit and payment due dates]
**Still to book or decide:** [LIST]
**Who's helping:** [planner, parents, friends - and what each will own]
**Special elements:** [e.g. "destination", "two ceremonies", "guests need travel and hotel info"]

Build a timeline that:
1. Works backward from the date in monthly blocks, then weekly for the final 6 weeks, then daily for the final week.
2. Covers: save-the-dates and invitations (with RSVP deadline), attire and fittings, rings, marriage license (check local rules and validity window - mark [CONFIRM]), hotel room blocks, menu tasting, music lists, decor, seating chart, vendor final confirmations, final payments, and tips.
3. Assigns an owner to every task, so it's not all on one person.
4. Builds in a 2-week buffer before the date with nothing new scheduled.
5. Includes a payment schedule: Vendor | Amount | Due date | Paid.

If our date is too soon for normal lead times, tell us which tasks to start this week.

Return: the timeline as a table (When | Task | Owner | Status), the payment schedule, and the 10 tasks most often forgotten. Next step: the wedding-day schedule.
variables: venue, vendors, with deposit and payment due dates
planner, parents, friends - and what each will own

title: Create a seasonal home maintenance checklist
description: A year-round maintenance calendar for your home type and climate, so small problems don't become expensive ones.
content:
Create a home maintenance checklist for my home and climate.

**Home type and age:** [e.g. "1960s single-family house", "2015 condo", "mobile home"]
**Climate:** [e.g. "cold snowy winters", "hot and humid", "wildfire area", "hurricane coast"]
**Systems:** [heating/cooling type, water heater (gas/electric/tankless), septic or sewer, well water, fireplace, gutters, deck, pool]
**Own or rent:** [if renting, focus on tenant tasks and what to report to the landlord]
**Skill level:** [BEGINNER / HANDY]

Give me:
1. A calendar by season (or month), with each task marked DIY or professional and a time estimate.
2. Safety tasks first: test smoke and carbon monoxide alarms monthly, replace their batteries, check fire extinguishers, clean dryer vents, and schedule fuel-burning appliance service.
3. Climate-specific tasks (e.g. preventing frozen pipes, storm prep, clearing brush).
4. Signs of trouble to watch for and when they need a professional quickly (e.g. gas smell - leave and call the gas company from outside; water stains; tripping breakers).
5. A simple home records template: appliance model numbers, filter sizes, warranty dates, and service history.

Return a table: Season | Task | DIY/Pro | Minutes | Notes. Keep it to what matters for my home - skip systems I don't have.

title: Create a year-round lawn and yard care calendar
description: A month-by-month yard plan for your grass type and climate, with water-wise and low-maintenance options.
content:
Create a lawn and yard care plan for me.

**Yard size and features:** [e.g. "quarter-acre, front lawn, back lawn with trees, flower beds"]
**Grass type (if known):** [e.g. "cool-season fescue", "Bermuda", "not sure"]
**Climate and region:** [REGION, rainfall, any watering restrictions]
**Problems:** [e.g. "bare patches", "weeds", "moss under trees", "standing water"]
**Goals:** [e.g. "lower maintenance", "safe for kids and dog", "pollinator-friendly"]
**Equipment and time:** [MOWER TYPE, HOURS PER MONTH]

Give me:
1. A month-by-month calendar: mowing height and frequency, watering, feeding, aerating, overseeding, leaf cleanup, and pruning. If I'm unsure of my grass type, tell me how to identify it.
2. Fixes for my listed problems, starting with cultural fixes (mowing higher, watering deeply and less often, improving drainage) before products.
3. Low-maintenance or water-saving alternatives for areas that struggle (ground covers, mulch beds, native plants).
4. Safety: follow product labels exactly, keep kids and pets off treated areas for the time the label says, mower and trimmer safety, and call 811 (in the US) before digging deep.
5. Tasks I may want to hire out (tree work near power lines, large tree removal).

Recommend a soil test through my local extension service before fertilizing. Return a calendar table: Month | Task | Notes.

title: Decide what to keep if I only have half the time
description: Stress-tests your workload against a 50% time cut to reveal what truly matters and what can shrink, slow down, or go.
content:
Help me work out what I'd keep if I suddenly had only half my working time.

**My current workload:** [PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, AND RECURRING WORK]
**My goals and what I'm accountable for:** [DETAILS]
**Why I'm asking:** [e.g. "upcoming leave", "taking on a new project", "I want to focus"]
**Period:** [e.g. "next 4 weeks"]

Steps:
1. Estimate the time each item takes now (mark estimates) and total it.
2. Assume I have 50% of that time. Keep only what has a real consequence if dropped: customer commitments, legal or compliance duties, my core goals, and work that unblocks others.
3. For everything else, decide: shrink (a smaller version), slow down (less often), hand off, or pause.

Return:
1. The 50% plan: | Item | Keep / Shrink / Slow / Hand off / Pause | New time | What changes |
2. What each shrunk version looks like (e.g. "the weekly report becomes 5 bullets in Teams").
3. Who would notice each change and what to tell them.
4. What this reveals: items I'm probably over-investing in even at full time.
5. Changes worth keeping permanently.

Be honest about trade-offs; don't pretend everything still gets done.
variables: PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, AND RECURRING WORK

title: Decide which meeting requests my executive should accept
description: A triage rule set for incoming meeting requests plus reply templates for accept, decline, delegate, and go-async.
content:
Help me build a triage system for meeting requests sent to my executive.

**My executive's role and top priorities this quarter:** [LIST 3-5]
**Typical requests they receive:** [e.g. "vendor demos, internal syncs, intro calls, mentoring, media"]
**Current weekly meeting hours vs. target:** [e.g. "32 hours, want 20"]
**People who always get time:** [NAMES OR ROLES]
**Who can stand in for them:** [deputies, chiefs of staff, team leads]

Create:
1. **Decision rules:** a short flowchart in text - who's asking, does it serve a current priority, does it need my executive specifically, could it be an email or a document instead, is there a deadline.
2. **Outcomes:** accept | accept shorter (15/25 min) | delegate to [name] | ask for an agenda first | send async | decline - with criteria for each.
3. **Reply templates** for each outcome, warm but brief, in my voice on my executive's behalf. The decline should leave the door open where appropriate without promising future time.
4. **Weekly caps:** how many slots to protect for each request type, and focus time to defend.
5. **A monthly review:** what to check to see whether the rules are working.

Keep the rules simple enough to apply in under a minute per request.
variables: deputies, chiefs of staff, team leads

title: Decide which tasks I should stop doing
description: Finds work you can eliminate, explains the risk of stopping each item, and drafts the message telling people.
content:
Help me decide what to stop doing.

**My current tasks, reports, meetings, and recurring commitments:** [PASTE]
**My main goals and what I'm accountable for:** [GOALS]
**Who asked for or uses each item (if known):** [DETAILS]
**Anything I must keep for legal, audit, or contractual reasons:** [DETAILS]

Test each item:
- Does anyone use the output? What would break if it stopped for a month?
- Does it serve my goals, or only a habit or a past need?
- Is someone else already doing it (duplicate work)?
- Could it be done less often, shorter, or to a lighter standard instead of stopped?

Return:
1. Table: | Item | Who relies on it | Value today | Risk if stopped | Verdict (Stop / Shrink / Keep) | Hours freed per month |
2. A stop-doing list, safest first.
3. For each Stop or Shrink: how to stop well - who to tell, a trial period (e.g. pause for 4 weeks and see who notices), and a fallback if it turns out to matter.
4. A short, professional message for each change that I can send by email, Teams, or Slack.
5. Total time freed and what I should put it toward.

Do not recommend stopping anything I flagged as required. Where you can't tell who relies on something, mark it [CHECK WITH OWNER] instead of guessing.

title: Decide which work notifications to turn off
description: Audits your apps and alerts and tells you which to switch off, batch, or keep, with the exact settings to change.
content:
Help me cut down the notifications that pull me away from work.

**Devices:** [e.g. Windows laptop, iPhone, Android]
**Apps and tools that notify me:** [e.g. Outlook, Teams, Slack, Jira, Asana, Salesforce, calendar, news, personal apps]
**Channels or groups I'm in:** [rough count, and which matter]
**Things I truly cannot miss:** [e.g. "my manager's DMs", "on-call alerts", "client emails"]
**When notifications bother me most:** [e.g. "during focus blocks", "in meetings", "evenings"]

Return:
1. **Notification audit table:** | App / channel | Current behavior | Decision (keep, batch, mute, turn off) | Reason |
2. **Settings checklist:** step-by-step changes for each app and device (banners, badges, sounds, keyword alerts, VIP lists, scheduled summary or focus modes). If you're unsure of a menu path in my version, say so rather than guessing.
3. **Safety net:** how the things I can't miss will still get through (VIP senders, @mention-only, priority alerts).
4. **Focus profile:** a work focus mode and an after-hours mode, with what each allows.
5. **One-week test:** what to watch for to check nothing important got missed.

Default to fewer interruptions, but never mute safety, security, or on-call alerts my job depends on.

title: Deep-clean my rental to get my deposit back
description: A room-by-room move-out cleaning checklist with photo documentation steps and a plan for disputed deductions.
content:
Help me prepare my rental for move-out so I get as much of my deposit back as possible.

**Home:** [ROOMS, flooring types, appliances]
**Lease cleaning terms:** [PASTE THE RELEVANT LEASE CLAUSE, or "not sure"]
**Move-in condition:** [e.g. "I have move-in photos", "there was already a carpet stain"]
**Known issues:** [e.g. "nail holes", "pet scratches on door", "oven never cleaned"]
**Time before handover:** [DAYS] and **help available:** [PEOPLE]
**Location:** [STATE/COUNTRY - deposit rules vary]

Give me:
1. A room-by-room checklist focused on what inspectors check most (oven, fridge, bathroom grout, baseboards, inside cabinets, windows, walls, floors), with a time estimate per room.
2. Which small fixes I can reasonably do myself (e.g. filling nail holes) versus leave alone, and to check my lease before painting or repairing anything.
3. A documentation plan: date-stamped photos and video of every room, meter readings, and returned keys.
4. A short, polite message to my landlord requesting a walk-through and the deposit return timeline.
5. What to do if deductions seem unfair: request an itemized list, compare with move-in records, and where to find my local tenant rights.

Deposit rules (deadlines, allowed deductions, normal wear and tear) vary by location - treat this as general information and check my local tenant agency or a tenant-rights organization.
variables: PASTE THE RELEVANT LEASE CLAUSE, or "not sure"

title: Define the minimum viable version of a deliverable
description: Strips a project or deliverable down to the smallest version that still achieves its purpose, so you can deliver sooner.
content:
Help me define the minimum viable version of a piece of work.

**The deliverable:** [e.g. "new onboarding guide", "sales dashboard", "policy update", "client proposal"]
**Its purpose - the decision or outcome it must enable:** [DETAILS]
**Who will use it, and what they need from it:** [AUDIENCE]
**The full version I had in mind:** [PASTE SCOPE OR OUTLINE]
**Deadline and time available:** [DETAILS]
**Must-haves set by others:** [e.g. "legal review", "brand template"]

Steps:
1. Restate the purpose in one sentence.
2. Sort every element into: essential to the purpose / improves it / nice to have.
3. Define the minimum version: the essentials only, done to a standard that won't embarrass me or mislead anyone.
4. Plan what goes into version 2 if the first one proves useful.

Return:
1. The purpose statement.
2. Scope table: | Element | Essential / Improves / Nice to have | Reason |
3. The minimum viable version, as a short paragraph and a checklist.
4. Time saved vs. the full version (estimate).
5. Risks of delivering the smaller version, and how to handle them.
6. A one-line note to set expectations with the requester ("This is version 1; next we'll add ...").

Never cut accuracy, required approvals, or compliance steps to make it smaller.

title: Define the scope and budget for my kitchen or bath renovation
description: A clear scope with must-dos, wants, and cuts, a realistic budget split by category, and a contingency fund before you talk to anyone.
content:
Help me define the scope and budget for my renovation. This is step 1 of renovating my kitchen or bathroom.

**Room:** [kitchen / bathroom - size and current layout]
**What's wrong with it now:** [e.g. "no counter space, cabinets falling apart, poor lighting"]
**What I want:** [WISH LIST]
**Budget:** [MAX AMOUNT and how I'm paying - savings, loan, credit]
**Home age and known issues:** [e.g. "1960s house, old wiring, slow drain"]
**How long I plan to stay:** [YEARS]
**DIY skills:** [none / some painting and demo / experienced]

Do this:
1. Sort my wish list into must-do (safety, function, failing parts), want, and nice-to-have. Point out whether moving plumbing, gas, or walls is driving the cost, and what keeping the current layout could save.
2. Split my budget across typical categories: design, demolition, cabinets, counters, fixtures, appliances, flooring, electrical, plumbing, labor, permits, and finishes. Mark all percentages and costs as [CONFIRM with local quotes].
3. Set a contingency of 10-20% (higher for older homes) and say what it covers: hidden rot, old wiring, mold, code upgrades.
4. Flag work that usually needs a permit and a licensed pro (electrical, plumbing, gas, structural) - rules vary by location.
5. Suggest a budget version, a mid version, and the version I described, with what changes between them.

Return a one-page scope summary and a budget table (Category | Low | High | Notes). Keep it - next I'll turn it into a design brief.
variables: kitchen / bathroom - size and current layout
MAX AMOUNT and how I'm paying - savings, loan, credit
e.g. "1960s house, old wiring, slow drain"
none / some painting and demo / experienced

title: Design a daily routine that fits my life
description: A realistic daily/weekly routine built around your energy, commitments, and goals.
content:
Help me design a routine I can actually stick to.

**My fixed commitments:** [work hours, commute, caregiving, classes]
**What I want to fit in:** [e.g. exercise, deep work, reading, side project, family time]
**My energy pattern:** [when I'm sharp vs. tired]
**What's failed before and why:** [HONEST NOTES]
**Sleep target:** [HOURS]

Create:
1. A weekday schedule and a weekend schedule (time blocks).
2. A "minimum version" for bad days — the 2–3 things that keep momentum.
3. Habit-stacking suggestions (attach new habits to existing ones).
4. One small change to start with this week, not a full overhaul.

Leave buffer time — no back-to-back blocks all day.
variables: e.g. exercise, deep work, reading, side project, family time

title: Design a low-distraction workday with an attention budget
description: Builds a daily template for your role that spends your best attention on the highest-value work and contains reactive tasks.
content:
Help me design a workday that spends my attention on purpose.

**My role and what I'm judged on:** [TITLE + 2-3 KEY OUTCOMES]
**A typical day now:** [DESCRIBE OR PASTE CALENDAR - meetings, email, deep work, admin]
**My energy pattern:** [when I'm sharp, when I fade]
**Reactive demands I can't avoid:** [e.g. support queue, approvals, client calls]
**Main distractions:** [e.g. Slack, open-plan noise, phone, constant small asks]

Treat my attention as a budget: I have a limited number of high-focus hours (assume 3-4 unless I say otherwise), a larger pool of medium-focus time, and low-energy time.

Return:
1. **Attention budget:** how many hours of high, medium, and low focus I have, and what each should be spent on, with my highest-value work in high-focus hours.
2. **Daily template:** a time-blocked day showing focus blocks, communication windows, meetings, admin batches, and breaks.
3. **Reactive-work container:** where incoming requests go and when I handle them, so they don't leak into focus time.
4. **Environment and tool rules:** 5-7 specific rules (e.g. "Slack closed during focus blocks", "phone in another room until 11").
5. **Overspend signals:** signs I've spent my budget badly that day, and the reset I'll use.
6. **A version for heavy-meeting days.**

Make it fit my real constraints. Where my job requires being reachable, design around that instead of ignoring it.
variables: when I'm sharp, when I fade
e.g. support queue, approvals, client calls
e.g. Slack, open-plan noise, phone, constant small asks

title: Design a shared-drive folder structure and naming convention
description: A logical folder structure, file naming rules, and access guidance so the team can find documents in seconds.
content:
Help me design a shared drive structure for my team or office.

**Team and what they produce:** [e.g. "12-person office: finance docs, contracts, HR records, marketing assets, board papers"]
**Tool:** [e.g. SharePoint, Google Drive, Dropbox]
**Current problems:** [e.g. "duplicates everywhere", "can't find the final version", "everything in one folder"]
**Sensitive material:** [HR, payroll, legal, board - who should and shouldn't see it]
**Retention requirements:** [how long certain records must be kept, if known]

Create:
1. **Top-level structure:** no more than 7-9 folders, organized by function or activity (not by person), with the purpose of each and 2 levels of subfolders as an example.
2. **Naming convention:** a pattern such as YYYY-MM-DD_Topic_DocType_v01, with rules for dates, versions, "FINAL" (avoid it), and characters to avoid. Give 5 before/after examples.
3. **Access model:** which folders are open, restricted, or confidential, and who owns access for each. Keep personal and sensitive records in restricted areas only.
4. **Archive and retention:** when files move to archive and how long to keep each record type - [CONFIRM WITH FINANCE/LEGAL] for statutory periods.
5. **Migration plan:** how to move from today's mess in stages without breaking links.
6. **A one-page guide** for staff with the 5 rules that matter most.
variables: HR, payroll, legal, board - who should and shouldn't see it
how long certain records must be kept, if known

title: Design a sustainable weekly routine around my highest-value work
description: Builds a repeatable weekly template that protects your most important responsibilities and keeps your hours sustainable.
content:
Redesign my typical week so it's built around my most important work and is sustainable.

**My role and highest-value responsibilities:** [e.g. "team leadership, pricing decisions, key client relationships"]
**Recurring commitments:** [meetings, reports, 1:1s, admin - with time for each]
**Target working hours per week:** [e.g. "45, no weekends"]
**Energy pattern:** [when I'm sharpest, when I'm drained]
**Non-negotiables outside work:** [e.g. "school pickup at 3:30 on Tuesdays"]

Steps:
1. Total my recurring commitments and compare them with my target hours.
2. Reserve time for my highest-value responsibilities first, in my best energy hours.
3. Fit recurring work around that, with admin and email batched into set windows.
4. Leave a 15-20% buffer for unplanned work.
5. If it doesn't fit, recommend what to shrink, move, or hand off.

Return:
1. A weekly template: | Day | Morning | Midday | Afternoon |, with themed blocks.
2. Hours by type (high-value work, recurring work, meetings, admin, buffer), compared with today if I gave enough detail.
3. The changes needed to make it real: meetings to shorten, reports to drop, requests to redirect.
4. Rules that protect it (e.g. no meetings before 11 on Tuesdays and Thursdays).
5. A monthly 15-minute check to see whether the routine still fits.

Make it work for a real job with real interruptions, not an ideal one, and never plan beyond my target hours.
variables: meetings, reports, 1:1s, admin - with time for each
when I'm sharpest, when I'm drained

title: Diagnose what is causing my work overload
description: Analyzes your workload to find the real sources of overload and where work keeps expanding, with a fix for each.
content:
Help me understand why I'm overloaded, not just how to get through this week.

**My role and what I'm meant to focus on:** [DETAILS]
**My current workload:** [PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, RECURRING WORK, AND MEETING LOAD]
**Where requests come from:** [e.g. "my manager, 3 internal teams, clients directly"]
**How long I've felt overloaded, and what changed:** [e.g. "since a colleague left in March"]
**Hours I'm working vs. contracted:** [OPTIONAL]

Look for these common causes:
- Volume: more work than one role can hold.
- Scope creep: tasks that grew bigger than agreed, or "small favors" that became permanent.
- Unclear ownership: work I picked up because no one else did.
- Process: rework, chasing inputs, manual steps, slow approvals.
- Meetings and interruptions eating focus time.
- My own habits: saying yes by default, perfectionism, not delegating.
- Inherited work from vacancies or reorganizations.

Return:
1. The top 3-5 sources of overload, each with the evidence from my inputs and an estimate of hours per week.
2. Where my workload is expanding unnecessarily, and how it happens.
3. For each source: one fix I control, and one that needs my manager or another team.
4. A short, factual summary I can take to my manager, framed around trade-offs rather than complaints.
5. Early warning signs to watch so it doesn't build up again.

Stick to what I've shared and label assumptions. If what I describe sounds like burnout (constant exhaustion, dread, health effects), say so gently and suggest talking to my manager, HR, or a health professional.
variables: PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, RECURRING WORK, AND MEETING LOAD
e.g. "my manager, 3 internal teams, clients directly"
e.g. "since a colleague left in March"

title: Extract decisions, actions, risks, and deadlines from a document
description: Turns any document or long update into a clear list of decisions made, actions with owners, risks, deadlines, and open questions.
content:
Go through the material below and pull out everything I need to track.

**Material:** [PASTE document, report, long email thread, or project update]
**Context:** [e.g. "steering committee pack for the CRM migration"]
**Today's date:** [DATE, so you can flag what's overdue]

Return five tables:
1. **Decisions made:** | Decision | Who made it | Date | Section or quote |
2. **Actions:** | Action | Owner | Due date | Status if stated | Section |
3. **Risks and issues:** | Risk or issue | Likely impact | Mitigation mentioned | Owner |
4. **Deadlines and milestones:** | Date | What is due | Who | Overdue or at risk? |
5. **Open questions:** | Question | Why it matters | Who could answer it |

Then:
- **Top 3 things to follow up on this week.**
- **Gaps** - actions with no owner, deadlines with no date, decisions that are implied but never confirmed.

Rules:
- Only list what the material says or clearly implies; mark implied items as (implied).
- Never invent owners or dates - write [NO OWNER] or [NO DATE].
- Keep each row to one line so I can paste the tables into Excel, a tracker, or a Teams or Slack message.
variables: PASTE document, report, long email thread, or project update
e.g. "steering committee pack for the CRM migration"
DATE, so you can flag what's overdue

title: Find and cut the interruptions that break my focus at work
description: Analyzes a log or description of your workday to find the biggest interruptions, needless context switches, and focus-draining meetings, with fixes for each.
content:
Help me find what is interrupting my work and which interruptions I can get rid of.

**My role:** [JOB TITLE]
**A log or description of 1-3 typical days:** [PASTE - what I worked on, every interruption, and roughly when; a rough list is fine]
**My recurring meetings:** [NAME, LENGTH, FREQUENCY, MY ROLE IN EACH]
**Work that keeps getting pushed back:** [TASKS]

Analyze:
1. **Interruption sources:** group every interruption by source (people, notifications, meetings, my own habits, tools, unclear processes) and estimate how often each happens and the focus time it costs, including the time to get back on track.
2. **Needless switches:** places where I jump between topics or tools without a reason, such as checking email between every task or splitting one project across many small slots.
3. **Focus-draining meetings:** meetings that cut my day into pieces or where my presence adds little value. For each, suggest: decline, send a delegate, go async, shorten, or move.
4. **Root causes:** which interruptions come from a process or information gap (e.g. people ask me because the answer isn't written down anywhere).

Return:
- A ranked table: | Source | Frequency | Est. focus cost per week | Can it be eliminated, reduced, or batched? | Specific fix |
- The top 3 changes to make this week, with any message I need to send.
- What to keep: interruptions that are actually part of my job and should stay.

Base estimates only on what I've shared and label them as estimates. Don't suggest ignoring my manager or customers in ways that would hurt my work.
variables: NAME, LENGTH, FREQUENCY, MY ROLE IN EACH

title: Find my highest-value work and where my time adds little value
description: Maps your responsibilities to business value so you can see what to protect, what to shrink, and where time is wasted.
content:
Help me see which parts of my work create the most value and which consume time without much return.

**My role and what I'm measured on:** [e.g. "finance business partner; measured on forecast accuracy and decision support"]
**My responsibilities and recurring activities:** [PASTE - add rough hours per week if you know them]
**Team or company goals this year:** [GOALS]
**What my manager or customers value most from me:** [IF KNOWN]

For each activity, assess:
- Value created: revenue, cost, risk reduced, decisions improved, customer or team impact.
- Whether it needs me specifically (my judgment, relationships, expertise) or could be done by someone or something else.
- Time vs. value: high value / low time, high value / high time, low value / high time, low value / low time.

Return:
1. Value map: | Activity | Hours/week | Value created | Needs me? | Quadrant | Recommendation |
2. My 3-5 highest-value activities, and what would happen if I gave them more time.
3. Where I spend time without meaningful value, with the likely reason (habit, unclear ownership, someone else's priority, perfectionism, a broken process).
4. Three changes for next week that move at least [e.g. 4] hours from low-value to high-value work.

Rules: Don't assume meetings or admin are worthless; some prevent risk or keep key relationships healthy. Where hours are missing, estimate and label them as estimates. Judge value from what I told you; don't invent metrics.
variables: PASTE - add rough hours per week if you know them

title: Find the avoidable stress and mental load in my work
description: Separates the pressure that comes with your job from avoidable strain caused by unclear priorities, open loops, rework, and broken processes.
content:
Help me find the parts of my work that create stress and mental load that don't need to be there. I'm not asking how to do less work overall - I want to find the strain that comes from how the work is set up.

**My role and main responsibilities:** [DETAILS]
**My workload:** [PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, RECURRING DUTIES, AND DEADLINES]
**What feels stressful and when:** [e.g. "Monday reporting crunch", "last-minute requests from leadership"]
**Things I keep track of in my head:** [e.g. "who owes me what", "which version is current", "promises I made in meetings"]
**What I can and can't change:** [e.g. "can't change client deadlines", "can propose process changes"]

Check for avoidable sources of pressure and mental load, such as:
- unclear priorities or conflicting requests from different people
- last-minute work caused by late inputs upstream
- rework from vague briefs or changing requirements
- tracking commitments in my head instead of a system
- too many open loops and half-finished tasks
- decisions I keep re-making because no rule or default exists
- approvals and handoffs that stall work
- recurring tasks rebuilt from scratch each time

Return:
1. **Pressure map:** | Source | Necessary or avoidable | Effect on me | Root cause | Who could fix it |
2. **Top 5 avoidable sources**, ranked by how much relief removing each would bring.
3. **Fix for each:** a concrete change (a system, template, rule, or agreement), who I'd need to talk to, and a first step for this week.
4. **Necessary pressure:** what is simply part of the job, with ways to make it easier to carry (preparation, buffers, checklists).
5. **A short message** I could use to raise the biggest issue with my manager, framed around the fix, not the complaint.

Base everything on what I've shared and label assumptions. If what I describe sounds like burnout (constant exhaustion, dread, numbness, health effects), say so plainly and suggest I talk to my manager, HR, an employee assistance program, or a doctor.
variables: PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, RECURRING DUTIES, AND DEADLINES

title: Fit a side hustle into my week without burning out
description: A realistic weekly time budget and routine that protects your day job, sleep, and relationships.
content:
Help me build a sustainable weekly routine for running a side hustle next to my full-time job.

**My day job hours and commute:** [DETAILS]
**Fixed commitments:** [family, caregiving, exercise, classes]
**Energy pattern:** [when I'm sharpest; when I'm useless]
**Side hustle tasks:** [e.g. making the product, client work, marketing, admin, customer messages]
**Hours I'm willing to give it:** [e.g. "8-10 hours a week"]

**Previous step (optional):** [PASTE my weekend demand test results, so the plan focuses on what worked]

Do this:

2. Assign each task type to a time block based on the energy it needs (deep work in good-energy slots, admin in low-energy slots).
3. Build a weekly calendar with protected rest time and at least one fully off evening.
4. Set boundaries for customer communication (response windows, auto-replies) so it never leaks into work hours.
5. List 3 early warning signs of burnout or slipping at my day job, and what to cut first if they appear.
6. Add a 15-minute weekly review checklist.

Output: the weekly schedule as a table (Day | Time | Block | Tasks), then the boundaries, warning signs, and review checklist.

title: Get from accepted offer to closing day without surprises
description: A dated checklist from inspection to keys, with how to read the inspection report, what to ask for, and closing-day checks.
content:
Help me get from an accepted offer to closing day. This is step 5 of buying my first home.

**Accepted offer details (from step 4, if I have it):** [price, contingencies and their deadlines, closing date]
**Inspection report findings:** [PASTE the summary or key issues, if I have it]
**Loan type and lender:** [DETAILS]
**My move-out situation:** [lease end date, or current home to sell]

lease end date, or current home to sell

title: Get my home ready before I leave on a trip

Help me get my home ready before I go away.

title: Interview a new executive to learn how they like to work
description: A structured intake conversation and working-style profile so I can support a new executive well from week one.
content:
Help me prepare to start supporting a new executive.

**Executive's role and when they start (or when I start):** [DETAILS]
**What I already know about them:** [background, previous company, reputation]
**What I'll be responsible for:** [calendar, inbox, travel, expenses, board, team events]
**How much time I'll get with them in the first week:** [e.g. "one 45-minute meeting"]

Create:

title: Make a checklist of documents to bring to an appointment or application
description: A tailored list of documents, copies, and proof to bring to a government office, bank, or benefits appointment so you don't get turned away.
content:
Help me prepare everything I need for an appointment or application.

**Where:** [office or organization, and my country or state]

Give me:

If I didn't paste the official requirements, give a typical list but mark every item [CHECK THE OFFICIAL LIST] and tell me where to look for it (the organization's official website or phone line). Don't invent fees, deadlines, or rules.
variables: office or organization, and my country or state
PASTE IT if I have it, or say "don't have it"

title: Make a family emergency plan
description: A household plan for fires, storms, and power outages with meeting points, contacts, and a supply checklist kids understand.
content:
Help me create an emergency plan for my family.

**Household:** [adults, kids with ages, older relatives, pets]
**Home type:** [apartment floor, house, mobile home]
**Local risks:** [e.g. "hurricanes", "wildfire", "earthquakes", "winter storms", "floods"]
**Special needs:** [medications, medical devices, mobility, allergies, infant supplies]
**Where kids spend their days:** [schools, daycare, activities]

Give me:
1. A one-page plan: two meeting places (near home and outside the neighborhood), an out-of-area contact, and how we'll reach each other if phones are down.
2. A fire escape plan: two ways out of each room, a practice schedule, and what to teach kids (get low, never go back inside).
