5. A kid-friendly version: what each child should know by heart, at their age, and a practice game.
6. A twice-yearly review checklist (batteries, food dates, contact updates).

Tell me to check my local emergency management office and my kids' schools for official evacuation routes and pickup policies, marked [CHECK LOCALLY]. Always: in a real emergency, call emergency services.
variables: adults, kids with ages, older relatives, pets

title: Make a moving timeline and checklist
description: A week-by-week moving plan from eight weeks out through the first week in your new home.
content:
Create a moving plan for me.

**Moving from and to:** [e.g. "apartment to house, same city", "cross-country", "abroad"]
**Moving date:** [DATE] and **today's date:** [DATE]
**Household:** [PEOPLE, KIDS' AGES, PETS]
**Home size and stuff:** [e.g. "2 bedrooms, lots of books"]
**Moving method:** [movers / rental truck / portable container / undecided]
**Budget:** [AMOUNT]
**Special items:** [e.g. "piano", "plants", "medications", "important documents"]

Build:
1. A week-by-week timeline working back from my moving date (8 weeks out to moving day), compressed if I have less time.
2. Admin tasks with timing: book movers or truck, notify landlord, transfer or set up utilities and internet, change address, update school records, move prescriptions, and update insurance.
3. A packing plan: room-by-room order (least-used first), box labeling system (room + contents + priority), and how many boxes to expect.
4. An "open first" box list and a separate bag for documents, medicines, chargers, and valuables that travels with me, not the truck.
5. A moving-day schedule, including plans for kids and pets that day.
6. The first-week checklist in the new home: test smoke and CO alarms, find the water shutoff and breaker panel, change locks if possible.

Return the timeline as a table: Week | Task | Owner | Done.
variables: movers / rental truck / portable container / undecided

title: Make a realistic weekly cleaning schedule
description: A cleaning routine sized to your home and energy, split into daily, weekly, and monthly tasks with time estimates.
content:
Create a cleaning schedule I can actually stick to.

**Home:** [e.g. "2-bed apartment, 1 bathroom, carpet in bedrooms"]
**Who lives here:** [PEOPLE, KIDS, PETS]
**Time I can give:** [e.g. "15 minutes on weekdays, 1 hour on Saturday"]
**What bothers me most:** [e.g. "bathroom gets gross fast", "clutter on counters", "pet hair"]
**What I let slip:** [TASKS YOU ALWAYS SKIP]
**Energy or health limits:** [e.g. "chronic fatigue", "bad back", "work night shifts"]

Build:
1. A daily "reset" list (10-15 minutes max).
2. A weekly plan with one zone per day, or a single cleaning block, whichever fits my time. Include time estimates per task.
3. Monthly and seasonal tasks (e.g. fridge clear-out, vacuum vents, wash pillows), spread out so no week is overloaded.
4. A minimal supply list. Include safety notes: never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar, or other cleaners; ventilate when using strong products; keep cleaners away from kids and pets.
5. A "bad week" version: the 3 tasks that keep the home livable when everything else slips.

Return the schedule as a table (Task | Frequency | Day | Minutes | Who) plus a one-page printable checklist. Keep it forgiving - the goal is good enough, consistently.
variables: e.g. "2-bed apartment, 1 bathroom, carpet in bedrooms"
e.g. "15 minutes on weekdays, 1 hour on Saturday"

title: Make a scholarship search and application tracker
description: A personalized list of scholarship types to search for, a deadline tracker, and a weekly routine for applying.
content:
Help me build a plan to find and apply for scholarships.

**About me:** [grade/year, state, intended major, GPA range, activities, work, community service, heritage or identity groups I'm comfortable using, first-generation status, special talents, parent employers or affiliations]
**When I need the money:** [e.g. "fall 2027 tuition"]
**Time I can spend per week:** [HOURS]
**Essays or materials I already have:** [e.g. "a personal statement", "two recommendation letters"]

Do this:
1. List the categories of scholarships I may qualify for (local, school-based, major-specific, employer, community organizations, identity-based, activity-based) and where to look for each: my school counselor or financial aid office, local foundations and clubs, professional associations, and well-known free search databases.
2. Give me red flags for scholarship scams: fees to apply, guaranteed winnings, requests for bank details, pressure tactics.
3. Build a tracker template with columns: Name | Amount | Deadline | Eligibility | Materials needed | Essay prompt | Status | Submitted date.
4. Show how to reuse one strong essay for several prompts by adapting it, not copying it.
5. Set a weekly routine to keep going.

Return the categories, scam checklist, tracker, reuse strategy, and routine. Don't invent specific scholarships, amounts, or deadlines; I'll fill them in after confirming on official sites.

title: Organize my family's busy week in one plan
description: A shared weekly family schedule that juggles school, work, activities, meals, and driving without daily chaos.
content:
Help me organize my family's week into one clear plan.

**Family members:** [adults and kids with ages]
**Fixed commitments:** [work hours, school times, activities, appointments, with days and times]
**Who can drive or cover what:** [DETAILS]
**Pain points:** [e.g. "Tuesday pickup clash", "no time for dinner", "forgetting forms and gear"]
**Weekly tasks:** [groceries, laundry, homework, practice, bills]

Give me:
1. A weekly grid: Day | Time | Who | What | Driver/owner. Highlight clashes and suggest fixes (carpools, swapping slots, dropping something).
2. A "daily launch" checklist for mornings and a 10-minute evening reset (bags packed, forms signed, clothes out).
3. A simple dinner plan that matches busy nights to quick meals.
4. A Sunday planning routine (15 minutes) to update the calendar together.
5. Ideas for a shared family calendar or whiteboard setup, and how to color-code by person.
6. Where we're overloaded: an honest look at whether any activity should pause, and how to decide.

Keep the plan realistic, with buffer time, and protect at least one unscheduled family block each week.

title: Pick my top five priorities and a must-do, should-do, can-wait list
description: Narrows a long workload to five clear priorities plus a must-do, should-do, can-wait list you can share with your manager.
content:
Help me cut my workload down to five clear priorities.

**Everything on my plate:** [PASTE TASKS, PROJECTS, AND REQUESTS]
**What my manager or team expects most from me right now:** [e.g. "close the audit findings", "ship the pricing page"]
**Time frame:** [this week / this month / this quarter]
**Hard deadlines and commitments I cannot move:** [DETAILS]

Rules:
- Top five means five. If two items are really one outcome, combine them; do not sneak in a sixth.
- Must-do = a real consequence if missed (deadline, customer, compliance, a commitment I made). Should-do = clear value but can slip a little. Can-wait = fine to defer or drop for this period.
- Write each priority as an outcome ("Signed vendor contract by May 15"), not an activity ("work on vendor stuff").
- If something is urgent but low value, say so instead of ranking it high.

Return:
1. My top five priorities, each with the outcome, why it made the list, and the next action.
2. Must-do / Should-do / Can-wait lists, one line per item with the reason.
3. Items that need a conversation (someone expects them but they landed in Can-wait), with a one-line message I can send.
4. A short version I can paste into Teams or Slack to align with my manager.

Mark anything you lack the facts to classify as [CONFIRM] rather than guessing.
variables: e.g. "close the audit findings", "ship the pricing page"
this week / this month / this quarter

title: Plan a cooking timeline for a holiday or dinner party
description: A reverse-scheduled cooking plan so every dish is ready on time, with make-ahead tasks and oven juggling.
content:
Help me plan the cooking so everything is ready at the same time.

**Occasion and serving time:** [e.g. "Thanksgiving dinner, eating at 4:00 pm"]
**Number of guests:** [NUMBER, plus any dietary needs or allergies]
**Menu:** [LIST EACH DISH - include recipe cook times and temperatures if you have them]
**Kitchen limits:** [e.g. "one oven", "4 burners", "small fridge", "no stand mixer"]
**Help available:** [e.g. "my partner can handle drinks and the table"]
**How much I can prep ahead:** [days before / morning of only]

Build:
1. A make-ahead list by day (2 days before, day before, morning of) with storage instructions.
2. A minute-by-minute timeline for the final 4 hours working backward from serving time, showing what's in the oven, on the stove, and resting. Flag oven-temperature conflicts and suggest fixes (stagger, use a slow cooker, serve at room temperature).
3. A shopping list grouped by store section, with quantities scaled to guest count.
4. Food-safety checkpoints: thawing time for any frozen meat or poultry (in the fridge, with days needed), safe internal temperatures, and keeping hot food hot and cold food cold (no more than 2 hours at room temperature).
5. Tasks I can hand to helpers or guests.

Keep it printable: a one-page timeline table with columns Time | Task | Equipment | Who.
variables: NUMBER, plus any dietary needs or allergies
e.g. "my partner can handle drinks and the table"

title: Plan a deep-work session for hard tasks
description: Sets up a focused work block with a clear output and few distractions.
content:
Act as a focus and execution specialist.

**Context**
I need to complete [TASK] within [TIME].

**Task**
Break the work into focused blocks. Define a concrete outcome for each block, identify likely interruptions, prepare the minimum inputs needed, and specify what should not be worked on during the session.

**Format**
Return:
| Block | Objective | Deliverable | Focus rule |
Then provide a 5-item distraction-control checklist.

**Task:** [PASTE]

title: Plan a deep-work workflow to finish a big project
description: Maps a multi-week project into deep-work sessions, prep steps, and re-entry notes so progress doesn't stall between interruptions.
content:
Help me design a deep-work workflow to get a large project done over the next few weeks.

**Project and final deliverable:** [e.g. "a 20-page market entry report", "a new pricing model in Excel"]
**Deadline:** [DATE]
**Hours I can realistically give it per week:** [NUMBER]
**Inputs I still need from others:** [DATA, APPROVALS, INTERVIEWS]
**What usually derails me on projects like this:** [e.g. "I research forever", "urgent work crowds it out", "I lose the thread between sessions"]

Return:
1. **Phases:** break the project into phases (e.g. gather, think, draft, refine), and mark which need deep focus and which can be done in short bursts.
2. **Session plan:** a week-by-week list of deep-work sessions, each with a concrete output and a length.
3. **Prep before each session:** what to have open and ready so I start in under 5 minutes.
4. **Re-entry note template:** a 3-line note I write at the end of every session (where I stopped, next step, open questions) so I can pick up fast.
5. **Dependency plan:** when to request inputs from others so I'm never waiting at the start of a deep session.
6. **Early warnings:** signs I'm falling behind and what I'll cut or ask for when I see them.

Be honest about the math: if the hours don't cover the work, show the gap and give me options (narrow scope, move date, get help).

title: Plan a kid's birthday party on a budget
description: A complete party plan with theme, schedule, activities, food, and a cost breakdown that stays within your budget.
content:
Help me plan my child's birthday party.

**Child's age and interests:** [AGE; favorite things]
**Number of kids and adults:** [ROUGH COUNT]
**Budget:** [AMOUNT]
**Location:** [home, park, rented space; indoor or outdoor]
**Date, time, and length:** [DETAILS]
**Must-haves or no-gos:** [allergies, dietary needs, no sugar overload, sensory sensitivities]

Give me:
1. 3 theme ideas that fit the interests and budget, then build the plan around the one I pick (default to the first).
2. A minute-by-minute schedule for the party length, with arrival, 2-3 activities, food, cake, and wind-down. Keep it realistic for this age's attention span.
3. Activities and games with materials and simple rules, plus one quiet option for kids who get overwhelmed.
4. A food and drink list with quantities for my guest count, labeled for common allergens.
5. A budget table: Item | Estimated cost | Cheaper swap. Use [ESTIMATE] and tell me to check local prices.
6. A countdown checklist: 3 weeks, 1 week, day before, party day.
7. Invitation text with RSVP and allergy question.

Include basic safety notes (supervision for water or trampolines, choking hazards for under-4s, balloon caution).
variables: home, park, rented space; indoor or outdoor

title: Plan a research paper with milestones up to the due date
description: A backward-planned schedule from topic to final draft, with small weekly milestones that fit your other classes.
content:
Help me plan my research paper so I'm not writing it all the night before.

**Assignment and requirements:** [TOPIC OR PROMPT, LENGTH, NUMBER OF SOURCES, CITATION STYLE]
**Due date (and any checkpoint dates set by my teacher):** [DATES]
**Today's date:** [DATE]
**Where I am now:** [no topic yet / have a topic / have sources / have a draft]
**Time I realistically have each week:** [e.g. "about 4 hours, mostly weekends"]
**Other big deadlines in this period:** [EXAMS, OTHER PAPERS, WORK SHIFTS]

Plan backward from the due date through these stages: choose and narrow topic, find sources, read and take notes, working thesis, outline, first draft, revision, citations and formatting, final proofread.

Rules:
- Break each stage into tasks of 30-90 minutes.
- Leave a buffer of at least 2 days before the deadline.
- Avoid stacking big tasks on days I've said are busy.
- Flag early if the timeline is too tight and suggest what to ask my teacher.

Return:
1. A table: Date or week | Task | Time needed | Done when... (a clear finish line).
2. The 3 dates I must not miss.
3. A short what-to-do-if-I-fall-behind plan.
variables: TOPIC OR PROMPT, LENGTH, NUMBER OF SOURCES, CITATION STYLE
no topic yet / have a topic / have sources / have a draft

title: Plan a sustainable work pace through busy seasons and deadlines
description: Maps your year of peaks and quiet periods, with prep before each crunch, limits during it, and real recovery after.
content:
Help me plan a working pace I can sustain across the whole year, including busy periods, instead of lurching from one crunch to the next.

**My role and recurring deadlines:** [e.g. "month-end close by day 5", "quarterly board pack", "annual budget in October"]
**Busy seasons and known peaks in the next 6-12 months:** [DATES AND WHAT DRIVES EACH]
**How the last peak went:** [hours worked, weekends, what slipped, how long recovery took]
**My pattern outside peaks:** [typical hours, evenings or weekends worked, last real time off]
**Commitments outside work:** [e.g. caregiving, study, commute]
**What I can influence:** [e.g. "can shift internal deadlines", "can request temporary help", "client dates are fixed"]

Steps:
1. Map my year into peak, normal, and quiet periods with the expected load in each. Mark estimates.
2. Find work that can be pulled forward out of peaks (prep, templates, early inputs) or pushed until after them.
3. Set crunch limits: the longest stretch and the maximum weekly hours I'll accept, and the trigger for asking for help.
4. Build recovery in: lighter days or a lighter week after each peak, and when to take leave.

Return:
1. **Year-at-a-glance:** | Period | Expected load (light / normal / heavy) | What drives it | Prep beforehand | Recovery after |
2. **Pre-peak checklist:** what to prepare 2-4 weeks before each peak.
3. **Crunch rules:** what pauses during a peak, what support I ask for, my hours limit, and the end date.
4. **Recovery plan:** how I recover after each peak, plus planned time off.
5. **Warning signs** that my pace is slipping, and the reset I'll use.
6. **Talking points** (3-5) to agree peak support and recovery time with my manager.

If the workload doesn't fit sustainable hours even outside peaks, say so plainly and help me frame that conversation instead of planning a heroic schedule. If I describe constant exhaustion, dread, or health effects, suggest I talk to my manager, HR, an employee assistance program, or a doctor.
variables: hours worked, weekends, what slipped, how long recovery took

title: Plan gifts and occasion messages for my executive's key contacts
description: A gift and occasions tracker, policy-safe gift ideas, and card templates for my executive's key relationships.
content:
Help me set up and plan gifts and occasion messages for my executive's key relationships.

**Key contacts:** [name or role, relationship, occasions to mark - birthdays, holidays, promotions, deals closed, bereavement]
**Company gift policy:** [value limits, rules for government officials or public-sector clients, approval needed, recording requirements]
**Budget:** [PER GIFT AND ANNUAL]
**What my executive usually likes to do:** [e.g. "handwritten notes", "books", "charity donations"]
**Known preferences of recipients:** [dietary, cultural, religious, alcohol-free]

Give me:
1. A tracker layout: contact | occasion | date | last gift/message | idea | budget | policy check | status.
2. Gift ideas for each type of relationship that are personal but appropriate - avoid anything that could look like an inducement.
3. **Policy checks:** flag recipients who may be restricted from accepting gifts (public officials, some regulated industries, procurement contacts) and gifts near value limits. Tell me to confirm with compliance where unsure.
4. Cultural considerations for international recipients (colors, numbers, timing, alcohol).
5. A reminder schedule: when to start ordering for each occasion given shipping times.
6. 3 short card-message templates in my executive's name for congratulations, thanks, and condolences, for them to personalize.

Never assume a recipient's preferences or beliefs; mark unknowns [ASK].

title: Plan my day in an ADHD-friendly way
description: Breaks tasks into tiny, concrete steps with timers, rewards, and low-friction starts.
content:
Help me plan today in a way that works with an ADHD brain.

**What needs to get done:** [BRAIN DUMP — messy is fine]
**Hard deadlines:** [TIMES]
**My energy right now:** [low / medium / high]
**What usually derails me:** [e.g. starting, switching tasks, phone, losing track of time]

Do this:
1. Pick the 3 things that truly matter today. Park the rest in a "later" list.
2. Break each into tiny, concrete first steps (each under 10 minutes; the first step should be almost too easy).
3. Build a simple schedule with timed sprints (e.g. 20 minutes on, 5 off), buffers, and a reward after each block.
4. Add "body doubling" or accountability ideas where useful.
5. Give me one line to read when I get stuck: the very next physical action.

Keep the output short and scannable. No guilt, no lectures.
variables: e.g. starting, switching tasks, phone, losing track of time

title: Plan my executive's business trip itinerary
description: A complete trip plan with meetings, travel, buffers, bookings to make, and a day-by-day itinerary my executive can carry.
content:
Help me plan a business trip for my executive.

**Destination(s) and dates:** [DETAILS]
**Purpose and fixed meetings:** [meetings with times and addresses, events, site visits]
**Departure city and preferences:** [airline/seat/class, hotel type, loyalty programs, dietary needs]
**Travel policy limits:** [class of travel, hotel rate caps, booking channel]
**Other travelers:** [who else is going]
**Budget:** [AMOUNT or "per policy"]

Produce:
1. **Plan and checks:** recommended flights or trains by time window (not specific fares - I'll book), hotel location logic (near which meetings), and ground transport between each stop with realistic travel times and buffers.
2. **Booking checklist:** everything to reserve, in the order to book it, with policy flags.
3. **Day-by-day itinerary:** time | activity | address | contact | confirmation number [ADD] | notes. Times in local time with home time in brackets.
4. **Risks:** tight connections, jet lag before a big meeting, late arrivals, public holidays or major events at the destination [CONFIRM].
5. **Pack for the trip:** documents, adapters, materials for each meeting, and gifts if relevant.
6. **Emergency sheet:** hotel, local contacts, my number, company travel provider - with placeholders.

Never invent flight numbers, prices, or confirmation codes. Mark anything I need to verify as [CONFIRM].
variables: meetings with times and addresses, events, site visits
class of travel, hotel rate caps, booking channel

title: Plan my thesis or dissertation timeline to submission
description: Builds a realistic backward-planned schedule from submission date, with chapter milestones, buffers, and advisor checkpoints.
content:
Help me build a realistic plan to finish my thesis or dissertation.

**Degree and submission deadline:** [e.g. "PhD, submit by 30 June"]
**Required structure:** [e.g. "intro, 3 empirical chapters, discussion" or "thesis by publication"]
**Status of each chapter or study:** [not started / data collected / analyzed / drafted / revised]
**Fixed commitments:** [teaching, job, conferences, fieldwork, caring responsibilities]
**Hours per week I can realistically give:** [NUMBER]
**Advisor and committee turnaround:** [e.g. "advisor takes 2-3 weeks per chapter"]
**Formal steps:** [ethics, committee meeting, formatting review, intent to submit, defense scheduling]

Steps:
1. Plan backward from the deadline, including institutional steps and feedback turnaround.
2. Estimate effort per chapter phase (analysis, first draft, revision), and add a 15-20% buffer.
3. Flag whether the plan is feasible as stated; if not, show what to cut, merge, or negotiate.
4. Set monthly milestones and a weekly rhythm (writing blocks, check-ins).
5. Identify the riskiest dependencies (data, co-authors, approvals) and a fallback for each.

Return: a feasibility verdict, a month-by-month milestone table (Month | Deliverable | Sent to advisor | Status check), a weekly template, and the top 3 risks with mitigations.
variables: not started / data collected / analyzed / drafted / revised

title: Plan my week
description: Turns your commitments and goals into a realistic weekly plan.
content:
Act as an executive productivity coach.

**Context**
I have the following commitments, goals, deadlines, meetings, and unfinished work for the coming week.

**Task**
Create a realistic weekly plan. Protect strategic work before meetings expand into all available time. Group related work, account for dependencies, and flag overload instead of pretending everything can fit.

**Format**
Return:
1. Weekly priorities
2. Monday-Friday plan
3. Focus blocks
4. Delegation opportunities
5. Items to defer
6. Main risk to the plan

**Inputs:** [PASTE]

title: Plan revision when I have several finals close together
description: A day-by-day timetable across all your exams, balanced by weight and risk, with a triage rule if you fall behind.
content:
Help me plan revision for several final exams that fall close together.

**Exam timetable:** [EACH EXAM: course, date, time]
**For each course:** [exam weight in final grade, my current grade, difficulty for me (easy / medium / hard), and top priority topics - paste from step 1 if you have them]
**Hours I can revise each day:** [DETAILS, including days with classes or work shifts]
**Fixed commitments:** [WORK, FAMILY, TRAVEL]
**Today's date:** [DATE]

Rules:
- Allocate hours by a mix of exam weight, my risk of a poor result, and difficulty, not just which exam comes first.
- Front-load the nearest exam, but keep later exams warm with short sessions so nothing goes cold.
- Mix subjects within a day to avoid fatigue; put the hardest work in my best hours.
- Protect sleep (at least 7 hours), meals, and one short break block per day. All-nighters reduce recall.
- Keep a small buffer each day.
- Include practice under timed conditions for each exam, not just rereading.

Return:
1. A day-by-day table until my last exam: Date | Session 1 | Session 2 | Session 3 | Notes.
2. A between-exams plan for the evening after each exam (rest, then switch).
3. A triage rule: if I fall a day behind, what to cut first.
4. A short checklist for the night before each exam.

If exam stress becomes overwhelming, suggest talking to my school's counseling or academic support services. This is step 4 of the "Ace your university final exams" pack. It works on its own, and can use the ranked topic lists from step 1 for each course.
variables: DETAILS, including days with classes or work shifts

title: Plan the renovation schedule and how we'll live through it
description: A phase-by-phase schedule with inspections and order deadlines, plus a plan for daily life without a working kitchen or bathroom.
content:
Help me plan the renovation schedule and how my household will cope during it. This is step 3 of renovating my kitchen or bathroom.

**Room and scope (from steps 1-2, if I have them):** [PASTE]
**Contractor's proposed start date and length:** [DETAILS, or "not hired yet"]
**Household:** [people, ages, pets, work from home?]
**Other kitchens or bathrooms in the home:** [e.g. "only one bathroom"]
**Fixed dates to work around:** [holidays, guests, travel]

Give me:
1. A phase-by-phase schedule: demolition, rough plumbing and electrical, inspections, insulation and drywall, cabinets, counters (measuring often happens after cabinets go in), tile, fixtures, final inspection, punch list. Show where delays usually happen and which phases depend on materials arriving.
2. A list of my own deadlines: decisions, orders, and payments the contractor needs from me, and when.
3. For a kitchen: a temporary kitchen setup (where, what appliances, no-cook and one-pot meal ideas, dishwashing plan). For a bathroom: options if it's our only one (gym, neighbors, a short-term rental for the worst days).
4. A plan for dust, noise, pets, kids' safety, and protecting floors and other rooms.
5. Questions to settle with the contractor before day 1: working hours, daily cleanup, where materials are stored, who pulls permits, and how we'll communicate.

Return the schedule as a table (Week | Phase | My tasks | Risks) plus the living-through-it plan. Next step: track costs and changes during the work.
variables: people, ages, pets, work from home?

title: Plan what to do with the time AI saves me or my team
description: A reclaimed-capacity plan that redirects hours saved by AI to priority work, instead of letting them disappear into more busywork.
content:
Help me plan what to do with the time AI is saving, so it turns into real value instead of more busywork.

**Where AI is saving time:** [TASKS and rough hours per week or month]
**Whose time it is:** [me / my team - roles and number of people]
**Our top priorities this quarter:** [GOALS]
**Work we never get to:** [e.g. customer follow-ups, process fixes, coaching, strategic projects, learning]
**Signs of overload or burnout:** [DETAILS, if any]

Steps:
1. Confirm how much capacity is real: deduct review time and any new work AI created. Mark estimates.
2. List options for using the reclaimed time: higher-value work, quality improvement, customer time, skills development, innovation, workload relief, or absorbing growth without hiring.
3. Score each option on value to the business, value to people, and ease.
4. Allocate the capacity across 2-4 options, with a deliberate share kept for recovery or slack where workload is unsustainable.

Return:
1. A capacity allocation table: Option | Hours/month | Owner | Expected outcome | How we'll measure it.
2. Ground rules to protect the time (e.g. calendar blocks, what we stop accepting).
3. What to tell my manager or team about how the saved time is being used.
4. A 30-day review checkpoint: what evidence shows the time is being used as planned.

Treat the hour figures as estimates unless I've given tracked data. Don't assume the default use of freed time is more of the same work.
variables: TASKS and rough hours per week or month
me / my team - roles and number of people

title: Prepare tomorrow's daily briefing for my executive
description: A one-page brief of tomorrow's meetings, prep needed, decisions waiting, and logistics so my executive walks in ready.
content:
Prepare a daily briefing for my executive for tomorrow.

**Tomorrow's calendar:** [PASTE MEETINGS - time, title, attendees, location or link]
**Notes on each meeting:** [purpose, related emails, documents, last time they met - whatever I have]
**Decisions or approvals waiting on them:** [LIST]
**Deadlines in the next 48 hours:** [LIST]
**Logistics:** [travel, car pickups, dress code, time zone changes]
**My executive's preferences:** [e.g. "bullets only", "wants the 3 most important things at the top"]

Build the briefing in this order:
1. **Top 3 for tomorrow:** the things that matter most, in one line each.
2. **Day at a glance:** table - time | meeting | who | purpose | prep needed | document link.
3. **Meeting notes:** for each important meeting, 2-4 bullets: why it's happening, what they want out of it, open issues, anything sensitive about the attendees.
4. **Decisions and sign-offs waiting:** what, for whom, by when, my recommendation if I've given one.
5. **Logistics:** travel times, buffers, where they need to be and when.
6. **Watch-outs:** back-to-back meetings with no break, meetings missing an agenda or document, overruns likely to cascade.

Rules:
- Use only what I've given you. Mark gaps as [CONFIRM] or [ADD DOCUMENT] - never invent a meeting purpose or attendee detail.
- Keep it to one screen; readable on a phone.
- After the briefing, list anything I should fix tonight (a missing agenda, a meeting to move) before sending it.
variables: PASTE MEETINGS - time, title, attendees, location or link
travel, car pickups, dress code, time zone changes

title: Prioritize my book of accounts for the week
description: Triage your customer accounts by risk, opportunity, and deadlines, and get a focused weekly action list.
content:
Help me decide which customer accounts to focus on this week.

**My accounts:** [PASTE LIST - for each: name, contract value, renewal date, health score or status, last contact date, open issues, any opportunities]
**Fixed commitments this week:** [MEETINGS, QBRS, DEADLINES]
**Time available for account work:** [e.g. "about 15 hours"]
**My targets this quarter:** [e.g. renewal rate, expansion revenue, adoption goals]

Triage the list:
1. Sort accounts into: Act now (risk or deadline in the next 30 days), Grow (expansion signals), Maintain (healthy, light touch), and Watch (data missing or mixed signals).
2. Flag accounts I haven't contacted in too long relative to their value and risk.
3. Pick the top 5-7 accounts for this week and give one specific action for each (e.g. "send usage review to sponsor", "book renewal call", "chase open ticket").
4. Group quick tasks I can batch (e.g. 5 check-in emails in one block).
5. Suggest what to deliberately skip this week and why.

Output: a table | Account | Category | Why now | This week's action | Time estimate |, then a short daily plan that fits my available hours.

Base everything on the data I provided. If an account is missing a key field, put it in Watch and note what to look up.
variables: e.g. renewal rate, expansion revenue, adoption goals

title: Prioritize my open requisitions and plan my recruiting week
description: A ranked view of my open roles and a realistic weekly plan that balances sourcing, interviews, and admin.
content:
Help me prioritize my open roles and plan my recruiting week.

**Open requisitions:** [for each: role, hiring manager, days open, business priority, pipeline by stage, next deadline]
**Fixed commitments this week:** [scheduled interviews, intake meetings, team meetings]
**Hours available for recruiting work:** [e.g. 35]
**Recurring admin:** [ATS updates, scheduling, reports]
**What's falling behind:** [e.g. sourcing for 2 roles, candidate follow-ups]

Do the following:
1. Rank my roles using business impact, urgency, pipeline health (how far each is from an offer), and risk of losing candidates. Show the ranking as a table with the reason for each.
2. Identify the single most important action per role this week (e.g. "get feedback on 3 finalists", "40 targeted outreaches", "reset requirements").
3. Build a day-by-day plan with time blocks: sourcing blocks in the morning, candidate calls, batched admin and scheduling, and a buffer for last-minute interviews.
4. List what to delegate, automate (e.g. scheduling links, templates), or push back on.
5. Draft a short note to a hiring manager if I need to set expectations on a lower-priority role.

Keep the plan realistic for my available hours - don't schedule more than about 80% of them.
variables: scheduled interviews, intake meetings, team meetings
e.g. sourcing for 2 roles, candidate follow-ups

title: Prioritize today's work
description: Ranks today's tasks by value, urgency, and dependencies and gives you a realistic plan.
content:
Act as a productivity strategist who prioritizes work by value, urgency, dependencies, and effort.

**Context**
I have the following workload and only [HOURS] of usable time today.

**Task**
Prioritize the work using business impact, urgency, strategic importance, dependencies, effort, and consequences of delay. Protect meaningful focus time and identify what should be deferred, delegated, or eliminated.

**Format**
Use:
| Task | Action | Priority | Why | Suggested time |
Actions: Do now, Schedule, Delegate, Defer, Eliminate.
Finish with my top 3 priorities.

**Tasks:** [PASTE]

title: Re-plan today's work when I'm short-staffed
description: A quick plan to prioritize work, reassign people, and communicate when absences leave the shift short.
content:
I'm short-staffed today. Help me re-plan the shift quickly.

**Who's in and their skills:** [NAME OR ROLE | skills | hours]
**Who's missing:** [ROLES/SKILLS MISSING]
**Today's workload:** [orders, appointments, jobs, tickets - with deadlines and customer commitments]
**Non-negotiables:** [safety-critical roles, legal minimum staffing, key customers, cutoffs]
**Options I might have:** [overtime, borrow from another team, temps, supervisor stepping in]

Give me, fast and in this order:
1. Must-do work today vs. what can be delayed, reduced, or rescheduled, with the impact of each delay.
2. A reassignment plan: who does what, keeping safety-critical and minimum-staffing roles covered by qualified people only.
3. Cover options ranked by cost and speed, and who I need to call.
4. Short messages: one to the team, one to my manager, and one to any customer or internal partner whose work will slip. Use [ADD] for times.
5. What to watch through the day (backlog, breaks, fatigue) and when to make the next call.

Don't reassign anyone to tasks they aren't trained or certified for. Afterwards, suggest 2-3 changes (cross-training, standby list) that would make the next short day easier.

title: Rebook and reschedule fast when my executive's travel is disrupted
description: A rapid recovery plan when a flight is canceled or delayed: rebooking options, meetings to move, and messages to send.
content:
My executive's travel has been disrupted. Help me recover fast.

**What happened:** [e.g. "6pm flight LHR-JFK canceled", "3-hour delay"]
**Where my executive is now:** [LOCATION]
**Original plan for the next 48 hours:** [flights, hotel, meetings with times and attendees]
**What's non-negotiable:** [e.g. "must be at the board meeting Thursday 9am"]
**Booking tools and contacts I have:** [travel agency, airline status, corporate account]

Give me, in priority order:
1. **Immediate actions (next 15 minutes):** what to do first - e.g. call the travel agency or airline, hold a backup option, secure a hotel - and what to tell my executive right now.
2. **Rebooking options to check:** alternative routes, nearby airports, train or car alternatives, with the trade-off of each against the non-negotiable commitments. Do not invent schedules; tell me what to look for.
3. **Meeting impact:** table - meeting | still possible? | move / switch to video / delegate / cancel | who to notify.
4. **Messages to send:** a 2-line text to my executive with options; short notes to each affected meeting host; hotel and car updates.
5. **Costs and records:** what to keep for expense claims and any compensation claims.

Keep each draft short. Mark anything I need to verify as [CONFIRM].
variables: flights, hotel, meetings with times and attendees
e.g. "must be at the board meeting Thursday 9am"
travel agency, airline status, corporate account

title: Redesign how I do a recurring task so it takes less time
description: Breaks down how you do a repeated task today and redesigns it with fewer steps, templates, and smoother handoffs.
content:
Help me redesign how I do a recurring task so it takes less time and causes fewer errors.

**The task:** [e.g. "monthly expense review", "onboarding a new client", "preparing the weekly sales pack"]
**How I do it now, step by step:** [PASTE - include tools, who I wait on, and where I copy and paste]
**How often, and how long it takes:** [FREQUENCY AND TIME]
**What usually goes wrong or slows me down:** [e.g. "chasing missing inputs", "rework after review"]
**What must stay the same:** [e.g. "manager sign-off", "the format the client expects"]

Check each step for waiting, rework, duplicate data entry, unnecessary checks, handoffs, and work done in the wrong order.

Return:
1. Current workflow: | Step | Time | Problem | Keep / Change / Remove |
2. The redesigned workflow as numbered steps, with what changed and why.
3. Quick wins I can apply next time: templates, checklists, saved views, Excel formulas, email rules, request forms.
4. The inputs to collect up front so I stop chasing people.
5. Time before vs. after, as an estimate with assumptions.
6. One change to test first, and how I'll know it worked.

Don't remove controls or approvals that exist for compliance or quality; mark them [CHECK BEFORE REMOVING] and explain the risk.
variables: e.g. "manager sign-off", "the format the client expects"

title: Reflect on my year and plan the next one
description: A structured annual review of wins, lessons, and priorities for next year.
content:
Guide me through a year-end review.

**The year:** [YEAR]
**Areas of my life to cover:** [e.g. work, health, relationships, money, learning, fun]
**Raw notes on what happened (optional):** [PASTE calendar highlights, journal notes, goals I set]

Ask me questions one area at a time (2–3 questions per area). After I answer all areas, produce:
1. **Highlights** — my biggest wins and proudest moments.
2. **Lessons** — what worked, what didn't, and patterns across areas.
3. **Unfinished business** — what I'm carrying forward and what I'm letting go.
4. **Next year** — 3 themes and up to 5 goals, each with a first step and a way to track it.
5. **A one-sentence intention** for the year.

Keep it honest and specific — no generic motivational language.
variables: e.g. work, health, relationships, money, learning, fun
PASTE calendar highlights, journal notes, goals I set

title: Rescue an overloaded day
description: Triage for days with too much to do: what to cut, move, renegotiate, or finish.
content:
Act as a pragmatic executive productivity coach.

**Context**
I have more work than available time today and need a realistic plan rather than an idealized one.

**Task**
Protect deadlines and high-impact outcomes first. Combine similar work, move non-critical tasks, identify delegation opportunities, and explicitly flag what will not get done.

**Format**
Return a time-blocked plan for the available hours, followed by:
- Move
- Delegate
- Drop
- Must complete

**Available time:** [PASTE]  
**Commitments:** [PASTE]

title: Resolve a calendar conflict with the fewest knock-on changes
description: A clear recommendation on which meetings to keep, move, or delegate when my executive is double-booked, plus the messages to send.
content:
Help me resolve a scheduling conflict in my executive's calendar.

**The conflicting meetings:** [for each: title, time, attendees, who requested it, how hard it was to schedule]
**The rest of the week:** [PASTE OR DESCRIBE open slots and fixed commitments]
**My executive's priorities right now:** [e.g. "closing the funding round", "board prep", "key customer renewal"]
**Rules I work by:** [e.g. "never move the CEO 1:1", "external before internal", "no meetings before 9am"]
**Who could attend instead:** [deputies or delegates, if any]

Work through it:
1. Rank the meetings by importance using my executive's priorities, seniority and external status of attendees, and how hard each is to reschedule (number of people, time zones, deadlines).
2. Recommend what to keep, move, shorten, or delegate - with one line of reasoning each.
3. For anything that moves, propose 2-3 new slots from the open time I listed and flag any that create back-to-backs or break my rules.
4. Note any knock-on effects (prep time lost, travel buffers, other attendees' calendars).

Then draft:
- A short note to my executive explaining the recommendation for a quick yes/no.
- The reschedule message for each moved meeting - polite, no over-explaining, offering the new slots.

Do not assume availability for other attendees; mark it [CHECK THEIR CALENDAR].
variables: PASTE OR DESCRIBE open slots and fixed commitments

title: Run a final walkthrough and punch list before the last payment
description: A room-specific inspection checklist, a clear punch list for the contractor, and the paperwork to collect before you pay in full.
content:
Help me do a final walkthrough of my renovation before I make the last payment. This is step 5 of renovating my kitchen or bathroom.

**Room and scope (from earlier steps, if I have them):** [PASTE SUMMARY or selections list]
**Final payment amount and contract terms for completion:** [DETAILS]
**Issues I've already noticed:** [LIST]
**Inspections passed:** [which ones, or "not sure"]

Give me:
1. A walkthrough checklist for this room, to do in daylight with all lights on:
   - Kitchen: cabinet doors and drawers align and close, counters level with clean seams, backsplash grout and caulk, sink and faucet with no leaks underneath, disposal and dishwasher run a full cycle, appliances installed and working, outlets and GFCI protection, lighting, range hood vented properly.
   - Bathroom: shower and tub tested for leaks and drainage, grout and caulk complete, tile flat with no hollow sounds, toilet secure, fan vents outside and is quiet, hot water reaches all fixtures, outlets protected, mirror and accessories secure.
   - Both: paint touch-ups, trim, flooring transitions, matches my selections list, site cleaned, debris removed.
2. A punch list template: # | Location | Issue | Photo taken | Agreed fix date | Done.
3. Paperwork to collect: final permit sign-off, warranties and manuals, product names and paint colors, lien releases where they apply [CONFIRM local rules], and receipts.
4. A polite message to the contractor listing the punch items and the completion date before final payment, per our contract.

Return the checklist, the template, the paperwork list, and the message.

title: Run an end-of-day review
description: A quick reflection on what mattered today and what to change tomorrow.
content:
Act as a reflective productivity coach focused on learning and improvement.

**Context**
These are my notes from today.

**Task**
Identify where I created meaningful value, where time was consumed without enough return, what remains genuinely important, and what I should change tomorrow. Avoid generic productivity advice.

**Format**
Return:
- Wins that mattered
- Time drains
- Unfinished priorities
- Lesson from today
- One thing to stop
- One thing to start
- Tomorrow's top priority

**Notes:** [PASTE]

title: Schedule deep-work blocks around my top priorities this week
description: Turns your priorities and calendar into protected focus blocks with clear outputs and a plan for interruptions.
content:
Help me schedule deep work around my top priorities this week.

**My top priorities this week:** [LIST - with deadlines]
**My calendar (meetings and fixed commitments):** [PASTE OR DESCRIBE BY DAY]
**When I focus best:** [e.g. "mornings before 11"]
**Typical interruptions:** [e.g. "Teams pings", "walk-ups", "urgent client emails"]
**Realistic deep-work capacity:** [e.g. "2-3 hours a day at most"]

Steps:
1. Identify which priorities need uninterrupted thinking (writing, analysis, design, decisions) and which can be done in short gaps.
2. Estimate the focus hours each one needs, and mark them as estimates.
3. Place 60-120 minute blocks in my best hours, around existing meetings, with a buffer before each deadline.
4. If the work does not fit, say how many hours are missing and what to move, decline, or shrink.

Return:
1. Focus block schedule: | Day | Time | Priority | Specific output by the end of the block |
2. A prep list: what to gather before each block so I don't stop mid-flow.
3. An interruption plan: status message, notification settings, and when I'll check email, Teams, or Slack.
4. A short calendar description for the blocks so colleagues understand them.
5. What to do when an urgent request takes over a block.

Don't fill every gap; leave room for reactive work.
variables: e.g. "2-3 hours a day at most"

title: Score my task list and turn it into a prioritized action plan
description: Scores every task on impact, urgency, effort, and strategic fit, then turns the ranking into a dated action plan.
content:
Turn my task list into a prioritized action plan.

**My tasks:** [PASTE LIST - include deadlines, who asked, and rough effort if known]
**My role and current goals:** [e.g. "regional sales ops lead; Q3 goals: cut quote turnaround, launch new CRM fields"]
**Time available over the period:** [e.g. "about 20 focus hours over the next 2 weeks"]
**Fixed deadlines or commitments:** [DATES]
**Weighting (optional):** [e.g. "strategic fit matters most this quarter" - or "use defaults"]

Steps:
1. Score each task 1-5 on Impact (value to the business or my goals), Urgency (cost of delay), Effort (5 = quick), and Strategic fit (link to my stated goals). Use weights of 35/25/15/25 unless I gave others.
2. Explain any score you had to guess, and mark missing facts as [CONFIRM].
3. Flag tasks that unblock other work and move them up, even if their own score is middling.
4. Check the plan against my available time. If it does not fit, say how many hours over I am and which tasks fall below the line.

Return:
1. Scoring table: | Task | Impact | Urgency | Effort | Strategic fit | Weighted score | Notes |
2. Action plan: | Rank | Task | First concrete step | Target date | Do / Delegate / Defer / Drop |
3. Below the line: tasks that will not fit, and who needs to be told.
4. The top 3 to start on tomorrow morning.

Do not invent deadlines or stakeholders. The scores are a starting point; I make the final call.
variables: e.g. "about 20 focus hours over the next 2 weeks"

title: Sequence my tasks by dependencies and find the biggest blocker
description: Maps which tasks depend on which, finds what is blocking the most work, and gives you the most efficient order.
content:
Help me put my tasks in the right order.

**Tasks:** [PASTE - include deadlines, owners, and rough effort]
**Known dependencies:** [e.g. "can't build the dashboard until IT grants data access" - or "work them out"]
**Things I'm waiting on from others:** [DETAILS]
**My available time:** [e.g. "3 hours a day for the next 2 weeks"]

Steps:
1. Map dependencies: what must finish before each task can start. Mark any dependency you inferred as [INFERRED] so I can check it.
2. Identify the task that blocks the most downstream work, and any external wait holding things up.
3. Group tasks that share inputs, tools, or people so they can be done together.
4. Build the most efficient order: clear blockers first, start long waits early, then work through the rest by deadline.

Return:
1. Dependency table: | Task | Depends on | Blocks | Owner | Effort | Deadline |
2. The single biggest blocker, why it matters, and the fastest way to clear it, including a short nudge message if it's someone else's.
3. The recommended sequence, day by day or step by step.
4. Tasks I can do in parallel while waiting.
5. Risks: circular dependencies, deadlines that can't be met in this order, and single points of failure.

Keep it plain: a list and a table, no project-management jargon.
variables: PASTE - include deadlines, owners, and rough effort
e.g. "3 hours a day for the next 2 weeks"

title: Set up communication windows for email, Teams, and Slack
description: Designs set times to check and answer messages, an urgent-request path, and a short note telling colleagues how to reach you.
content:
Help me stop living in my inbox by setting fixed communication windows.

**Channels I use:** [e.g. Outlook, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp, phone]
**Typical volume:** [rough messages per day in each]
**Response times people expect from me:** [e.g. "clients within 4 hours", "my manager same day"]
**Truly urgent situations in my job:** [e.g. "production outage", "client escalation"]
**My work hours and time zones of key colleagues:** [DETAILS]

Return:
1. **Window schedule:** how many check-ins per day, at what times, and how long each one lasts - matched to the response times people actually need.
2. **What happens in a window:** a triage routine (reply, delegate, schedule, archive) in the order I should run it.
3. **Urgent path:** how someone reaches me for a real emergency outside a window, and what qualifies.
4. **Settings to change:** notification, status, and focus-mode settings for each channel.
5. **Message to my team:** a short, friendly note (under 120 words) explaining when I respond and how to flag urgent items.
6. **Exceptions:** periods (launches, month-end, travel) when the windows should loosen, and how.

If my role genuinely needs near-real-time replies, say so and design shorter, more frequent windows instead of pretending I can go dark for hours.
variables: e.g. Outlook, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp, phone
rough messages per day in each
e.g. "clients within 4 hours", "my manager same day"

title: Set up email rules to filter, sort, and forward my mail
description: A folder structure and step-by-step filter rules for your email app so the right messages land in the right place automatically.
content:
Help me set up email rules so my inbox sorts itself.

**Email app:** [e.g. "Gmail", "Outlook desktop", "Outlook web", "Apple Mail"]
**Account type:** [personal / work / shared mailbox]
**What floods my inbox:** [e.g. "newsletters", "system alerts", "invoices", "client emails mixed with team chatter"]
**Messages that must reach me fast:** [senders, keywords, or types]
**Messages that should go to someone else:** [what, and to whom]
**Folders or labels I already use:** [LIST or "none"]

Give me:
1. A simple folder or label structure (no more than 8), with what goes in each.
2. A rules table: Rule name | Condition (sender, domain, subject words, keywords, to/cc) | Action (label, move, mark read, forward, flag) | Order | Stop processing further rules? (yes/no).
3. Step-by-step setup for each rule in my email app, using its current menu names - if you are unsure of the exact menu path, say so and describe what to look for.
4. How to test each rule on existing mail before relying on it.
5. Pitfalls: rule order conflicts, rules that catch too much, server-side vs client-only rules, and messages important senders could miss.
6. A weekly 5-minute review habit to keep it working.

Before setting up any auto-forwarding, check: is it allowed by my organization's policy, could it send confidential or personal data outside the company, and does the recipient need everything or just a notification? Prefer forwarding within my organization over external addresses.

title: Sort a pile of messy notes into organized topics with tags
description: Untangle notes written at different times into clean topic groups, with tags, a merged version, and an index you can search.
content:
Help me organize my notes.

**Notes:** [PASTE NOTES - they may mix unrelated topics and dates]
**What I use them for:** [work projects / study / personal knowledge base / writing ideas]
**Tool they will live in:** [e.g. Notion, Obsidian, OneNote, Google Docs, plain folders]
**Topics I already use (optional):** [LIST]

Steps:
1. Split the notes into individual ideas, even when one note covers several unrelated things.
2. Group the ideas into 5-12 clear topics. Reuse my existing topics where they fit; propose new ones only when needed.
3. Within each topic, merge duplicates and near-duplicates, keep the most complete wording, and keep dates where they matter.
4. Suggest 3-6 tags per topic: lowercase, no spaces (use underscores), no repeats, including any people or projects named.
5. Flag open questions, to-dos, and anything that looks outdated or contradictory.

Rules:
- Do not rewrite my meaning or drop content. If something does not fit, put it under "Unsorted".
- If you spot passwords, API keys, account numbers, or other secrets, do not repeat them. Just tell me which note contains one so I can move it to a password manager.

Return:
1. A topic index: topic, one-line summary, tags, number of notes.
2. Each topic as a section with its cleaned, merged notes.
3. A to-do and open-questions list.
4. A suggested folder or page structure for my tool.
variables: PASTE NOTES - they may mix unrelated topics and dates
e.g. Notion, Obsidian, OneNote, Google Docs, plain folders

title: Sort information into what needs my attention and what I can ignore
description: Separates signal from noise: the 10 points that matter, what needs action from you, and what you can safely skip.
content:
Help me cut through the information below and tell me what actually matters to me.

**My role and current priorities:** [e.g. "finance manager; closing Q3, hiring two analysts"]
**What I'm responsible for or accountable for:** [AREAS]
**Information:** [PASTE updates, newsletters, reports, long threads, announcements]

Return:
1. **Needs my action** - items where I must do, decide, or reply, with the deadline if stated. Most urgent first.
2. **Need to know** - things that affect my work or priorities but need no action now. One line each.
3. **The 10 most important points overall**, ranked, each in one sentence with a note on why it ranks there.
4. **Safe to ignore** - what I can skip, grouped, with a short reason (not relevant to my role, repeats something above, already resolved, purely informational, low impact).
5. **Watch list** - items that are not important yet but could become important, and the signal that would change that.

Rules:
- Judge relevance against my role and priorities, not general importance.
- Don't drop anything with a deadline, a request addressed to me, money, legal, or safety implications into "ignore"; when in doubt, put it under "need to know" and say why.
- Be brief. The point is to save me reading time.
variables: e.g. "finance manager; closing Q3, hiring two analysts"

title: Sort my task list into deep work, shallow work, and async work
description: Tags every task by focus needed, sync vs. async, strategic vs. admin, and reactive vs. proactive so you know how to schedule each.
content:
Help me sort my task list by the kind of attention each task needs.

**My role:** [JOB TITLE AND MAIN RESPONSIBILITIES]
**My task list:** [PASTE - include recurring work, not just this week's to-dos]
**What counts as high-value in my role:** [e.g. "shipping the roadmap", "closing renewals", "accurate month-end close"]

For each task, decide:
- **Focus level:** Deep (needs 60+ uninterrupted minutes and real thinking), Shallow (can be done in short bursts), or Mixed.
- **Sync or async:** must happen live with others, or can be handled by message, doc comment, recorded video, or shared file.
- **Strategic or administrative:** moves a goal forward, or keeps the lights on.
- **Proactive or reactive:** I chose to do it, or it arrived as a request or fire.

Return:
1. A table: | Task | Focus level | Sync/async | Strategic/admin | Proactive/reactive | Suggested handling |
2. A summary: what share of my list is deep, strategic, and proactive, and whether that matches what my role is judged on.
3. The 3 sync tasks most worth converting to async, with how (e.g. "send a short recorded walkthrough and a chat thread instead of a call").
4. The deep tasks that most need protected time, in priority order.
5. Admin and reactive work that could be batched into one or two daily slots.

If a task is too vague to classify, ask me rather than guessing.
variables: PASTE - include recurring work, not just this week's to-dos

title: Sort my tasks into automate, delegate, eliminate, or do myself
description: Applies a clear four-way test to every task, including what AI could handle and what needs your personal judgment.
content:
Sort my tasks into automate, delegate, eliminate, or do myself.

**My tasks (one per line, with frequency and time if known):** [PASTE]
**My role:** [ROLE]
**People I could delegate to, and their skills:** [e.g. "analyst - strong in Excel; coordinator - good with scheduling" - or "none"]
**Tools I have:** [e.g. Microsoft 365 Copilot, ChatGPT, Power Automate, Zapier, none]
**Sensitive data or approvals involved:** [e.g. "salary data", "client contracts", "none"]

Decision tests:
- Eliminate: no one would notice or care if it stopped.
- Automate or AI-assist: repetitive, rule-based, or a first draft from clear inputs, where errors are easy to catch.
- Delegate: someone else can do it well with instructions, or it would help them grow.
- Do myself: needs my judgment, accountability, authority, or relationships, or involves sensitive decisions about people, money, or legal risk.

Return:
1. Table: | Task | Verdict | Why | How (tool, prompt idea, or person) | Human check needed | Time saved/week |
2. The tasks that need my personal judgment, and why AI or delegation would be risky for each.
3. For AI-assisted tasks: what the AI does, what I review, and what data must never go into the tool.
4. The three moves that save the most time, in order.

Be realistic: if AI would only save a few minutes or adds review burden, say so. Follow my company's AI and data policies; if I haven't mentioned them, remind me to check.

title: Sort tasks by urgency and impact
description: Applies an urgent/important framework so you know what to do, schedule, delegate, or drop.
content:
Act as a decision-oriented productivity advisor.

**Context**
I need to classify a set of tasks so I can decide how to spend my limited attention.

**Task**
Classify every task based on urgency and impact. Consider whether the task creates meaningful value, prevents risk, enables other work, or is mainly administrative. Recommend the appropriate action.

**Format**
Use:
| Task | Urgency | Impact | Recommendation | Reason |
Recommendations: Do Now, Schedule, Delegate, Eliminate.

**Tasks:** [PASTE]

title: Stop procrastinating on an assignment I keep avoiding
description: A judgment-free look at why you're stuck and a tiny first step you can start in the next 10 minutes.
content:
Help me get started on an assignment I keep putting off.

**The assignment:** [WHAT IT IS, how big, due date]
**How long I've been avoiding it:** [e.g. "a week"]
**What I do instead:** [e.g. "phone, cleaning, other homework"]
**How I feel when I think about it:** [e.g. "overwhelmed", "bored", "scared it won't be good enough", "don't know where to start"]
**Time and energy available today:** [e.g. "1 hour, pretty tired"]

Do this:
1. Name the most likely reason I'm avoiding it (unclear first step, task too big, fear of a bad grade, boredom, low energy) based on what I said. Ask one question if you're not sure.
2. Match a strategy to that reason, e.g. make the first step tiny, set a 15-minute timer, write a deliberately bad first version, work beside a friend, or remove the phone from the room.
3. Break the assignment into small steps, each with a clear finish line.
4. Give me one step I can start within 10 minutes and finish in under 25.

Return: the likely reason, the strategy, the step list, and the one thing to do right now. Keep it short and kind; no lectures.

If the avoidance is part of a bigger pattern of feeling low, hopeless, or unable to cope, suggest I talk to my school counselor or a trusted adult. If I mention thoughts of harming myself, tell me to contact a crisis line right away (in the US, call or text 988).
variables: WHAT IT IS, how big, due date

title: Track my executive's open loops in a weekly summary
description: A weekly status of everything waiting on or from my executive, so nothing stalls and they can clear decisions fast.
content:
Turn my notes into a weekly open-loops summary for my executive.

**Items I'm tracking:** [PASTE - pending decisions, approvals, replies owed, promises they made in meetings, things others owe them]
**This week's key outcomes:** [WHAT GOT DONE]
**Upcoming deadlines (next 2 weeks):** [LIST]
**My executive's preferences:** [e.g. "max one page", "wants my recommendation on each"]

Produce:
1. **Needs your decision (top):** item | context in one line | options | my recommendation (only if I've given one) | needed by.
2. **You owe:** replies, documents, or follow-ups they promised - to whom, since when.
3. **Waiting on others:** item | who | since | next chase date.
4. **Coming up:** deadlines and events in the next 2 weeks with prep needed.
5. **Done this week:** short list.
6. **Aging alert:** anything open more than [2] weeks, with a suggested action - close it, chase it, or drop it.

Rules:
- One line per item where possible. Group by priority, not by when I added it.
- Don't invent dates or owners; mark [CONFIRM].
- At the end, list the chase messages I should send this week and draft the two most important ones.
variables: e.g. "max one page", "wants my recommendation on each"

title: Triage and prioritize my team's analytics request queue
description: A fair, transparent way to rank incoming data requests by value and effort, with replies for the ones you push back on.
content:
Help me triage and prioritize my team's queue of analytics and data requests.

**Requests:** [PASTE list: requester, team, request, date asked, any stated deadline]
**Team capacity:** [people and hours available this week or sprint]
**Current priorities or OKRs:** [company or team goals]
**Recurring pain points:** [e.g. "lots of one-off pulls", "urgent asks from execs", "requests already answered by a dashboard"]

Steps:
1. Classify each request: answerable by existing dashboard or self-serve, quick data pull, analysis, new dashboard or pipeline, or unclear.
2. Score each on: decision value (what decision it informs and its size), urgency (real deadline vs. preference), effort (t-shirt size), and alignment with priorities. Show the scoring rule so it is transparent.
3. Spot duplicates and requests that can be bundled.
4. For unclear requests, write the one question that would clarify them.
5. Recommend what to do now, schedule, redirect to self-serve, or decline.

Return:
- A prioritized table: Request | Type | Value | Urgency | Effort | Score | Action | Notes.
- A plan for this week that fits within capacity.
- Short, friendly replies for redirected or declined requests that explain why and offer an alternative.
- 3 process improvements to reduce repeat requests (e.g. intake form fields, a FAQ of where to find common numbers, office hours).

Do not invent deadlines or values; mark unknowns as [ASK].
variables: people and hours available this week or sprint

title: Triage marketing requests from other teams
description: A fair intake and prioritization system for the flood of requests from sales, product, and leadership, plus replies for each.
content:
Help me triage and prioritize the requests coming into my marketing team.

**Current requests:** [PASTE LIST: requester, what they want, deadline they gave, why]
**Our team and capacity:** [PEOPLE, skills, approximate hours available this month]
**Marketing priorities this quarter:** [OKRs or top goals]
**Work already committed:** [LAUNCHES, campaigns, recurring work]

Do this:
1. Score each request on: impact on our quarterly goals or revenue, urgency (real external deadline vs. preferred date), effort (S/M/L), and whether a self-serve option exists (template, existing asset, brand toolkit).
2. Sort into: do now, schedule, redirect to self-serve or another team, decline. Explain each call in one line.
3. Spot patterns: recurring requests that should become templates or a self-serve library, and requesters who need a standing slot.
4. Draft short, respectful replies for each "schedule", "redirect", and "decline", offering an alternative where possible.

Then design a lightweight intake process:
- A request form with required fields (goal, audience, metric, deadline, decision-maker, budget, existing assets).
- Service levels by request type (e.g. social graphic 3 days, landing page 2 weeks).
- A weekly prioritization slot and how to escalate conflicts to leadership with a clear trade-off ("If we do X, Y moves to next month").

Return the triage table (Request | Requester | Impact | Urgency | Effort | Decision | Reason), the replies, and the intake form fields.
variables: PEOPLE, skills, approximate hours available this month

title: Turn a document or policy into a checklist
description: Converts a policy, procedure, standard, or long document into a clear checklist people can tick off, with nothing important left out.
content:
Turn the document below into a practical checklist.

**Document:** [PASTE - policy, procedure, standard, guideline, contract obligations, or instructions]
**Who will use the checklist:** [ROLE]
**When they'll use it:** [e.g. "before submitting a purchase request", "during a site audit", "on a new hire's first day"]
**Format:** [printable page / Excel / Word / Teams or Slack message]

Build it:
1. Pull out every action, requirement, and check in the document. Ignore background and explanation.
2. Write each item as one action someone can tick off ("Attach the signed quote"), starting with a verb.
3. Group items by stage or timing (before / during / after) in the order they happen.
4. Mark mandatory items clearly, and separate them from recommended ones.
5. Add the owner and deadline or timing where the document states them.

Return:
1. **The checklist** - grouped, numbered, with a checkbox for each item and the section of the document it comes from.
2. **Critical items** - the ones that cause the most harm if missed (compliance, safety, money), highlighted.
3. **Unclear requirements** - places where the document is vague, marked [CLARIFY].
4. **Coverage check** - confirm every requirement in the document is either on the checklist or listed as left out on purpose, with the reason.

Use only what the document says; don't add requirements from general practice unless labeled (suggested).
variables: printable page / Excel / Word / Teams or Slack message

title: Turn a goal into a realistic plan
description: Breaks a goal into milestones, weekly actions, and checkpoints.
content:
Act as an experienced program manager.

**Context**
I need to achieve the following outcome but the path from goal to execution is not yet clear.

**Task**
Break the goal into milestones, deliverables, dependencies, risks, owners, decision points, and immediate actions. Identify assumptions that could invalidate the plan.

**Format**
Return:
- Goal
- Success measure
- Milestones
- Dependencies
- Risks
- Owners
- Next 5 actions

**Goal:** [PASTE]

title: Turn a pile of updates into my next 5 actions for today
description: Picks out what truly needs you today from a stack of updates and turns it into 5 ordered actions that fit your schedule.
content:
Go through everything below and turn it into a short action plan for today.

**What's in front of me:** [PASTE updates, emails, Teams or Slack messages, reports, task lists]
**My role and current priorities:** [ROLE and the 2-3 things that matter most this period]
**Time I actually have today:** [e.g. "back-to-back meetings until 3pm, then 2 hours free", "travelling, phone only"]
**People I can hand things to:** [NAMES or roles - optional]
**Today's date:** [DATE, so you can spot deadlines]

Steps:
1. **Needs me today** - pick only the items with a deadline today or tomorrow, an escalation, a decision only I can make, or real risk if they wait. One line each on why.
2. **My next 5 actions**, in order. Each starts with a verb and has: estimated time, what "done" looks like, and which item it comes from. The total must fit the time I have; if it doesn't, say what to drop or move.
3. **Hand off** - items someone else can take, with who and a ready-to-send one-line handoff message.
4. **Can wait** - everything else, with a suggested day to look at it (not a full summary).
5. **Looks urgent but isn't** - and anything quiet that could become a problem this week if ignored.

Rules: judge urgency from deadlines, who's asking, and impact - not from exclamation marks or the word "urgent". Don't invent deadlines; if one is unclear, mark it [CHECK DEADLINE]. Never put anything involving money, legal, safety, or a direct request from my manager into "can wait" without flagging it. I make the final call on priorities.
variables: ROLE and the 2-3 things that matter most this period
DATE, so you can spot deadlines

title: Turn a recurring task into a reusable template and checklist
description: Creates a fill-in template plus a step checklist so a repeated task is faster, consistent, and easy to hand over.
content:
Turn a task I repeat into a reusable template and checklist.

**The recurring task:** [e.g. "monthly board report", "new vendor setup email", "quarterly access review"]
**How often I do it:** [FREQUENCY]
**A past example of the finished output:** [PASTE ONE OR TWO]
**What changes each time:** [e.g. "dates, figures, client name"]
**What must stay consistent:** [structure, tone, required sections, approvals]
**Where it will live:** [Word, Excel, Outlook template, OneNote, Confluence, Google Docs]

Return:
1. The template, with every variable as a labeled [PLACEHOLDER] plus a short hint, and the fixed text left in place.
2. A start-to-finish checklist: inputs to gather first, who to ask, the steps, and the quality checks before sending.
3. A "done means" definition: what a correct, complete output looks like.
4. Common mistakes in this task, and the line in the template or checklist that prevents each.
5. Setup tips for the tool I named (e.g. save as an Outlook template, lock formula cells in Excel).
6. A one-paragraph handover note so a colleague can use it without me.

Strip names, figures, and confidential details from my example so the template is clean. Don't invent required sections; ask me if something looks missing.

title: Turn an overwhelming workload into a realistic plan
description: Takes everything on your plate and builds a plan that fits your actual hours, including what to drop and renegotiate.
content:
I'm overwhelmed. Help me turn my workload into a realistic plan.

**Everything on my plate:** [PASTE - tasks, projects, requests, half-finished work]
**Deadlines and who's waiting:** [DETAILS]
**Hours I actually have for this work per week:** [after meetings and admin]
**Planning window:** [e.g. "next 2 weeks"]
**Help available:** [people, tools, budget - or "none"]

Steps:
1. Put everything in one list and merge duplicates.
2. Estimate the hours each item needs (mark estimates) and total them against my available hours.
3. Show the gap plainly: "You have X hours of work and Y hours of time."
4. Close the gap in this order: drop, shrink scope, delay, delegate, ask for help.
5. Sequence what remains by deadline and dependency.

Return:
1. The reality check: total work vs. capacity.
2. The plan: | Week | Task | Hours | Deadline | Notes |
3. What I'm not doing in this window, and who needs to know.
4. Messages to renegotiate deadlines or scope, ready to send by email, Teams, or Slack.
5. The first 3 things to do today, each under 90 minutes.
6. A check-in point to re-plan if things change.

Keep the tone calm and practical. Don't make the plan fit by assuming I'll work evenings or weekends. If the overload sounds chronic, say so and suggest raising it with my manager, backed by the numbers above.
variables: PASTE - tasks, projects, requests, half-finished work

title: Turn my executive's voice notes and scribbles into tasks and drafts
description: Messy dictation or handwritten notes converted into a clean task list, drafted emails, and questions to clarify.
content:
Turn my executive's rough instructions into organized tasks and drafts.

**Their notes:** [PASTE - voice-note transcript, dictation, typed-up handwritten notes, or chat messages]
**Context I know:** [e.g. "'the Denver thing' is the Q3 offsite", names of people they refer to]
**My usual tools:** [task list, calendar, email]

Do this:
1. **Interpret:** list each separate instruction in plain words. Where something is ambiguous ("sort out Tom"), give my best interpretation and mark [CHECK WITH EXEC].
2. **Task list:** task | type (schedule / email / book / research / file / remind) | for whom | due date if stated | priority (from their wording - "asap", "when you get a chance").
3. **Drafts:** write any emails or messages they asked for, short and in a neutral professional voice (I'll adjust to their voice).
4. **Calendar actions:** meetings to set up, with suggested attendees, length, and purpose.
5. **Reminders:** anything they said they'd do themselves that I should remind them about, and when.
6. **Clarifying questions:** a short list I can send in one message, grouped so they can answer in 30 seconds.

Never fill in a name, date, or number they didn't give. Keep the output skimmable.

title: Write a design brief and selections list for my renovation

Help me write a design brief and a selections list for my renovation. This is step 2 of renovating my kitchen or bathroom.

title: Write our wedding-day schedule and run sheet

Help us write our wedding-day schedule. This is step 5 of planning our wedding.

**Planning timeline and vendor list (from step 4, if we have it):** [PASTE]

2. A vendor run sheet: arrival time, setup location, contact person, and cues for each vendor (when the DJ starts music, when the photographer must be where).
3. A family photo shot list grouped to minimize reshuffling, with names of who to gather.
4. A contact sheet: Role | Name | Phone | Arrival time.
5. A plan B for rain, heat, a late vendor, or a missing item, with who decides.
6. A day-of emergency kit list.
