title: Agree on authorship and contributions before a collaboration
description: Drafts a fair authorship and contribution agreement using recognized criteria, to prevent disputes on collaborative papers.
content:
Help me set up an authorship and contribution agreement for a collaborative research project.

**Project and planned outputs:** [e.g. "2 papers and a dataset"]
**Collaborators and expected roles:** [NAMES or roles, career stage, institutions]
**Field norms:** [e.g. "first and last author matter", "alphabetical order", "large consortium"]
**Journal or institutional policy:** [e.g. "ICMJE criteria", or "unknown"]
**Known sensitivities:** [e.g. "a student and a postdoc both want first author", "data provider expects authorship"]

Draft:
1. The authorship criteria we will use (e.g. ICMJE or field equivalent), explained in plain terms, and who qualifies for acknowledgment instead.
2. A contributions table using the CRediT taxonomy (conceptualization, methodology, software, formal analysis, investigation, data curation, writing - original draft, review and editing, supervision, funding acquisition, etc.) with each person's expected role and level.
3. Proposed author order for each output, with the reasoning.
4. Rules for change: what happens if contributions shift, someone leaves, or new people join, and when we revisit (e.g. at each draft milestone).
5. A dispute process, including who to involve (e.g. research integrity office).

Return the agreement as a 1-2 page document plus a short, friendly email to propose it to collaborators. Note that institutional policies take precedence and should be checked.
variables: NAMES or roles, career stage, institutions

title: Analyze a patient safety event with a root cause analysis
description: A just-culture root cause analysis of a safety event or near miss, focused on systems and processes, with strong corrective actions and measures.
content:
Help me run a root cause analysis (RCA) of a patient safety event at our clinic.

**Event type:** [e.g. wrong patient label on a specimen, missed abnormal result follow-up, medication sample dispensing error, fall in exam room, near miss]
**What happened:** [FACTUAL SEQUENCE with times, using roles not names]
**Harm level:** [no harm / near miss / temporary harm / serious harm]
**Processes and systems involved:** [e.g. EHR inbox routing, specimen labeling, check-in, handoffs]
**Contributing conditions noted so far:** [e.g. staffing, interruptions, new workflow, unclear policy]
**Team members available for the review:** [ROLES]

Work through:
1. A timeline of events and decision points.
2. What should have happened under our process versus what did happen.
3. Contributing factors across categories: communication, policies and procedures, staffing and training, equipment and EHR design, environment, patient factors, and organizational culture. Use "5 whys" for the key gaps.
4. Root causes stated as system issues, not individual blame, following just-culture principles.
5. Corrective actions ranked by strength: stronger (forcing functions, standardization, removing hazards), intermediate (checklists, redundancy, software changes), weaker (training, reminders, new policy alone). Recommend at least one stronger or intermediate action.
6. A measurement plan to verify each action works.

Return an RCA summary, a fishbone-style factor list, and an action table: Action | Strength | Owner | Due | Measure. Do not draw clinical conclusions about care quality; those belong to our medical director. If the event caused serious harm, check reporting obligations to the state, accreditor, or patient safety organization, and patient disclosure policy, with risk management.
variables: FACTUAL SEQUENCE with times, using roles not names
no harm / near miss / temporary harm / serious harm
e.g. EHR inbox routing, specimen labeling, check-in, handoffs
e.g. staffing, interruptions, new workflow, unclear policy

title: Analyze spend and find savings
description: Categorizes spend and identifies cost-saving opportunities.
content:
Role: Act as a category manager doing spend analysis for cost optimisation.

Context: Spend data (by supplier, sub-category, business unit, geography, contract vs off-contract, PO vs non-PO): [SPEND_DATA]. Time range and any known data-quality issues: [RANGE_QUALITY]. Contracts in place and their pricing mechanisms: [CONTRACTS]. Demand / specification context (is demand controllable, is the spec gold-plated): [DEMAND_SPEC]. Market conditions for the category: [MARKET]. Constraints (switching cost, business resistance, single-source): [CONSTRAINTS].

Goal: Give procurement leadership a clear picture of where the money goes and a prioritised list of savings opportunities that are real and executable, with the risk of each.

Task: Produce: (1) the spend picture - concentration by supplier and sub-category, contract vs maverick spend, tail spend, price variance for like items across BUs; (2) the savings levers with an estimated range and the basis - consolidation/leverage, renegotiation/benchmarking, specification/demand management, payment terms, process/automation, supplier rationalisation; (3) each opportunity sized, with effort, time to realise, one-off vs recurring, and the business or supply risk; (4) a prioritised plan (value vs effort vs risk) with the first 3 to pursue; (5) what data or benchmark would firm up the estimates.

Constraints: Estimate savings as ranges with the basis stated - never a single confident number. Distinguish addressable spend from committed/contracted spend. Note where a saving creates a supply, quality or relationship risk. Do not assume demand is reducible where the input says it is not.

Examples: Opportunity row: 'Consolidate [sub-category] from 6 suppliers to 2 -> est. 4-8% of $[spend] (~$[range]/yr), based on volume-leverage benchmarks; effort: M; time: 2 quarters; risk: medium (transition, single-source on [item]).'

Format: Sections: Spend picture | Savings levers & opportunities (table) | Prioritised plan & first 3 | Data/benchmark to firm up. ~700 words.

Verification: Show the spend concentration and price-variance figures; flag opportunities based on assumption rather than data, and any distorted by the data-quality issues.

Validation: Pressure-test the top opportunity with the business stakeholder who owns the demand: is the saving real and will they support it, or will it be resisted into nothing? Re-rank accordingly.

title: Assess a troubled project I just inherited
description: A structured two-week health check plan, interview questions, and a findings template for taking over a struggling project.
content:
Help me assess a troubled project I have just taken over.

**What I know so far:** [GOAL, timeline, budget, team, sponsor]
**Symptoms:** [e.g. "missed two milestones", "sponsor has lost confidence", "team morale low", "no one agrees on scope"]
**Documents available:** [charter, plan, status reports, RAID log, budget tracker]
**Why the previous manager left:** [if known]
**Time I have before I must report back:** [e.g. 2 weeks]

Create a project health check that covers: scope and requirements clarity, schedule realism, budget and forecast, team capacity and morale, stakeholder alignment, governance and decision-making, vendor performance, technical or delivery risk, and quality.

Return:
1. **A day-by-day plan** for the assessment period: what to read, who to talk to, and in what order.
2. **Interview questions** for the sponsor, team members, key stakeholders, and vendors (5-7 each), designed to get honest answers.
3. **Documents to check and red flags** in each (e.g. a plan that has not been updated in a month, risks with no owners).
4. **A findings template**: area | rating (red/amber/green) | evidence | root cause | recommended action.
5. **Quick wins** to build trust in the first week without making big promises.
6. **The report-back structure** - including options to reset, recover, or recommend stopping the project.

Remind me to separate what I have verified from what I have been told.
variables: charter, plan, status reports, RAID log, budget tracker

title: Assess the impact of a change request
description: Evaluates a scope change's impact on time, cost, quality, and risk.
content:
Role: Act as a delivery lead assessing a change request for the change control board.

Context: The change requested and who raised it: [CHANGE_REQUEST]. Reason / driver: [DRIVER]. Current baselines (scope, schedule, cost, quality): [BASELINES]. Current status and critical path: [STATUS_CP]. Dependencies and other in-flight changes: [DEPENDENCIES]. Benefits case it affects: [BENEFITS_CASE].

Task: Produce: a clear statement of the change and its rationale; the impact on scope, schedule (including critical path), cost, resources, risk, and the benefits case if accepted; the impact of NOT making the change; 2-3 options (accept as-is / accept modified / defer / reject) with pros, cons and cost; a recommendation with the reasoning; and the approvals needed.

Format: Sections: Change & rationale | Impact analysis (scope / schedule / cost / risk / benefits) | Do-nothing impact | Options | Recommendation | Approvals. ~450 words.

Verification: Quantify schedule and cost impact against the baselines and show the assumption; flag any impact you cannot size without more input.

Validation: Challenge as a sponsor watching the budget: is the recommendation driven by benefit and risk, or by avoiding a hard conversation? Re-justify if needed.

title: Audit my CRM data quality and fix the biggest gaps
description: A CRM hygiene audit that finds the data problems hurting forecasting and reporting, with fixes, owners, and rules to prevent them.
content:
Help me audit the quality of our CRM data and create a cleanup plan.

**CRM and objects in scope:** [e.g. Salesforce accounts, contacts, opportunities]
**What I can share:** [field fill rates, sample export, report results, or a description of known issues]
**Reports that depend on this data:** [e.g. forecast, pipeline coverage, attribution, territory assignment]
**Team size and who can make changes:** [admins, RevOps, reps]

Check for:
1. Opportunities: past close dates, missing next steps, no activity in 30+ days, amount of zero, stage not matching age or evidence, missing close-lost reason.
2. Accounts and contacts: duplicates, missing owner, missing industry/size/region fields used for routing or territories, contacts with no account.
3. Ownership: records owned by departed users or inactive queues.
4. Field design: fields nobody fills in, free-text fields that should be picklists, picklist values that overlap.
5. Process causes: where bad data enters (imports, integrations, manual entry) and why reps skip fields.

Return:
- A table: Issue | Records affected (from my data, or [CHECK]) | Impact on reporting | Fix | Owner | Effort.
- A prioritized cleanup plan for the next 30 days.
- Prevention rules: validation rules, required fields by stage, automation, and duplicate matching rules.
- A short weekly hygiene dashboard with 5 metrics to track.

Do not invent record counts. If I haven't given a number, tell me which report to run to get it.

title: Audit my project plan for missing owners, deadlines, and unaddressed risks
description: Checks your plan or tracker for tasks with no owner, no deadline, vague deliverables, and risks nobody is managing.
content:
Audit my project plan for gaps before they turn into problems.

**Plan, tracker, or task list:** [PASTE - include owner and date columns even if blank]
**Risk log:** [PASTE, or "none"]
**Recent status notes or meeting notes:** [PASTE, to catch commitments that never reached the plan]

Check for:
1. Ownership gaps: tasks with no owner, shared owners ("team", "IT", two names), or owners who have left or aren't on the team list.
2. Deadline gaps: tasks with no due date, "TBD", or dates already passed without an update.
3. Vague tasks: no clear deliverable, so nobody can say when they're done.
4. Unmanaged risks: risks with no owner, no mitigation, no review date, or concerns raised in notes that never reached the risk log.
5. Orphaned actions: commitments in notes or emails that aren't in the tracker.
6. Workload signals: one owner holding far more open tasks than others.

Return:
1. A gap table: Item | Gap type | Why it matters | Suggested fix (proposed owner role, date, or rewording).
2. Risks not being addressed: Risk | Evidence | Likely impact | Suggested owner role | First mitigation step.
3. A summary count of each gap type, so I can track it week to week.
4. A short message I can send to the team in Teams or Slack asking owners to fill the gaps by a set date.

Suggest owner roles, not names, unless the name is already in my data. I decide who owns what.
variables: PASTE - include owner and date columns even if blank
PASTE, to catch commitments that never reached the plan

title: Audit whether teams are actually following a procedure
description: A short process audit plan with observation questions and a scoring sheet to check whether an SOP is followed in practice.
content:
Help me check whether a procedure is actually being followed on the floor.

**The procedure:** [PASTE THE SOP OR KEY STEPS]
**Why I'm checking:** [e.g. "errors are rising", "new procedure", "audit coming up"]
**Where and who:** [areas, shifts, roles]
**How much time I have for audits:** [e.g. "15 minutes per audit, twice a week"]

Build:
1. An observation checklist of 8-12 questions, each tied to a critical step, phrased so the answer is observable (yes/no/partly) - e.g. "Is the label scanned before the carton is sealed?" not "Is labeling done correctly?"
2. Who audits and how often (layered audits: supervisors frequently, managers less often), and a rotation across shifts.
3. A scoring sheet and how to record what was seen, not just the score.
4. How to talk to the person doing the work: ask them to walk you through it, ask what makes it hard to follow, and treat gaps as information about the procedure, not only the person.
5. How to classify findings: the procedure is unclear, it's unworkable as written, people weren't trained, or the right tools aren't available - each needs a different fix.
6. A simple tracker for findings and actions, and what trend would trigger a procedure rewrite.

Keep audits respectful and short; this is about making the process work, not catching people out.
variables: PASTE THE SOP OR KEY STEPS
e.g. "errors are rising", "new procedure", "audit coming up"
e.g. "15 minutes per audit, twice a week"

title: Brief a subcontractor or white-label partner on client work
description: A brief that sets a subcontractor up to deliver to my standard, with scope, quality bar, client contact rules, and confidentiality.
content:
Write a brief for a subcontractor or partner who will deliver part of a client project for me.

**The client project and what they're doing:** [SUMMARY and their portion]
**Deliverables and deadlines:** [LIST]
**Quality standard:** [examples of good work, style guides, tools, file formats]
**Budget and how they'll be paid:** [fixed / hourly, invoicing terms]
**Client visibility:** [will the client know they exist, or is this white-label?]
**Confidentiality concerns:** [what's sensitive]

Create a brief with:
1. Background: the client's goals and why this piece matters (only what they need to know).
2. Scope and deliverables with acceptance criteria, plus explicit exclusions.
3. Timeline with internal review points that leave me time to fix issues before the client sees anything.
4. Rules of engagement: who talks to the client (and who doesn't), how to raise questions, response times, and which brand or email to use if they're client-facing.
5. Quality checklist I'll review their work against.
6. Confidentiality and ownership reminders: client data handling, no portfolio use without permission, and IP assignment as set out in our agreement.
7. Payment terms and what happens if deadlines slip.

Also list the clauses my subcontractor agreement should cover (NDA, IP assignment, non-solicitation of the client), and recommend having that agreement reviewed by a lawyer.
variables: examples of good work, style guides, tools, file formats
will the client know they exist, or is this white-label?

title: Build a contract-to-close timeline with every deadline
description: A dated transaction checklist covering contingencies, earnest money, appraisal, loan, title, and closing, with owner and reminders.
content:
Build a contract-to-close timeline for my real estate transaction.

**My side:** [buyer / seller / both / transaction coordinator]
**Acceptance (effective) date:** [DATE]
**Contract deadlines:** [EARNEST MONEY DUE, INSPECTION, APPRAISAL, FINANCING / LOAN COMMITMENT, TITLE REVIEW, HOA DOCS REVIEW, SALE-OF-HOME, FINAL WALKTHROUGH, CLOSING - as written in the contract, calendar or business days]
**Financing:** [CONVENTIONAL / FHA / VA / CASH, LENDER]
**Property specifics:** [HOA/CONDO, WELL/SEPTIC, PRE-1978 BUILD, TENANT-OCCUPIED, NEW CONSTRUCTION]
**Parties and contacts:** [AGENTS, LENDER, TITLE/ESCROW OR ATTORNEY, INSPECTOR]

Build:
1. A chronological table: Date | Deadline or task | Owner | What must be delivered | Reminder date | Consequence if missed.
2. Calculate dates from the effective date using the counting method I specify. If I do not specify how weekends and holidays count, flag it as [CONFIRM COUNTING RULE] rather than guessing.
3. Add property-specific items (lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978, septic or well tests, HOA resale certificate, tenant estoppel).
4. Add standard items: utility transfers, closing disclosure review timing, wire-fraud warning to the client, walkthrough checklist.
5. List the five deadlines where a missed date costs my client the most.

End with a short weekly status email template for my client. Remind me that the signed contract and my broker's guidance control; this is a planning aid, not legal advice.
variables: AGENTS, LENDER, TITLE/ESCROW OR ATTORNEY, INSPECTOR

title: Build a fair staff shift schedule that covers demand
description: A shift schedule that matches staffing to hourly or daily demand while respecting availability, skills, rest rules, and fairness.
content:
Help me build a staff shift schedule for my team.

**Period:** [e.g. "next 2 weeks", "Mon-Sun"]
**Demand by time block:** [e.g. "Mon-Fri 8-12: 6 people, 12-4: 4 people; Sat: 3 people" - or volume data I have]
**Team:** [NAME OR ID | contracted hours | skills/certifications | availability or restrictions]
**Rules I must follow:** [minimum rest between shifts, max hours per week, break rules, union or contract terms]
**Fairness preferences:** [e.g. "rotate weekends", "share closing shifts evenly"]
**Known absences:** [leave, training days]

Steps:
1. Check whether total available hours can cover demand. If not, show the gap by time block before scheduling.
2. Make sure every shift has at least one person with each critical skill: [CRITICAL SKILLS - e.g. "forklift license", "keyholder", "first aider"].
3. Build the schedule as a table: day | shift times | people assigned | skills covered.
4. Show a summary per person: total hours vs. contracted, number of weekend/late shifts.

Then:
- Flag any rule I might be breaking (rest periods, overtime, under-contracted hours).
- Highlight thin spots where one absence would leave us short, and suggest who could cover.
- Note where demand data looked uncertain.

Working time rules vary by country, state, and contract; check the result against local law and any agreements before publishing.

title: Build a one-page project dashboard for executives in Excel or PowerPoint
description: Designs a one-page project dashboard with the right KPIs, RAG indicators, and layout, built from your project data.
content:
Help me turn my project information into a one-page dashboard for executives.

**Project data:** [PASTE the tracker, status reports, milestone list, budget figures, risk log]
**Who reads it and what they decide:** [e.g. "COO, decides on funding and priority each month"]
**Format:** [Excel / PowerPoint slide / Power BI or Tableau]
**Update frequency:** [weekly / monthly]

Steps:
1. Pick 5-7 measures that answer: Are we on time? On budget? Delivering the scope? What could hurt us? What do you need from me? Typical choices: milestone status, schedule variance, budget spent vs plan, forecast at completion, scope change count, open high risks, decisions pending.
2. For each measure, say exactly how to calculate it from my data and what threshold turns it amber or red.
3. Lay out the page: headline and overall RAG at the top, then key measures, a milestone strip, top 3 risks, and "decisions needed".

Return:
1. The measure list: Measure | Formula or source | Green / amber / red threshold | Why an executive cares.
2. The page layout, section by section, with what goes where.
3. This period's values filled in from my data. Anything you can't calculate stays as [ADD DATA].
4. For Excel: the sheet structure, key formulas, and which chart to use for each measure. For PowerPoint: the slide layout and a headline that states the takeaway.
5. 3 things to leave off the page and why.

Use only numbers from my data. Keep the page readable in under one minute.
variables: e.g. "COO, decides on funding and priority each month"
Excel / PowerPoint slide / Power BI or Tableau

title: Build a plan to reduce chronic absenteeism at my school
description: A tiered, data-driven attendance plan with root causes, interventions, and family outreach steps.
content:
Help me build a plan to reduce chronic absenteeism.

**School level and size:** [e.g. "middle school, 640 students"]
**Current rate:** [% of students missing 10%+ of enrolled days, and trend]
**Groups most affected:** [grades, student groups, neighborhoods]
**Known causes:** [e.g. transportation, illness, caregiving, anxiety, suspension, disengagement]
**Staff and partners:** [e.g. attendance clerk, counselors, social worker, community agencies]
**State or district rules:** [truancy thresholds, required letters or meetings]

Build the plan in three tiers:
1. Tier 1 (all students): welcoming culture, attendance messaging, recognizing improvement (not just perfect attendance), and early warning reports.
2. Tier 2 (missing 10-19%): personal outreach, attendance contracts, mentors, barrier-removal (bus passes, alarm clocks, health referrals).
3. Tier 3 (20%+): case management, home visits, wraparound services, coordinated plans with families.

For each tier give: who owns it, trigger, actions, timing, and how we track it.

Also include:
- A weekly attendance team meeting agenda using student-level data.
- Draft language for a first-contact message to families that is supportive, not punitive.
- 3 leading indicators to watch monthly.

Note where legal truancy steps apply and mark state requirements as [CONFIRM]. Avoid approaches that push out students, such as suspensions for absences.
variables: truancy thresholds, required letters or meetings

title: Build a plan to reduce patient no-shows
description: A targeted no-show reduction plan based on your appointment data, with reminder cadence, scheduling rules, and a fair missed-appointment policy.
content:
Help me reduce patient no-shows at our clinic.

**Specialty and setting:** [e.g. "pediatric primary care", "outpatient behavioral health"]
**Current no-show rate:** [OVERALL %, and by visit type, provider, day, or lead time if known]
**Patient population factors:** [e.g. transportation barriers, shift workers, high Medicaid share, language needs]
**Current reminder process:** [channels, timing, two-way confirmation or not]
**Scheduling rules today:** [booking lead times, double-booking, waitlist, same-day slots]
**Current missed-appointment policy:** [fees, dismissal rules, or none]
**Tools we have:** [EHR/PM system, texting platform, telehealth]

Give me:
1. The likely drivers based on my data, and which extra data to pull to confirm them (e.g. no-show rate by lead time, new vs. established, payer).
2. A reminder cadence (e.g. 7 days, 2 days, same day) with two-way confirm/cancel and an easy reschedule path.
3. Scheduling changes: shorter lead times for high-risk visit types, waitlist backfill, targeted overbooking rules by slot, and telehealth conversion where appropriate.
4. Barrier support: transportation resources, interpreter scheduling, evening slots.
5. A missed-appointment policy that is fair and consistently applied. Note that Medicaid and some payer contracts restrict charging no-show fees; mark that as [CONFIRM WITH BILLING/COMPLIANCE].
6. A 90-day pilot plan with one target metric, owner, and weekly check.

Keep all reminder content to the minimum necessary information, and do not suggest dismissing patients without a documented process and proper notice.
variables: channels, timing, two-way confirmation or not
booking lead times, double-booking, waitlist, same-day slots

title: Build a preventive maintenance schedule for my equipment
description: A maintenance plan that sets tasks and intervals per asset, balances workload, and tracks compliance.
content:
Help me build a preventive maintenance (PM) schedule.

**Equipment list:** [ASSET | type | age | how critical (high/med/low) | hours of use per week]
**Manufacturer recommendations:** [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE, if available]
**Failure history:** [common breakdowns, downtime, repair costs]
**Maintenance resources:** [technicians, hours available, outside contractors]
**Production windows for maintenance:** [e.g. "weekends", "between shifts"]

Do this:
1. Rank assets by criticality (impact of failure on safety, output, quality) and condition.
2. For each asset, list PM tasks: task | interval (time- or usage-based) | duration | skill needed | parts. Use manufacturer guidance where given; otherwise propose intervals and mark them [CONFIRM WITH MANUFACTURER].
3. Spread the tasks into a 12-month calendar that fits our maintenance hours and production windows, avoiding pile-ups in one week.
4. A daily or weekly operator checklist (clean, inspect, lubricate) for simple tasks operators can own.
5. Metrics to track: PM completion rate, overdue PMs, unplanned downtime, mean time between failures.
6. Where failure history suggests condition-based checks (vibration, temperature, wear measurements) would beat fixed intervals.

Safety-related tasks (lockout/tagout, guarding, pressure systems, lifting equipment) may have legal inspection requirements; flag them and tell me to confirm with a qualified person.

title: Build a process FMEA for a new or changed production step
description: A process FMEA table with failure modes, effects, causes, current controls, and severity/occurrence/detection ratings, plus prioritized actions.
content:
Help me build a process FMEA (PFMEA) for a production step.

**Process step(s):** [e.g. "Op 30: press-fit bearing into housing"]
**What changed or why now:** [new line / new part / process change / customer complaint / annual review]
**Product requirements this step must deliver:** [special or critical characteristics, tolerances, torque, dimensions]
**Equipment and controls in place today:** [machines, fixtures, poka-yokes, gauges, inspection frequency]
**Known history:** [past defects, scrap reasons, complaints, or "none"]
**Rating scale we use:** [AIAG-VDA 2019 with Action Priority / classic RPN / our own 1-10 tables]

Work through the step like a cross-functional team would:
1. Break the step into its process functions and requirements.
2. For each, list realistic failure modes (what goes wrong at this step), the effect on the next operation, the end customer, and safety or regulatory compliance, and the causes at the 4M level (man, machine, method, material) plus environment and measurement.
3. List current prevention controls and detection controls separately. Do not count an operator visual check as strong detection.
4. Suggest severity, occurrence, and detection ratings with a one-line reason each, and mark every rating [TEAM TO CONFIRM].
5. Rank by Action Priority (High/Medium/Low) or RPN, whichever scale I named.

Return:
- A table: Function/requirement | Failure mode | Effect | S | Cause | Prevention control | O | Detection control | D | AP or RPN | Recommended action | Owner | Due date.
- The top 5 risks with an action that lowers occurrence or improves detection, preferring error-proofing over added inspection.
- Questions the team must answer on the floor before finalizing.

Do not invent defect rates or history. A PFMEA is a team document: treat this as a first draft for the team review, not a finished analysis.
variables: machines, fixtures, poka-yokes, gauges, inspection frequency
past defects, scrap reasons, complaints, or "none"

title: Build a production budget for a commercial or video shoot
description: A line-item production estimate covering pre-production, shoot days, crew, post, and contingency, with assumptions the client can sign off.
content:
Help me build a production budget for a shoot.

**Deliverables:** [e.g. "one 30s spot, two 15s cutdowns, 6 vertical social edits, 10 stills"]
**Creative scope:** [SCRIPT OR TREATMENT SUMMARY - locations, cast size, special requirements like animals, stunts, drones, kids, night work]
**Shoot days and location:** [NUMBER OF DAYS, city or country, studio vs location]
**Rates I know:** [crew day rates, equipment quotes, talent fees, post house quotes]
**Client budget ceiling:** [AMOUNT, if known]
**Who is producing:** [in-house agency production / external production company / hybrid]

Organize the estimate into these sections, similar to a standard production bid form:
- Pre-production (casting, location scouting, permits, tech scout, prep days).
- Shoot crew by department, with day rates, prep and wrap days, and overtime assumptions.
- Equipment (camera, grip, electric, specialty).
- Talent (session fees and usage noted separately), wardrobe, hair and makeup, art and props.
- Locations, permits, studio, travel, catering, insurance.
- Post-production (edit, grade, sound mix, music, VFX, versioning).
- Production fee, markup, and contingency.

Return:
1. A budget table: section | line item | quantity | rate | days | total | source of rate (quote / my rate / estimate).
2. Subtotals per section and a grand total.
3. The assumptions and exclusions the client must accept.
4. Three ways to bring the cost down, with the creative trade-off of each.

Never present an estimated rate as a quote: label it [ESTIMATE - GET QUOTE]. Note where union rules, local permits, or insurance need checking.
variables: NUMBER OF DAYS, city or country, studio vs location

title: Build a punch list and closeout plan to finish the job
description: An organized punch list by area and trade plus a closeout checklist for documents, inspections, and final payment.
content:
Help me close out a construction project.

**Project and contract type:** [e.g. "restaurant build-out, GC with 12 subs"]
**Raw punch items from walkthroughs:** [PASTE NOTES - any order is fine]
**Areas or rooms:** [LIST]
**Subs and trades:** [LIST]
**Target dates:** [SUBSTANTIAL COMPLETION, CERTIFICATE OF OCCUPANCY, OWNER MOVE-IN, FINAL COMPLETION]
**Closeout requirements in my contract or specs:** [e.g. O&M manuals, as-builts, attic stock, training, warranties - or "not sure"]

Steps:
1. Clean up the punch items: one item per line, specific location, clear description of what "done" means. Merge duplicates.
2. Assign each item to a trade and sort by area so each sub can walk it in one pass.
3. Flag items that block a final inspection, CO, or owner occupancy as priority.
4. Build the closeout checklist: final inspections and sign-offs, CO, as-built drawings, O&M manuals, warranties with start dates, attic stock, owner training, keys and access, final cleaning, final lien waivers from all subs and suppliers, consent of surety if bonded, and release of retainage.

Return:
- Punch list table: #, Area, Item, Trade, Priority, Due date, Status, Verified by.
- Per-trade punch summary I can send to each sub.
- Closeout checklist with owner and due date for each item.
- A short email to subs setting the punch completion deadline.

Mark contract-specific requirements I have not confirmed as [CHECK SPEC SECTION].
variables: PASTE NOTES - any order is fine

title: Build a RAID log (risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies)
description: Captures and tracks the risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies on a project.
content:
Role: Act as a project manager compiling and structuring a RAID log.

Context: Project context: [PROJECT_CONTEXT]. Raw notes / status inputs mentioning risks, assumptions, issues, dependencies: [NOTES]. Scoring scale for risk (likelihood x impact): [RISK_SCALE]. Escalation thresholds: [ESCALATION]. Review cadence: [CADENCE].

Task: Produce: a categorised RAID log - Risks (description, cause, likelihood, impact, score, response strategy, owner, next action, date); Assumptions (statement, validity, what happens if false, owner); Issues (description, impact now, severity, owner, action, target date); Dependencies (what, on whom, needed-by date, status, owner). Then the items breaching escalation thresholds and a proposed agenda for the next RAID review.

Format: Four tables (Risks / Assumptions / Issues / Dependencies) + escalations + review agenda.

Verification: Do not invent items not implied by the notes; flag notes that are too vague to log and need clarification. Apply the risk scale consistently.

Validation: Check the log against the project's biggest known threat: is it captured with a real response and owner, or buried? Elevate it if so.

title: Build a recovery plan for a project that is behind schedule
description: Turns a late project's facts into ranked recovery options (crash, fast-track, de-scope) with cost, risk, and a recommendation.
content:
Help me build a recovery plan for a project that is behind schedule.

**Project and goal:** [WHAT WE ARE DELIVERING and for whom]
**Committed date vs. current forecast:** [e.g. "June 30 committed, now forecasting Aug 15"]
**Why we slipped:** [CAUSES - be honest: late dependencies, underestimates, scope added, people lost]
**Remaining work:** [MILESTONES or major tasks still open, with estimates]
**Levers I could pull:** [extra budget, more people, overtime, vendor help, scope that could move to a later release]
**Hard constraints:** [fixed date? fixed budget? regulatory scope that cannot be cut?]

Analyze recovery using these options, and say which ones actually apply:
- **Crashing** - adding people or money to critical-path tasks (watch for onboarding drag and Brooks's law).
- **Fast-tracking** - running sequential tasks in parallel (note the rework risk).
- **De-scoping** - moving features to a later release (name what users lose).
- **Re-sequencing** - delivering the highest-value slice first.
- **Moving the date** - and what that costs.

Rules: do not invent estimates or costs - where I have not given a number, mark [ESTIMATE NEEDED]. Be realistic about how much time each option really buys back.

Return:
1. A one-paragraph diagnosis of the slip.
2. An options table: option | days recovered (range) | added cost | new risks | who must approve.
3. My recommended combination and the new forecast date with a confidence level.
4. What I must stop, start, and change this week.
5. A short message to my sponsor presenting the options and my recommendation.
variables: WHAT WE ARE DELIVERING and for whom
MILESTONES or major tasks still open, with estimates

title: Build a response plan for a supply chain disruption
description: A first-72-hours action plan when a supplier, port, or route fails: impact, allocation, recovery options, and communications.
content:
Help me build a response plan for a supply chain disruption happening now.

**What happened:** [e.g. "supplier fire", "port closure", "carrier bankruptcy", "customs hold"]
**What is affected:** [PARTS, SKUS, LANES, SITES]
**What we know and don't know:** [FACTS SO FAR, EXPECTED DURATION IF STATED]
**Inventory on hand and in transit:** [UNITS AND WEEKS OF COVER PER ITEM]
**Open demand at risk:** [CUSTOMER ORDERS, PRODUCTION SCHEDULE]
**Possible alternatives:** [OTHER SUPPLIERS, ROUTES, MODES, SUBSTITUTE PARTS]
**Response team:** [NAMES OR ROLES]

Build the plan in phases:
1. First 24 hours: confirm facts, secure in-transit stock, freeze or reallocate inventory, stand up a daily call.
2. 24-72 hours: quantify the gap by week, run allocation rules (which customers or products get priority and why), activate alternatives, book capacity before competitors do.
3. Recovery: rebuild buffers, review contracts (force majeure notices, our obligations to customers), lessons learned.

For allocation, suggest criteria (contractual commitments, margin, strategic customers, safety-critical items) and ask me to confirm before applying them.

Use only facts I provide; mark unknowns [CONFIRM]. For force majeure or contract questions, note that legal should review.

Return:
1. A gap table: Item | Cover (weeks) | Demand at risk | Gap start date | Recovery option.
2. The phased action plan with owners and deadlines.
3. Short drafts: internal leadership update, customer notice, and a note to sales on what they can promise.
4. The 5 metrics to track daily until recovery.
variables: FACTS SO FAR, EXPECTED DURATION IF STATED
UNITS AND WEEKS OF COVER PER ITEM
OTHER SUPPLIERS, ROUTES, MODES, SUBSTITUTE PARTS

title: Build a supplier sustainability questionnaire and scoring guide
description: Targeted ESG questions for suppliers plus a scoring rubric that separates real evidence from vague claims.
content:
Build a sustainability (ESG) questionnaire for my suppliers and a guide to score their answers.

**Categories and suppliers in scope:** [e.g. "top 50 suppliers by spend", "packaging and logistics"]
**Why we're doing this:** [CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS, REGULATION, SCOPE 3 TARGETS, BRAND COMMITMENTS]
**Our priorities:** [e.g. emissions, labor rights, conflict minerals, deforestation, water, packaging waste]
**Frameworks we report against, if any:** [e.g. a science-based target, a reporting standard - or "none yet"]
**Supplier maturity:** [mostly large multinationals / mostly small firms / mixed]

Requirements:
- Keep it short enough that small suppliers will complete it: a core set of about 15-20 questions, plus optional depth for strategic suppliers.
- Ask for evidence, not opinions: certificates, audit reports, measured data with the year and method, named policies.
- Cover emissions (scope 1 and 2 data, reduction targets, whether they can share product-level data), human rights and labor, health and safety, environmental management, business ethics, and their own supplier oversight.
- Avoid yes/no questions that invite greenwashing; ask "how" and "show".

Return:
1. The questionnaire grouped by section, with answer format for each question.
2. A scoring rubric: 0-3 per question, with what counts as evidence at each level.
3. Red flags that should trigger follow-up or an audit.
4. A cover email explaining why we're asking and how the data will be used.
5. Suggested follow-up actions by score band (develop, monitor, escalate).

Ask me to confirm any regulatory requirement before stating it as mandatory.
variables: e.g. "top 50 suppliers by spend", "packaging and logistics"
mostly large multinationals / mostly small firms / mixed

title: Build a three-week look-ahead schedule for my jobsite
description: A day-by-day look-ahead by trade and area with constraints, inspections, and deliveries flagged before they cause delays.
content:
Build a three-week look-ahead schedule for my jobsite.

**Project and phase:** [e.g. "3-story wood frame, framing to MEP rough-in"]
**Master schedule milestones in this window:** [MILESTONES AND DATES]
**Activities planned:** [ACTIVITY, AREA/FLOOR, CREW OR SUB, DURATION]
**Crews available:** [TRADE AND HEADCOUNT]
**Deliveries and long-lead items:** [ITEM, EXPECTED DATE, CONFIRMED OR NOT]
**Inspections needed:** [e.g. "framing, rough electrical, rough plumbing, insulation"]
**Open RFIs, submittals, or permits holding work:** [LIST]
**Work days and weather risk:** [e.g. "Mon-Fri, rain likely next week"]

Steps:
1. Lay out activities by day and area, following a logical trade sequence (e.g. rough-in before insulation inspection before drywall).
2. For each activity, run a constraint check: design answered, materials on site, prior work complete, crew available, inspection passed, access and equipment ready. Mark it Ready or Constrained and name the constraint.
3. Flag trade stacking where two crews need the same area at once.
4. Show inspection call-in dates with buffer for re-inspection.
5. Identify the activities on the path to the next milestone.

Return:
- A table: Week, Day, Activity, Area, Trade, Crew size, Status (Ready/Constrained), Constraint, Owner to clear it.
- A constraints list sorted by date needed.
- 5 bullet talking points for the weekly subcontractor coordination meeting.

Do not invent durations or dates; mark gaps as [CONFIRM].
variables: e.g. "3-story wood frame, framing to MEP rough-in"
ACTIVITY, AREA/FLOOR, CREW OR SUB, DURATION
ITEM, EXPECTED DATE, CONFIRMED OR NOT
e.g. "framing, rough electrical, rough plumbing, insulation"

title: Build a troubleshooting flowchart for a piece of equipment
description: A how-it-works explanation plus a step-by-step fault-finding flowchart, with safety stops, for any appliance, machine, or system.
content:
Help me build a troubleshooting guide and flowchart for a piece of equipment.

**Equipment:** [TYPE, MAKE, MODEL - e.g. "gas-fired pool heater", "commercial dishwasher", "rooftop HVAC unit"]
**Who will use the guide:** [homeowner / in-house maintenance / trained technician]
**Symptoms or error codes we see most:** [LIST]
**Manual or spec excerpts I can share:** [PASTE, or "none"]

Give me:
1. How it works: the normal operating sequence in numbered steps (e.g. call for heat, safety checks, ignition, proving, run, shutdown), naming the component responsible at each step.
2. A sequence diagram of that process as Mermaid flowchart code.
3. A fault-finding flowchart (Mermaid) for each common symptom: start at the symptom, check the cheapest and most likely causes first, and branch on yes/no observations.
4. A troubleshooting table: Symptom or code | Likely causes (most to least likely) | Check to perform | Fix | Who should do it (user / technician).
5. Preventive maintenance tasks with frequency.
6. Tools and test equipment needed.

Rules:
- Mark every step that involves gas, high voltage, refrigerant, pressure, or moving parts with a SAFETY note, including isolation or lockout before work, and route it to a qualified technician if the user is not one.
- If I name error codes you cannot confirm for this model, mark them [CHECK MANUAL] rather than guessing their meaning.
- If anyone smells gas or sees scorching or smoke, the first instruction is to stop, shut off supply if safe, leave the area, and call the gas utility or emergency services.

title: Build a weekly staff schedule that hits my labor cost target
description: A forecast-driven front- and back-of-house schedule that controls labor cost and follows break and scheduling rules.
content:
Help me build next week's staff schedule.

**Department:** [e.g. restaurant FOH and BOH / housekeeping / front desk]
**Forecast by day and daypart:** [COVERS, SALES, OR OCCUPIED ROOMS AND ARRIVALS/DEPARTURES]
**Productivity standards:** [e.g. 1 server per 20 covers, 14 rooms cleaned per attendant per shift, 1 cook per 60 covers]
**Labor cost target:** [e.g. 28-30% of sales, or hours per occupied room]
**Staff:** [NAMES OR IDS, ROLE, PAY RATE, AVAILABILITY, MAX HOURS, MINORS]
**Fixed positions and management:** [ROLES ALWAYS ON]
**Rules that apply:** [break and meal periods, overtime threshold, minor work hours, predictive scheduling notice or clopen rules in my city - or "unsure"]

Steps:
1. Convert the forecast into required staff by hour or shift using my standards; show the curve.
2. Build shifts that match the curve with staggered starts and cuts instead of everyone on a full shift.
3. Assign people by availability and skills, spreading weekend and closing shifts fairly.
4. Flag overtime risk, clopens (close then open), minor hour limits, and missing breaks.
5. Calculate scheduled hours, labor cost, and labor % by day and for the week; show what to cut first if sales come in under forecast and who is on call if over.

Return the schedule as a table (day, shift, role, person, hours), the labor cost summary, a list of rule conflicts to check, and a short note to post for staff. Scheduling laws vary by city and state; confirm with HR or local law, and do not schedule in breach of a rule I named.
variables: e.g. restaurant FOH and BOH / housekeeping / front desk
COVERS, SALES, OR OCCUPIED ROOMS AND ARRIVALS/DEPARTURES
e.g. 28-30% of sales, or hours per occupied room
NAMES OR IDS, ROLE, PAY RATE, AVAILABILITY, MAX HOURS, MINORS

title: Build an annual compliance calendar for our legal entities
description: Creates a calendar of corporate filings, annual meetings, renewals, and registrations per entity so deadlines are never missed.
content:
Help me build an annual corporate compliance calendar for our group of legal entities.

**Entities:** [for each: legal name, entity type, jurisdiction of incorporation, registration number, financial year end, date of incorporation]
**Places each entity is registered or qualified to do business:** [LIST]
**Known deadlines and filings we already track:** [LIST]
**Who owns each type of task:** [e.g. "paralegal: filings; finance: tax returns; company secretary: meetings"]
**Registered agents / corporate service providers:** [if any]

For each entity, list the recurring obligations to check, such as:
- Annual reports / confirmation statements and registered office or agent renewals
- Annual financial statements and audit filing deadlines
- Annual general meeting or annual shareholder/director approvals
- Beneficial ownership or register updates
- Business licenses, permits, and foreign qualifications
- Director and officer changes to be filed within a set period
- Tax registrations (flag only; finance owns the returns)
- Powers of attorney, signatory lists, and bank mandates to review

Rules:
- Do not state specific statutory deadlines from memory as fact. Put the obligation and a proposed date, mark each [CONFIRM DEADLINE WITH REGISTRY OR LOCAL COUNSEL], and note the typical trigger (e.g. "X months after year end").
- Add an internal reminder date 30 days before each deadline.

Return:
1. A table: Entity | Jurisdiction | Obligation | Trigger | Proposed due date | Reminder date | Owner | Source to confirm.
2. A month-by-month view of the year.
3. A short list of information I am missing.

Requirements vary by jurisdiction and change; a qualified lawyer or local agent must confirm each deadline.
variables: CONFIRM DEADLINE WITH REGISTRY OR LOCAL COUNSEL

title: Build an incident response playbook for one type of attack
description: Creates a step-by-step playbook for a specific threat like ransomware or account takeover, with roles and decision points.
content:
Build an incident response playbook for one attack scenario.

**Scenario:** [e.g. "ransomware on a file server", "business email compromise", "compromised admin account", "lost laptop with sensitive data"]
**Our environment:** [key systems, identity provider, EDR, backup tool, cloud platforms]
**Team and roles:** [who is on call, IT, security, legal, comms, leadership, outside IR firm or insurer]
**Constraints:** [e.g. "24/7 operations", "regulated data", "cyber insurance requires notice within X hours"]

Structure it around the NIST incident response phases:
1. Detection and triage: signals that trigger this playbook, initial severity criteria, who to page.
2. Containment: immediate steps (with the order that preserves evidence), and the decisions that need an approver (e.g. shutting down production).
3. Evidence preservation: what to capture before changing anything, and chain of custody basics.
4. Eradication and recovery: removing the attacker, rotating credentials, restoring from clean backups, verifying before reconnecting.
5. Communication: internal updates cadence, when to involve legal, insurer, law enforcement, customers, or regulators.
6. Post-incident: lessons learned meeting and control improvements.

Include decision points as "If X, then Y" lines, and for each step: owner, tool, and target time.

Return: a one-page quick-reference checklist, the full playbook, and a contact roster template with [ADD] placeholders. Flag steps that need legal advice (e.g. ransom payment, breach notification) rather than making those calls.

title: Build an integrated program roadmap across workstreams
description: Combines several workstream plans into one roadmap showing milestones, cross-workstream dependencies, and integration points.
content:
Help me build an integrated roadmap for a program with several workstreams.

**Program goal:** [OUTCOME and target date]
**Workstreams:** [LIST each with its lead, scope, and key milestones with dates]
**Known dependencies between workstreams:** [e.g. "Training can't start until the system is configured"]
**External dates:** [regulatory deadlines, contract dates, business calendar events, freeze periods]
**Planning horizon and granularity:** [e.g. "18 months, by month"]

Steps:
1. Lay out each workstream's milestones on a common timeline.
2. Map cross-workstream dependencies and check each one: does the provider's date land before the consumer needs it? Flag conflicts and tight handoffs (less than 2 weeks of buffer).
3. Identify integration points - moments where outputs from several workstreams must come together (e.g. end-to-end testing, launch readiness) - and treat these as program-level milestones.
4. Find periods of overload where several workstreams peak at once and compete for the same people or approvals.
5. Suggest program-level checkpoints for leadership review.

Rules: keep each workstream's dates as given; flag problems rather than silently moving dates. Mark any assumption as [ASSUMED].

Return:
1. A roadmap table: period | workstream | milestone | depends on | integration point?
2. A dependency list with status: OK / tight / conflict.
3. The top 5 program-level risks from the roadmap.
4. A one-page summary view for executives: phases, major milestones, and decision points.
5. A description of how to draw it as a swimlane chart.
variables: LIST each with its lead, scope, and key milestones with dates
e.g. "Training can't start until the system is configured"

title: Build an offboarding checklist that removes every access
description: Creates a role-specific checklist to revoke accounts, devices, and data access when someone leaves, with timing.
content:
Create an IT offboarding checklist for a departing employee.

**Role and department:** [e.g. "sales manager", "DevOps engineer"]
**Type of exit:** [planned resignation / involuntary termination / contractor end]
**Last working day and time:** [DATE, TIME, TIME ZONE]
**Systems they use:** [e.g. "Entra ID, Google Workspace, Salesforce, AWS, GitHub, VPN, building badge"]
**Devices they hold:** [laptop, phone, tokens, keys]
**Shared or privileged access:** [admin accounts, shared mailboxes, service accounts, password vault entries, API keys they created]

Build the checklist in phases:
1. Before the exit: inventory their access, identify data and files to transfer, find accounts and automations owned by this person.
2. At the exit time: disable sign-in, revoke sessions and tokens, remove MFA devices, disable VPN and remote access, block mobile email.
3. Same day: rotate any shared passwords, secrets, or keys they knew; remove from privileged groups; collect devices.
4. Within 30 days: transfer file and mailbox ownership, set auto-reply or forwarding per policy, reassign licenses, wipe and reimage devices, then delete or archive accounts per retention policy.

For an involuntary exit, make disabling access happen at the same moment as the conversation, coordinated with HR.

Return a table: Step | System | Action | Owner | When | Done (checkbox). Add a short list of the access items most often missed. Follow our data retention and legal hold rules; mark anything that needs HR or legal sign-off as [CONFIRM WITH HR/LEGAL].

title: Build evaluation criteria and a scoring plan for a public solicitation
description: Weighted, defensible proposal evaluation criteria, scoring guides, and evaluator instructions that hold up if a bidder protests.
content:
Help me design the evaluation criteria and scoring plan for a public solicitation.

**Solicitation type:** [RFP / RFQ / best value / qualifications-based selection]
**What we are buying:** [SCOPE SUMMARY]
**Estimated value and contract length:** [DETAILS]
**What matters most to us:** [e.g. "technical approach", "past performance", "price", "local or small business participation if allowed"]
**Rules or policies that apply:** [e.g. "state procurement code", "federal grant rules", "price must be at least 30% weight"]
**Evaluation committee:** [number and roles of evaluators]

Create:
1. **Pass/fail responsiveness checks** (required forms, licenses, insurance, deadlines) kept separate from scored criteria.
2. **Scored criteria** with weights totaling 100, a one-line rationale for each weight, and how price will be scored (formula shown).
3. **A scoring guide** for each criterion: what earns high, middle, and low scores, written as observable evidence in the proposal.
4. **Evaluator instructions**: conflict-of-interest and confidentiality attestations, score independently before consensus, document strengths and weaknesses for every score, no contact with bidders.
5. **A scoring sheet layout**: Criterion | Weight | Score | Weighted score | Strengths | Weaknesses.
6. **Protest-proofing checks**: criteria in the solicitation match criteria used, no unstated criteria, consistent treatment of all bidders.

Rules: criteria must be tied to the scope and disclosed in the solicitation; do not invent legal requirements or preference programs; mark anything unconfirmed [CONFIRM WITH PROCUREMENT].
variables: RFP / RFQ / best value / qualifications-based selection

title: Capture lessons learned from a project
description: A blameless lessons-learned write-up with actions for next time.
content:
Role: Act as a PMO analyst capturing lessons learned from a completed project or phase.

Context: Project summary and outcome vs plan: [PROJECT_SUMMARY]. Inputs (retro notes, review findings, RAID history, stakeholder feedback): [INPUTS]. The knowledge base structure and tags: [KB_STRUCTURE]. Audience who would reuse this: [AUDIENCE].

Task: Produce: 6-10 lessons, each as - situation, what happened, why (root cause), the impact, the recommendation for future projects, and the type of project/phase it applies to; group them (estimation, stakeholders, delivery, procurement, etc.); add the KB tags; and list the 3 lessons most worth turning into a checklist item or template change.

Format: Sections: Lessons (grouped, each with the 6 fields) | KB tags | Turn-into-standard candidates.

title: Check supply readiness for a new product launch
description: A launch readiness plan that confirms parts, suppliers, capacity, inventory build, and logistics are ready before the launch date.
content:
Help me plan and check supply chain readiness for a new product launch.

**Product and launch date:** [PRODUCT, LAUNCH DATE, MARKETS AND CHANNELS]
**Bill of materials:** [COMPONENTS, SUPPLIERS, LEAD TIMES, QUALIFICATION STATUS - new or existing parts]
**Launch volume forecast:** [INITIAL STOCKING, FIRST 3 MONTHS, CONFIDENCE LEVEL]
**Production:** [IN-HOUSE OR CONTRACT MANUFACTURER, CAPACITY, PILOT RUN DATES]
**Distribution:** [WAREHOUSES, CHANNEL PARTNERS, RETAILER SETUP REQUIREMENTS, SHIPPING MODE]
**Item setup:** [ITEM MASTER, BARCODES, PACKAGING, LABELING, COMPLIANCE MARKINGS]
**Known risks:** [LONG-LEAD PARTS, NEW SUPPLIERS, UNCERTAIN DEMAND]

Steps:
1. Work backwards from launch date to find the latest date each long-lead component must be ordered; flag any already late.
2. Check qualification, first article, and certification status for new parts and the product.
3. Size the launch inventory build, with an upside and downside demand scenario, and the commitment exposure if demand is weak.
4. Confirm distribution steps: inbound to warehouse, retailer or marketplace onboarding, channel fill timing.
5. Confirm systems and data: item setup, pricing, barcodes, packaging specs.
6. Define go/no-go criteria for launch.

Use only my dates and lead times; flag anything I haven't confirmed as [CONFIRM].

Return:
1. A readiness tracker: Workstream | Item | Owner | Due date | Status (red/amber/green) | Risk.
2. The critical path and the 5 items most likely to delay launch.
3. Inventory build plan with exposure in each scenario.
4. A one-paragraph readiness summary for the launch team.
variables: PRODUCT, LAUNCH DATE, MARKETS AND CHANNELS
INITIAL STOCKING, FIRST 3 MONTHS, CONFIDENCE LEVEL
IN-HOUSE OR CONTRACT MANUFACTURER, CAPACITY, PILOT RUN DATES
LONG-LEAD PARTS, NEW SUPPLIERS, UNCERTAIN DEMAND

title: Close a client matter with a closing letter and file checklist
description: A closing letter that formally ends representation, plus an internal checklist for trust balances, file return, and record retention.
content:
Help me close a completed client matter at my law firm.

**Client and matter:** [NAME, MATTER NUMBER, DESCRIPTION]
**How the matter ended:** [e.g. "settled and dismissed", "deal closed", "will signed"]
**Remaining obligations the client has:** [e.g. "file annual report", "comply with settlement terms by June 1" - or "none"]
**Trust account balance for this client:** [AMOUNT]
**Outstanding fees or costs:** [AMOUNT]
**Original documents we hold:** [LIST]
**Our file retention period:** [e.g. "7 years" - per firm policy]

Give me:
1. A client closing letter that: thanks the client; states clearly that the representation has ended; summarizes the outcome in two or three sentences; lists any ongoing obligations or future dates the client must track themselves; explains what happens to the trust balance; offers return of originals; states how long we keep the file and that it may then be destroyed; and invites them to contact us for future matters as a new engagement.
2. An internal closing checklist: final bill, trust balance refunded or applied with documentation, unearned fees returned, originals returned with receipt, docket entries cleared or handed off, conflicts database updated to "former client", file archived with destruction date, and any malpractice-relevant notes.
3. A short client feedback request I could send two weeks later.

Do not add dates or amounts I have not given you; mark gaps as [ADD]. Check my state's trust accounting and file retention rules before finalizing.

title: Connect my online store's payments, accounting, and inventory
description: A plan for integrating your payment gateway with accounting and inventory systems, with tool options, data flows, and reconciliation checks.
content:
Help me connect my online store's payment processing with my accounting and inventory systems.

**Store platform:** [e.g. Shopify, WooCommerce, custom]
**Payment gateway(s):** [current or candidates]
**Accounting software:** [e.g. QuickBooks, Xero, other]
**Inventory system:** [built into store, separate app, spreadsheet, ERP]
**Sales channels:** [website, marketplaces, in-person POS]
**Monthly orders and countries/currencies:** [DETAILS]
**Current pain points:** [e.g. manual entry, stock mismatches, payouts that don't match sales]
**Budget and technical help available:** [DETAILS]

Cover:
1. **Data flows** - a simple map of what moves where: orders, payments, fees, refunds, chargebacks, taxes, payouts, stock levels.
2. **Integration options** - native connectors, integration apps or middleware, and custom API work: pros, cons, rough effort, and fit for my size. Name tool categories and what to look for; mark specific products and prices as [CONFIRM].
3. **Accounting setup** - recording sales vs. payouts, gateway fees, refunds, sales tax/VAT, and multi-currency; summary journals vs. per-order entries.
4. **Inventory sync** - single source of truth for stock, timing of updates, oversell prevention, returns back to stock.
5. **Reconciliation** - a daily/weekly check that payouts match orders minus fees and refunds, and what to do with mismatches.
6. **Security** - keep card data with the gateway (PCI scope), API key handling, user access.
7. **Rollout plan** - test with sample orders, run in parallel, cutover date.

Return a recommended setup for my situation and a checklist. Confirm accounting and tax treatment with my accountant.
variables: built into store, separate app, spreadsheet, ERP

title: Contain a suspect lot before it reaches more customers
description: A first-48-hours containment plan that traces affected lots, quarantines stock everywhere it sits, and tells the customer what they need to know.
content:
Help me contain a suspected quality problem in product that may already be shipped.

**The problem:** [defect, how it was found, by whom, and when]
**Safety or regulatory risk:** [could it injure someone, violate a regulation, or stop a customer line?]
**Known affected lots/serials and production dates:** [DETAILS]
**Traceability available:** [lot genealogy, raw material lots, machine, shift, operator, date codes]
**Where product may be:** [WIP, finished goods, warehouses, in transit, at customers, in the field]
**Customers involved and their requirements:** [e.g. "automotive OEM requires notification within 24 hours"]

Build a containment plan:
1. Define the suspect range: work backward to the last known good part and forward to the first verified good part after the fix. Explain the logic, and widen the range if the cause is unknown.
2. Use traceability to find related product: same material lot, same machine, same tooling, same shift.
3. Quarantine actions at each location (WIP, finished goods, warehouse, in transit, customer stock), with who does it and how the stock is tagged and recorded.
4. Sorting or inspection method to release good product (100% inspection, test, and how to verify the sort works).
5. A clean-point marking for the first certified good shipments.
6. A customer notification draft: what we know, what we don't, lots affected, actions taken, next update time.
7. When to escalate to a formal recall or regulatory report, and who must decide.

Return: an action list with owners and deadlines for the first 48 hours, the customer note, and a log template.

Do not invent lot numbers or quantities; use [ADD]. Recall and regulatory reporting duties depend on your industry and jurisdiction; involve quality leadership and legal counsel.
variables: defect, how it was found, by whom, and when
e.g. "automotive OEM requires notification within 24 hours"

title: Coordinate the first hour of an operational disruption
description: A step-by-step response plan and update templates for when a site, system, or supplier failure is happening right now.
content:
Something has gone wrong in my operation right now. Help me run the response.

**What's happening:** [DESCRIBE - e.g. "WMS is down, trucks are arriving", "power loss on line 2", "supplier didn't deliver"]
**When it started and what we know:** [FACTS SO FAR]
**Who and what is affected:** [customers, orders, staff, sites]
**People I have available:** [ROLES]
**Any safety risk:** [YES/NO/UNSURE - describe]

Give me, briefly and in priority order:
1. **Immediate checks:** safety first (if there is any risk to people, stop and follow emergency procedures, call emergency services if needed), then contain the impact.
2. **Roles:** who leads, who fixes, who communicates, who logs the timeline. One person per role.
3. **Workarounds:** options to keep the most critical work flowing (manual process, reroute, prioritize key customers), with the risks of each.
4. **Decision points:** what I need to decide in the next 15, 30, and 60 minutes, and the information I need for each.
5. **Update templates:** a 3-line internal update for leadership and a holding message for affected customers or teams. Use [ADD] for facts we don't have yet.
6. **What to log now** so the post-incident review has an accurate timeline.

Don't speculate about the cause; list possible causes only as hypotheses to check.

title: Create a client onboarding kit for my freelance business
description: A welcome email, intake questionnaire, and kickoff agenda so every new client starts smoothly.
content:
Create a client onboarding kit for my freelance business.

**My service:** [WHAT I DELIVER]
**Typical project length and steps:** [DETAILS]

2. An intake questionnaire (10-15 questions) tailored to my service, with a short explanation of why each question matters.
3. A 30-minute kickoff call agenda with timings and the decisions to leave with.
4. A checklist of what must be in place before work starts (signed agreement, deposit paid, access granted, assets received).
5. Short templates for: a weekly status update, a feedback request with a deadline, and a polite note when the client is holding up the project.
6. A scope-change note that explains what's outside the agreement and offers a quote.

Keep the tone warm and professional. Have my contract terms reviewed by a qualified professional; this kit supports the agreement, it doesn't replace it.

title: Create a mutual success plan with a new customer
description: A shared plan that turns a new customer's goals into milestones, owners, and dates both sides agree to.
content:
Help me create a mutual success plan for a new customer.

**Customer and use case:** [COMPANY TYPE, WHAT THEY'RE USING US FOR]
**Business outcomes they want:** [e.g. "cut onboarding time by 30%", "replace spreadsheets by Q3"]
**Their key people:** [EXEC SPONSOR, PROJECT LEAD, ADMINS, END USERS]
**Our team:** [CSM, IMPLEMENTATION, SUPPORT, OTHERS]
**Contract start, go-live target, and renewal date:** [DATES]
**Known constraints:** [e.g. IT security review, data migration, limited admin time, holidays]

Produce:

2. Milestones table: | Milestone | Success criteria | Customer owner | Our owner | Target date | Dependencies |. Cover kickoff, technical setup, data/integration, admin training, pilot group, full rollout, first value review.
3. Success metrics: 3-5 leading indicators (adoption, activity) and 2-3 outcome metrics, with how and when each is measured.
4. Risks to the plan, each with an early warning sign and a mitigation.
5. Communication rhythm: cadence of check-ins, who attends, and how we escalate blockers on both sides.
6. A short cover note I can send with the plan asking them to review and confirm.

Mark any date or metric I haven't provided as [CONFIRM]. Keep it to a plan both sides can sign off on, not an internal project plan.

EXEC SPONSOR, PROJECT LEAD, ADMINS, END USERS

title: Create a new supplier onboarding checklist and questionnaire
description: A risk-based onboarding pack with the documents, checks, and approvals to collect before a new supplier gets a first PO.
content:
Create a supplier onboarding checklist and questionnaire for my organization.

**What we buy from this type of supplier:** [e.g. direct materials, contract manufacturing, IT services, logistics]
**Risk level of this supplier:** [LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH - and why, e.g. "handles customer data", "safety-critical part"]
**Our industry and any regulations we must meet:** [e.g. food safety, medical devices, defense, data privacy]
**Internal teams involved:** [PROCUREMENT, QUALITY, FINANCE, LEGAL, IT SECURITY, SUSTAINABILITY]
**Systems:** [ERP OR SUPPLIER PORTAL WHERE DATA IS ENTERED]
**Our current gaps or past problems:** [e.g. "bank detail fraud", "no insurance on file"]

Build the onboarding in tiers so low-risk suppliers aren't overloaded and high-risk ones are checked properly. Cover:

title: Create a project plan with a work breakdown and schedule
description: WBS, milestones, dependencies, resources, and a realistic timeline.
content:
Role: Act as a project manager building the WBS and schedule.

Context: Scope and deliverables: [SCOPE_DELIVERABLES]. Known constraints (fixed dates, resource availability, external dependencies): [CONSTRAINTS]. Team and skills available: [TEAM]. Estimating basis / any historical data: [ESTIMATING_BASIS]. Methodology (predictive / agile / hybrid): [METHODOLOGY]. Risk areas: [RISK_AREAS].

Task: Produce: (1) a WBS decomposing each deliverable to work-package level with a one-line definition of done for each; (2) rough effort and duration per work package with the estimating assumption; (3) the dependency map and the resulting phased schedule with milestones; (4) the critical path and the work packages with the least float; (5) where the schedule is most fragile and the buffer or fast-track options.

Format: Sections: WBS (indented, with DoD) | Estimates (table) | Dependencies & schedule (phases + milestones) | Critical path & low-float items | Schedule risks & options. ~550 words.

Verification: Flag every estimate that lacks a basis and every dependency without a confirmed date; note where the WBS may be incomplete.

Validation: Pressure-test the critical path: if the two riskiest work packages slip by 20%, what is the end-date impact and the earliest mitigation? State it.

title: Create a QA/QC review checklist for drawings before they are issued
description: A discipline-specific quality control checklist and review workflow for construction documents before permit or bid issue.
content:
Help me create a quality control review checklist for a drawing set before it is issued.

**Firm type and disciplines:** [e.g. "architecture with MEP and structural consultants", "civil engineering"]
**Project type:** [e.g. "tenant fit-out", "healthcare", "site development"]
**Issue milestone:** [e.g. "50% CD", "permit set", "bid set", "issued for construction"]
**Applicable codes and standards:** [e.g. "local building code edition adopted by the jurisdiction, accessibility standard, energy code" - list what applies]
**Recurring problems from past projects:** [e.g. "door schedules not matching plans", "spec sections referenced but missing", "consultant sheets on outdated backgrounds"]
**Reviewer available:** [e.g. "senior architect not on the project team"]

Build:
1. A checklist grouped by area: general and cover sheets, code analysis, life safety and egress, accessibility, coordination between disciplines, details and sections, schedules, specifications cross-checks, title blocks and seals, and permitting authority submittal requirements.
2. A cross-discipline coordination list (e.g. structural openings vs. MEP penetrations, ceiling heights vs. ductwork, grid lines and levels consistent across all sheets).
3. Items specific to the milestone I chose - what must be complete now vs. later.
4. A review workflow: who reviews, how comments are recorded and closed out, and sign-off before issue.
5. A comment log template: sheet | comment | category | severity | assigned to | resolved (Y/N) | back-checked by.

Keep items as checkable yes/no questions. Do not state code requirements from memory - phrase them as checks against the adopted code [VERIFY AGAINST ADOPTED CODE]. The checklist supports, but does not replace, review by the licensed professional in responsible charge.
variables: e.g. "senior architect not on the project team"

title: Create a quality inspection checklist for a product or service
description: A practical inspection checklist with clear pass/fail criteria, sampling guidance, and what to do when something fails.
content:
Help me create a quality inspection checklist.

**What's being inspected:** [e.g. "incoming pallets", "finished units before shipping", "completed field service job", "hotel room after cleaning"]
**Specifications or standards:** [PASTE SPECS, DRAWINGS, CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS, OR DESCRIBE]
**Common defects or complaints:** [WHAT GOES WRONG]
**Who inspects and how much time they have:** [ROLE, MINUTES PER CHECK]
**Volume:** [units per day/shift]

Build:
1. A checklist of 10-20 items in the order the inspector would naturally check them. For each: what to check | how (look, measure, test) | pass criteria with tolerances or a clear description | tool needed.
2. Critical vs. minor items: which failures stop shipment or need immediate escalation.
3. Sampling: how many to check and how often, and when to tighten sampling (after a failure, new supplier, new operator).
4. What to do on a fail: quarantine, label, record, notify, and who decides on rework or reject.
5. A recording format so results can be trended later.
6. Ideas for visual aids (photos of good vs. bad) for the hardest-to-judge items.

Use the specs I give; where a tolerance or criterion is missing, mark [DEFINE SPEC] instead of guessing. For regulated products, align with the applicable standard and our quality system.
variables: PASTE SPECS, DRAWINGS, CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS, OR DESCRIBE

title: Create a risk register with mitigations
description: Identifies, scores, and plans responses to project or business risks.
content:
Role: Act as a delivery lead building and analysing the project risk register.

Context: Project scope, approach and phase: [SCOPE_PHASE]. Known risk sources (technical, resource, external, commercial, change, dependency): [RISK_SOURCES]. Risk scale and appetite: [SCALE_APPETITE]. Schedule and budget baselines: [BASELINES]. Contingency available (time / budget): [CONTINGENCY]. Lessons from similar projects: [LESSONS].

Goal: Give the project board a clear view of the risk exposure and a credible plan to keep it within appetite.

Task: Produce: (1) the risk register - each risk with cause, trigger, likelihood, impact (schedule/cost/quality), score, and proximity; (2) a response per risk (avoid / reduce / transfer / accept) with the specific actions, owner and cost; (3) contingency plans for the top risks with the trigger that activates them and the reserve they draw on; (4) the overall exposure vs contingency and whether it is within appetite; (5) the 5 risks to review weekly.

Constraints: Score consistently on the given scale; base likelihood on evidence or the lessons, not optimism. Contingency plans must name a concrete trigger, not 'if things go wrong'. Make clear where residual risk still exceeds appetite.

Examples: Register row: 'Risk: key integration partner delivers late. Cause: their competing priorities. Trigger: no API spec by [date]. L: high, I: 3-wk slip. Response: reduce - weekly joint checkpoint + parallel stub build. Owner: [name]. Contingency: if trigger hits, activate stub (draws 2 wks reserve).'

Format: Sections: Risk register (table) | Responses & costs | Contingency plans (trigger -> action -> reserve) | Exposure vs contingency | Weekly-review list. ~700 words.

Verification: Recompute total potential schedule/cost exposure of the un-mitigated top risks and compare to contingency; flag risks scored on assumption alone.

Validation: Stress-test as a sceptical project board: if the top two risks both materialise, does the contingency actually cover it? State the honest answer and the pre-emptive move.

title: Create a role-based IT setup checklist for new hires
description: Builds a provisioning checklist per role so every new starter gets the right accounts, devices, and access on day one.
content:
Create a role-based IT provisioning checklist for new hires.

**Roles we hire for:** [e.g. "sales rep, engineer, finance analyst, store manager"]
**Core systems everyone gets:** [e.g. "M365, Slack, HR portal, password manager"]
**Role-specific systems:** [WHICH systems for which role, with permission level if known]
**Devices:** [laptop models, phones, peripherals; imaging or zero-touch tool like Autopilot or Jamf]
**Lead time we get from HR:** [e.g. "5 business days"]
**Security requirements:** [MFA, security training, policy acknowledgments, device encryption]

Build:
1. A timeline from offer accepted to end of week one: what IT does at each point (order device, create accounts, assign licenses, enroll device, ship or set up desk).
2. A base checklist for every hire.
3. An add-on checklist per role, applying least privilege: start with the minimum and list who approves extra access.
4. Day-one steps for the new hire: sign in, set up MFA, password manager, and where to get help, written so a non-technical person can follow it.

title: Create a tagging taxonomy so our team's documents are easy to find
description: Designs categories, tags, synonyms, and required metadata so people can find documents in SharePoint, Confluence, Notion, or a shared drive.
content:
Help me design a taxonomy so our team's knowledge is easy to search and find.

**Team and what we do:** [e.g. "12-person marketing ops team"]
**Where the documents live:** [e.g. SharePoint, Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, Teams]
**Sample of what we have:** [PASTE a list of document titles, folder names, or short descriptions - 30+ is ideal]
**How people search today and what goes wrong:** [e.g. "people can't tell which version is current", "everything is in 'Misc'"]
**Who will maintain it:** [ROLE]

Design:
1. **Top-level categories** (5-9) based on how people look for things (by task, process, client, or product - say which principle you chose and why).
2. **Tag sets (facets)** - e.g. document type, process, audience, product, status, year. For each: allowed values, a definition, and an example.
3. **Synonyms** - terms people search for mapped to the official tag (e.g. "PO" -> "purchase order").
4. **Required metadata** per document: owner, last reviewed date, status (draft / current / archived).
5. **Mapping** - show where 10-15 of my sample documents would sit.
6. **Governance** - who can add new tags, how often to review, how to retire old content.
7. **Retagging plan** - how to apply the taxonomy to existing content in stages, starting with the most-used documents.
8. **A one-page guide** for the team: which tags to use, with examples.

Keep it simple enough to use without training: no more than 3 levels deep and no more than 6 tag sets. Use only tags the sample supports; mark anything you are guessing about our content as [CONFIRM].
