- A table: Issue | Where it appears | Why it matters | How to fix it.
- A method for redoing it myself: read, cover the source, explain it aloud, write from memory, then compare.
- The correct in-text citation format for my style, using my source details.

Do not write a new paraphrase for me. If the passage should simply be quoted instead (because the exact wording matters), say so.

title: Clean pasted text of junk symbols, duplicates, and links
description: Strip decorative characters, repeated lines, leftover markup, and URLs from copied text while keeping every meaningful word.
content:
Clean up the text below so only the meaningful content remains.

**Text:** [PASTE TEXT]
**Where it came from:** [e.g. "AI chat output", "PDF copy-paste", "web page", "exported notes"]
**Remove URLs?** [yes - delete them / yes - keep the link text only / no]
**Keep formatting for:** [plain text / Markdown / email]

Remove:
- Decorative characters and box-drawing symbols (e.g. ░ ═ │ ■ >>> ###) and divider lines.
- Leftover markup or placeholders that carry no meaning (e.g. "null", "{...}", stray HTML tags, "### start ###").
- Exact or near-exact repeated lines, headings, and paragraphs (keep the first, most complete version).
- Broken line breaks in the middle of sentences, extra blank lines, and double spaces.
- URLs, if I asked for that, in any form (http, https, www, bare domains).

Keep:
- Every sentence that carries meaning, word for word. Do not summarize, shorten, reword, or fix grammar.
- Headings, paragraphs, numbered steps, and bullet lists that show the real structure.
- Numbers, names, code snippets, and quotes exactly as written.

Return:
1. The cleaned text only, ready to paste.
2. A short list of what you removed (e.g. "14 divider lines, 3 duplicated paragraphs, 6 URLs") and anything you were unsure about, so I can check it.
variables: yes - delete them / yes - keep the link text only / no

title: Clean up and structure a messy document
description: Reorganizes and formats messy notes, pasted text, or exported content into a clean, consistent document.
content:
Turn the content below into a clean, well-structured document.

**Output format:** [Markdown / Google Doc–ready / plain text / table]
**Purpose:** [e.g. "internal wiki page", "client handout", "notes I can scan later"]

**Content:**
[PASTE — notes, copied web text, PDF text, transcript]

Do this:
- Fix broken line breaks, stray characters, and inconsistent spacing or numbering.
- Group related content under clear headings in a logical order.
- Convert lists of comparable items into tables where it helps.
- Keep all original information and wording — do not summarize, add, or remove content unless it is an exact duplicate (list any duplicates you removed at the end).
- Flag anything garbled or incomplete as [UNCLEAR: …].
variables: Markdown / Google Doc–ready / plain text / table
PASTE — notes, copied web text, PDF text, transcript

title: Connect the chapters of my nonfiction book into one story
description: Finds the throughline across your chapters and writes transitions, callbacks, and exercises that make the book feel unified.
content:
Help me make my nonfiction book read as one connected whole instead of a set of separate essays.

**Book topic and promise to the reader:** [WHAT THE READER WILL GET]
**Framework or method it is built on:** [e.g. "a Jungian process for everyday life", "a 5-step budgeting method", "none"]
**Chapter list with a one-line summary each:** [PASTE]
**Exercises or practices in the book:** [LIST, by chapter]
**What feels disconnected:** [e.g. "chapters 4-6 feel like detours", "the exercises feel bolted on"]

Give me:
1. The throughline: the single transformation or question that carries the reader from chapter 1 to the end, in one sentence, plus 2 alternatives.
2. A chapter map table: Chapter | Role in the arc (foundation / deepening / turning point / integration) | Concept it builds on | Concept it sets up | Recurring motif or story.
3. Chapters that don't fit the arc, with options: move, merge, cut, or reframe.
4. Transitions: a draft closing paragraph and opening paragraph for each chapter boundary that hands the reader forward.
5. Recurring threads: 2-3 stories, case examples, or images that can return across chapters, and where.
6. Exercise integration: how each exercise builds on the previous one, so practices form a progression, with a brief reflection prompt linking them.
7. Reflection questions I can ask myself while revising to test cohesion.

Keep my voice and ideas; do not add new claims, research, or quotes. If a psychological or health method is involved, keep exercises within self-help and suggest a note pointing readers to professional support where appropriate.

title: Design the structure of a report before writing it
description: Creates a decision-focused outline for a report so the writing is easy and the reader gets what they need.
content:
Act as a strategy consultant who designs reports around decisions rather than information volume.

**Context**
I need a report about [TOPIC] for [AUDIENCE]. The report should help the reader understand the issue and act.

**Task**
First identify the report's purpose, key decision, audience needs, evidence required, and logical narrative. Then create the structure.

**Format**
Return:
- Report objective
- Audience
- Core decision
- Recommended table of contents
- Purpose of each section
- Evidence required
- Key question answered by each section

title: Develop a stronger thesis statement for my essay
description: Coaching questions and feedback that help you sharpen your own thesis into a clear, arguable claim.
content:
Help me develop a strong thesis statement for my essay by coaching me, not by writing it for me.

**Assignment prompt:** [PASTE IT]
**Essay type:** [argumentative / analytical / compare-and-contrast / research / literary analysis]
**My topic and what I've read or found so far:** [NOTES, SOURCES, IDEAS]
**My current thesis attempt(s):** [PASTE ONE OR MORE, even if rough]
**Length of the essay:** [e.g. "5 pages", "1,200 words"]

Do this:
1. Test my current thesis against these checks: Does it take a position someone could disagree with? Is it specific, not a statement of fact or a topic? Does it answer the actual prompt? Is it narrow enough for the length? Does it hint at the reasons I'll use?
2. For each check that fails, explain why in one or two sentences.
3. Ask me 4-6 questions that push my thinking, e.g. "So what?", "According to whom?", "What's the strongest counterargument?"
4. Show me the pattern of a strong thesis using a different, unrelated topic, so I can see the structure without copying.

Return the checklist results, your questions, and the unrelated example. When I reply with a revision, review it again with the same checks. Do not write a thesis on my topic for me.
variables: PASTE ONE OR MORE, even if rough

title: Edit my writing to be clearer and tighter — in my own voice
description: Line-edits your draft for clarity and flow while keeping it sounding like you.
content:
Edit the text below so it is clearer, tighter, and easier to read — without making it sound like someone else wrote it.

**Who will read it:** [AUDIENCE]
**What it needs to achieve:** [PURPOSE — e.g. "get approval", "explain a change", "persuade readers to sign up"]

**Text:**
[PASTE TEXT]

How to edit:
- Keep my voice, vocabulary, and point of view. Edit like an editor, not a ghostwriter.
- Cut filler, repetition, and hedging. Shorten long sentences. Replace vague words with specific ones.
- Fix structure only where the reader would get lost (order of ideas, paragraph breaks, missing transitions).
- Do not add new facts, claims, or examples.

Return:
1. **Edited version** — clean, ready to use.
2. **Key changes** — 3–5 bullets on what you changed and why.
3. **Still unclear** — anything I should clarify myself because only I know the answer.

title: Escalate an unresolved complaint to a regulator or ombudsman
description: Turns a complaint a company ignored into a well-organized escalation to the right ombudsman, regulator, or consumer agency.
content:
Help me escalate a complaint that the company didn't resolve.

**Company and industry:** [e.g. my bank, energy supplier, phone company, insurer, airline, landlord agency]
**What went wrong:** [the original problem, with dates]
**What I've done so far:** [each contact: date, method, who, what they said - paste key emails]
**Their final response, if any:** [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE, or "no reply after X weeks"]
**What I want now:** [e.g. refund of AMOUNT, correction, compensation, an apology, a fixed service]
**My location:** [COUNTRY/STATE]

Steps:
1. Identify the kinds of bodies that typically handle complaints for this industry where I live (e.g. an ombudsman, a sector regulator, a consumer protection agency, a state attorney general's office). Mark names [CONFIRM] unless you're certain, and note that many require me to complain to the company first and wait a set time.
2. Check whether I seem to have completed the company's complaint process; if not, tell me what step is missing.
3. Build a clear timeline of events from my notes.
4. Draft the escalation: who I am, the company, the issue in two sentences, the timeline, what the company did or didn't do, the outcome I want, and a list of attached evidence.

Rules: factual, calm, specific. Use only facts and amounts I provide. Keep the summary under 400 words.

Return: the timeline table, the escalation text, an evidence checklist, and what to expect after filing. This is general information, not legal advice.
variables: PASTE OR SUMMARIZE, or "no reply after X weeks"

title: Fix broken words and line breaks in text copied from a PDF
description: Rejoins words split by hyphens and line breaks while keeping real hyphenated words and the original formatting intact.
content:
Clean up text I copied from a PDF or scan so it reads normally.

**Text:** [PASTE TEXT]
**Format to keep:** [plain text / Markdown / keep the existing headings and lists]
**Language:** [e.g. English]

Fix only these problems:
1. Words split across lines with a hyphen (e.g. "infor- mation" or "infor-\nmation") - rejoin them into one word.
2. Real compound words and hyphenated terms (e.g. "well-known", "COVID-19", "long-term") - keep the hyphen. If you cannot tell whether a hyphen is real, keep it and list the word at the end.
3. Hard line breaks in the middle of sentences - join them into normal paragraphs, but keep real paragraph breaks, headings, list items, and table rows.
4. Stray page numbers, running headers, or footers repeated in the text - remove them and list what you removed.
5. Obvious extraction artifacts like doubled spaces or ligature errors (e.g. "ﬁ" shown as a broken character).

Rules: do not reword, correct grammar, change spelling, or summarize anything. The output must contain the same words in the same order.

Return:
1. The cleaned text.
2. A short list of uncertain hyphens and anything removed, so I can check them.
variables: plain text / Markdown / keep the existing headings and lists

title: Get brutally honest feedback on my draft or idea
description: A candid, specific critique of a draft, plan, or idea — what works, what doesn't, and how to fix it.
content:
Give me honest, specific feedback on the work below. I want critique, not praise.

**What it is:** [e.g. blog draft, pitch, essay, business idea, cover letter]
**Who it's for:** [AUDIENCE]
**What success looks like:** [GOAL]
**How harsh:** [gentle / direct / brutal]

**Work:**
[PASTE]

Evaluate:
1. **Overall verdict** — does it achieve its goal? One paragraph, no softening.
2. **Biggest problems** — the 3 issues that most hurt it, ranked, each with a quoted example and a specific fix.
3. **Clarity and structure** — where a reader would get confused, bored, or lost.
4. **Argument/substance** — weak claims, missing evidence, gaps in logic.
5. **What's working** — only what is genuinely strong, so I keep it.
6. **Top 3 edits to make next.**

Be specific: point to exact sentences. Do not rewrite the whole thing unless I ask.
variables: e.g. blog draft, pitch, essay, business idea, cover letter

title: Get feedback on my lab report before I submit it
description: Section-by-section feedback on your lab report's structure, data presentation, and reasoning so you can fix it yourself.
content:
Review my lab report and give me feedback so I can improve it myself.

**Course and level:** [e.g. "AP Biology", "General Chemistry II lab"]
**Lab instructions and required format:** [PASTE, including required sections and citation style]
**My lab report draft:** [PASTE, including tables or a description of graphs]
**Grading rubric, if available:** [PASTE]

Check each section:
- **Title and abstract:** does the abstract state purpose, method, key result, and conclusion briefly?
- **Introduction:** background, purpose, and a testable hypothesis.
- **Methods:** could someone repeat it? Past tense, no step-by-step list unless required.
- **Results:** data in labeled tables and graphs (titles, axes, units, significant figures), with text describing trends but not interpreting them yet.
- **Discussion:** does it interpret results, compare them with the hypothesis and expected values, calculate percent error if relevant, and name specific sources of error (not just "human error")?
- **Conclusion and references.**

Return:
1. A table: Section | What's working | What's missing or unclear | How to fix it.
2. The 3 most important fixes.
3. Any claims that go beyond what my data shows.

Rules: do not change my data or calculations; if a number looks wrong, point it out and ask me to recheck. Do not write sections for me; explain what each needs.
variables: PASTE, including required sections and citation style
PASTE, including tables or a description of graphs

title: Make AI-sounding text sound natural and human
description: Removes the robotic tells from AI drafts so the writing sounds like a real person.
content:
Rewrite the text below so it reads like a thoughtful person wrote it, not an AI.

**Where it will be used:** [e.g. LinkedIn post, email to a client, blog, essay]
**The voice I want:** [e.g. "plain and friendly", "confident expert", "dry and witty"]

**Text:**
[PASTE TEXT]

Remove the common AI tells:
- Stock openers and closers ("In today's fast-paced world", "In conclusion", "I hope this helps").
- Buzzwords and inflated words (delve, leverage, seamless, robust, unlock, elevate, game-changer, landscape, tapestry).
- Formulaic patterns: "It's not X, it's Y", rule-of-three lists everywhere, every paragraph the same length, excessive em dashes.
- Generic claims with no specifics; hedging that says nothing.

Then make it human:
- Vary sentence length. Use concrete details and plain words.
- Keep my meaning, facts, and structure unless a change clearly helps.
- Do not add fake personal anecdotes or invented facts.

Return the rewritten text, then a short list of the patterns you removed.
variables: e.g. LinkedIn post, email to a client, blog, essay

title: Plan where to add images and figures in my book or report
description: A section-by-section visual plan showing where diagrams, charts, and photos would help readers most, with briefs for each.
content:
Review my manuscript and plan where images, diagrams, and other visuals would help readers.

**Manuscript:** [PASTE TEXT, or chapter-by-chapter summaries]
**Type and audience:** [e.g. "health guide for newly diagnosed adults", "technical report for managers", "children's science book"]
**Format:** [print / ebook / both; color or black and white; page size]
**Visual budget:** [e.g. "about 1 visual per chapter", "up to 40 figures", "no budget for custom illustration"]
**Style:** [e.g. "clean line diagrams", "photos", "friendly illustrations"]

For each chapter or section:
1. **Where:** the exact paragraph or concept the visual should sit next to.
2. **Why:** what the reader would struggle with in text alone (a process, comparison, data, anatomy, location, emotion).
3. **Visual type:** diagram, flowchart, chart, table, photo, illustration, or callout box, and why that type fits.
4. **Brief:** what it should show, labels, and the key takeaway, so an illustrator or designer can create it.
5. **Caption draft** and alt text.
6. **Priority:** must-have / nice-to-have.

Then give me:
- A summary table: Chapter | Location | Visual type | Purpose | Priority.
- Places where a table or bulleted summary would work better than an image.
- Sourcing notes: what needs custom creation, what could use licensed stock, and permissions to check.

For medical, scientific, or technical content, flag visuals that need expert review for accuracy.
variables: print / ebook / both; color or black and white; page size

title: Proofread for mistakes without rewriting my style
description: Catches grammar, spelling, punctuation, and consistency errors and changes nothing else.
content:
Proofread the text below. Fix only genuine errors — do not restyle or rewrite.

**Language/variant:** [e.g. US English, UK English]
**Style rules to follow (optional):** [e.g. "Oxford comma", "sentence-case headings", house style guide]

**Text:**
[PASTE TEXT]

Check for: spelling, grammar, punctuation, typos, repeated or missing words, inconsistent capitalization, numbers, names, and terminology.

Return:
1. **Corrected text** with every fix applied.
2. **Change list** as a table: | Original | Correction | Reason |
3. **Judgment calls** — places where the text is correct but could be read two ways, so I can decide.

If there are no errors, say so plainly instead of inventing changes.

title: Remove corporate jargon and buzzwords from my message
description: Strips out jargon, buzzwords, and filler so your message says plainly what you mean.
content:
Remove the corporate jargon from my message so it says plainly what I mean.

**My message:** [PASTE]
**Reader:** [WHO]
**Terms that are genuinely needed:** [e.g. "our product names", "agreed industry terms" - keep these]

Steps:
1. Find every piece of jargon, buzzword, or empty phrase, such as: leverage, synergy, align on, move the needle, bandwidth, circle back, deep dive, best-in-class, value-add, going forward, in order to, at this point in time, unlock, drive impact, holistic.
2. For each, ask what it actually means here. If it means something specific, replace it with the plain word. If it means nothing, delete it.
3. Turn vague nouns back into verbs ("make a decision" to "decide", "provide an update" to "update").
4. Replace abstract claims with the concrete detail if my message contains it ("improve efficiency" to "cut approval time from 5 days to 2"). If no detail is given, flag it [ADD SPECIFIC] rather than inventing a number.

Return:
1. **The rewritten message.**
2. **Jargon table** - | Original phrase | Replaced with | Why |
3. **Vague claims** that need a specific fact or example to be convincing.
4. **Word count** before and after.

Keep my tone, meaning, and level of formality. Don't make it casual if the original was formal.

title: Report a local problem to my city or town so it gets fixed
description: A clear, specific report about a pothole, broken streetlight, illegal dumping, or other local issue, plus how to follow up.
content:
Help me report a problem in my neighborhood to my local government.

**The problem:** [e.g. pothole, broken streetlight, missed trash collection, blocked sidewalk, overgrown lot, unsafe crossing, noise]
**Exact location:** [street address, nearest cross streets, landmarks]
**How long it's been going on:** [DATES]
**Why it matters:** [e.g. safety risk for kids walking to school, wheelchair users can't pass]
**Evidence:** [photos, dates I noticed it, others affected]
**Reported before?** [yes/no, case number if any]
**How my city takes reports:** [e.g. 311 app or line, online form, email to council office, don't know]

Give me:
1. The right type of office or service to contact, with a note to confirm on my city's official website [CONFIRM].
2. A short report (under 120 words) that fits an online form: what, where, since when, and the risk.
3. A longer version for email to a council member or department, with a clear request and a reasonable timeline.
4. A follow-up message for if nothing happens in [NUMBER] weeks, referencing my case number.
5. Tips for getting it prioritized: specific location details, photos, safety impact, and neighbors filing too.

Keep the tone constructive and factual. If the problem is an immediate danger (e.g. downed power line, gas smell, flooding), tell me to call emergency services or the utility first.
variables: street address, nearest cross streets, landmarks
photos, dates I noticed it, others affected

title: Request a disability accommodation from a business, school, or agency
description: A clear, confident request for the accessibility support you need, sharing only necessary information, with follow-up steps.
content:
Help me write a request for a disability or accessibility accommodation.

**Who I'm asking:** [e.g. my landlord, my child's school, a college disability office, a government office, a doctor's office, an event venue]
**Who needs the accommodation:** [me / my child / my parent]
**What I need:** [e.g. a ground-floor appointment, a sign language interpreter, large-print documents, extra time on tests, a service animal, a ramp, phone appointments instead of in person]
**Why, in as much detail as I'm comfortable sharing:** [how the barrier affects access - I don't need to give a diagnosis]
**Supporting documents I have:** [e.g. letter from a doctor, previous accommodation plan]
**Deadline or event date:** [DATE]
**My location:** [COUNTRY/STATE]

Requirements:
- State the request in the first two sentences and be specific about what would work.
- Explain the barrier and how the accommodation removes it. Share only what's needed - not my full medical history.
- Offer alternatives that would also work, if any.
- Ask for a reply by a date in bold and for the response in writing.
- Tone: confident and cooperative, not apologetic.

Return:
1. The request letter or email.
2. A note on rights that may apply where I live, with law names marked [CONFIRM] - general information, not legal advice.
3. What to do if they refuse or don't respond: ask for the reason in writing, propose alternatives, and where to get free help (e.g. disability rights organizations) [CONFIRM].
variables: e.g. letter from a doctor, previous accommodation plan

title: Rewrite a message or document for a senior executive
description: Rewrites for a time-poor senior reader: bottom line first, decisions clear, detail trimmed.
content:
Act as an executive communications advisor who understands how senior leaders consume information.

**Context**
I need to communicate the following information to a senior executive who has limited time and wants the key issue, business impact, and required action quickly.

**Task**
Rewrite the content for executive consumption. Lead with the most important point. Remove operational detail that does not affect the decision. Make business impact, risk, decision required, and next step explicit. Preserve facts and clearly flag anything uncertain.

**Format**
Use this structure:
- **Headline**
- **What matters**
- **Business impact**
- **Decision or action required**
- **Next step**

Keep the final message under 150 words.

**Input:** [PASTE]

title: Rewrite a message so it sounds professional
description: Turns a rough, emotional, or casual message into a clear, professional one with the same meaning.
content:
Act as an expert business communication editor who writes clear, concise, human professional communication.

**Context**
I need to send the message below to a workplace audience. My intent and facts must remain unchanged. The message may currently contain unnecessary detail, weak phrasing, jargon, or an inconsistent tone.

**Task**
Rewrite the message so it is clear, confident, concise, professional, and natural. Preserve the original meaning. Remove filler and unnecessary repetition. Strengthen the request or next step. Do not invent facts or make the message sound overly formal.

**Format**
Return:
1. **Subject or opening line**
2. **Final message**
3. **Key improvement:** one sentence explaining the biggest improvement

**Input:** [PASTE MESSAGE]

title: Rewrite a technical document for business stakeholders
description: Translates a technical document into business language: what it means, the cost, risk, and timing, and what decision is needed.
content:
Rewrite the technical document below for a business audience.

**Document:** [PASTE - e.g. architecture proposal, engineering report, IT incident review, data analysis]
**Audience:** [e.g. "department heads with no technical background"]
**What they need to do with it:** [approve budget / choose an option / understand impact / just stay informed]
**Length:** [e.g. "one page", "half the original"]

Rewrite it so that:
1. It opens with a 3-sentence summary: what this is, why it matters to the business, and what is needed from the reader.
2. Each technical point is translated into its business effect - cost, time, risk, customer impact, or capability gained.
3. Jargon is removed or explained in a few plain words the first time it appears.
4. Options are compared on business criteria (cost, risk, time to deliver, what we give up).
5. Numbers keep their exact values; round only where precision doesn't matter, and say so.

Return:
1. The rewritten document.
2. A short glossary of any technical terms that had to stay.
3. A list of points you simplified, so a technical reviewer can check the meaning is still correct.
4. Questions business readers are likely to ask, with answers drawn from the original.

Don't add claims, estimates, or benefits that aren't in the original; mark anything uncertain as [CONFIRM WITH TECHNICAL OWNER].
variables: e.g. "department heads with no technical background"

title: Rewrite my message for a global audience and non-native English readers
description: Makes a message easy to understand across countries and cultures: no idioms, clear dates, and plain international English.
content:
Rewrite my message so it works for a global audience, including people who read English as a second language.

**My message:** [PASTE]
**Where readers are based:** [COUNTRIES OR REGIONS]
**How it will be read:** [email / Teams or Slack / intranet / may be machine-translated]

Rewrite it using these rules:
1. **Plain international English** - short sentences (under 20 words), one idea each, common words.
2. **No idioms, slang, or sports metaphors** ("touch base", "ballpark", "hit it out of the park", "circle back").
3. **No ambiguous dates, times, or numbers** - write dates as 3 March 2026 style, include time zones (e.g. 15:00 CET / 09:00 ET), and state currency codes.
4. **Expand acronyms** and explain company-specific terms the first time.
5. **Avoid culture-bound references** - local holidays, humor, or assumptions about workweeks and seasons.
6. **Explicit, polite asks** - direct enough for readers who expect clarity, respectful enough for readers who expect formality.
7. **Translation-friendly** - avoid phrasal verbs where a single word works ("find out" to "learn"), and avoid sarcasm or irony.

Return:
1. **The rewritten message.**
2. **Changes made** - a short list of the idioms, dates, and terms I replaced.
3. **Cultural notes** - anything that may land differently in the regions I listed (e.g. directness, deadlines over holidays). Keep these general and avoid stereotypes.

Keep all facts and the original meaning.
variables: email / Teams or Slack / intranet / may be machine-translated

title: Rewrite text in a different tone, length, or style
description: Adapts the same message for a new tone, audience, length, or point of view without changing the facts.
content:
Rewrite the text below for a new purpose without changing its facts or intent.

**Change it to:** [TARGET — e.g. "warmer and more casual", "more direct", "half the length", "for a 10-year-old", "first person", "executive and strategic"]
**Audience:** [WHO WILL READ IT]
**Must stay exactly the same:** [names, numbers, commitments, key phrases — or "nothing specific"]

**Text:**
[PASTE TEXT]

Rules:
- Keep every fact, claim, and commitment. Add nothing new.
- Apply the change consistently from the first line to the last.
- Sound natural — no clichés, filler, or forced enthusiasm.

Return:
1. **Rewritten version.**
2. **Two alternatives** that interpret the change differently (e.g. more/less formal, shorter/longer), each labeled.
3. **One-line note** on anything you had to cut or soften to make it fit.

title: Teach AI to write in my personal style
description: Analyzes samples of your writing and produces a reusable style guide, then writes in that voice.
content:
I want you to learn how I write so you can draft in my voice.

**Samples of my writing (2–5 pieces, ideally 300+ words total):**
[PASTE SAMPLES]

**What I'll use this for:** [e.g. LinkedIn posts, client emails, newsletter]

Step 1 — Analyze my samples and describe my style precisely:
- Tone and attitude
- Sentence length and rhythm
- Vocabulary (words I use often; words I never use)
- How I open and close pieces
- Structure and formatting habits (lists, headings, paragraph length)
- Use of humor, questions, stories, data
- Quirks that make it recognizably mine

Step 2 — Turn that into a **"Write like me" style guide** of 10–15 concrete rules I can paste into future chats.

Step 3 — Write a short sample on this topic using the guide: [TOPIC]

Base everything only on the samples. If the samples are too short or inconsistent to judge something, say so rather than guessing.
variables: e.g. LinkedIn posts, client emails, newsletter

title: Translate text so it sounds native, not translated
description: Translates and localizes text for a specific audience while keeping meaning and tone.
content:
Translate the text below.

**From → to:** [SOURCE LANGUAGE] → [TARGET LANGUAGE and region, e.g. "Spanish (Mexico)"]
**Audience and context:** [e.g. "customers on our website", "formal letter to a government office", "casual message to a friend"]
**Tone:** [formal / neutral / friendly / marketing]
**Terms to keep untranslated:** [brand names, product names, technical terms]

**Text:**
[PASTE TEXT]

Rules:
- Translate meaning, not word-for-word. It should read as if written by a native speaker in that region.
- Adapt idioms, units, dates, and cultural references when a literal version would confuse the reader.
- Keep formatting (headings, lists, links) intact.

Return:
1. **Translation.**
2. **Notes** — any idioms, puns, or culturally sensitive phrases you adapted, and anything ambiguous in the original that I should confirm.
variables: brand names, product names, technical terms

title: Turn a policy or process document into an employee FAQ
description: Anticipates the questions employees and new starters will actually ask about a policy or process and answers them from the document.
content:
Turn the document below into an FAQ for the people who will use it.

**Document:** [PASTE - policy, process, procedure, system guide, or announcement]
**Who will read the FAQ:** [e.g. "all employees", "new hires in finance", "store managers"]
**Where it will live:** [intranet page, Teams or Slack post, onboarding pack, knowledge base]
**Questions people have already asked, if any:** [PASTE]

Steps:
1. Read the document as a new employee would. List the questions they would ask: what it is, does it apply to me, what do I do, by when, what if I'm an exception, who do I ask, what happens if I get it wrong.
2. Add the edge cases and "what if" questions experienced staff would ask.
3. Answer each from the document.

Return:
1. **FAQ** - 12-25 questions grouped under clear headings, phrased the way people would actually type them, each with a 1-3 sentence answer and the section of the document it comes from.
2. **Unanswered questions** - questions the document doesn't answer, marked [NEEDS ANSWER FROM ...], so the owner can fill them.
3. **Confusing parts** - places in the document likely to cause misunderstanding, with a suggested clarification.

Rules:
- Answer only from the document. Never guess at policy, entitlements, or deadlines.
- Plain language; define acronyms. Keep wording consistent with the document's terms.

title: Turn clinician instructions into a patient-friendly handout
description: Rewrites approved clinician instructions at a plain-language reading level, keeping the clinical content exactly the same and adding clear when-to-call guidance.
content:
Rewrite these clinician-approved instructions as a patient handout.

**Original instructions:** [PASTE - approved by our clinician]
**Topic:** [e.g. "preparing for a colonoscopy", "caring for a wound after a minor procedure", "what to expect at your first PT visit"]
**Audience:** [e.g. adults, parents of young children, older adults]
**Reading level target:** [e.g. 6th grade]
**Language(s):** [e.g. English; Spanish version to be professionally translated]
**Our contact details and after-hours line:** [DETAILS]

Rules:
- Keep every clinical instruction, number, time, and dose exactly as written. Do not add, remove, or soften any clinical content. If something is unclear or seems contradictory, flag it as [CLINICIAN TO CONFIRM] instead of resolving it.
- Short sentences, everyday words, active voice. Define any medical term you must keep.
- Organize as: What this is for, Before, Day of, After, When to call us, When to call 911 or go to the emergency room. Use only warning signs given in the original; if none are given, insert [CLINICIAN TO ADD WARNING SIGNS].
- Use numbered steps for sequences and checkboxes for things to bring.
- Fit on one double-sided page.

Return:
1. The handout.
2. A list of every change from the original, so the clinician can approve it quickly.
3. The estimated reading level and any words still above target.

The handout must be reviewed and approved by the responsible clinician before use.
variables: e.g. adults, parents of young children, older adults
e.g. English; Spanish version to be professionally translated

title: Turn complex or technical writing into plain language
description: Makes dense, technical, or legal text easy for a non-expert to understand.
content:
Act as an expert plain-language editor.

**Context**
The content is technically correct but may be difficult for a smart non-specialist to understand.

**Task**
Rewrite it using simple language, shorter sentences, concrete examples, and minimal jargon. Preserve the technical meaning. Do not oversimplify important nuance.

**Format**
Return:
- Simplified version
- Terms that were simplified
- One real-world example

**Text:** [PASTE]

title: Turn information into a clear recommendation
description: Builds a recommendation with options, reasoning, risks, and a clear ask.
content:
Act as a business strategy advisor.

**Context**
I need to turn the information below into a clear recommendation for a decision-maker.

**Task**
Define the problem, summarize relevant evidence, clarify options and trade-offs, identify decision criteria, and formulate a recommendation only from the evidence provided. Flag uncertainties that could materially change the recommendation.

**Format**
Use:
- Decision required
- Situation
- Key evidence
- Options
- Trade-offs
- Recommendation
- Risks
- Next steps

**Information:** [PASTE]

title: Turn my notes or ideas into a polished article
description: Converts rough notes, bullets, or a transcript into a structured, publishable article or thought-leadership piece.
content:
Act as an experienced thought-leadership editor.

**Context**
I have rough notes and want to turn them into a useful, credible article for [AUDIENCE].

**Task**
Develop a coherent argument from the notes. Create a strong opening, logical progression, practical examples, useful insights, and a conclusion that reinforces the main idea. Do not invent supporting evidence.

**Format**
Return:
- Headline
- Opening hook
- Article
- 3 key takeaways
- Suggested CTA

**Notes:** [PASTE]

title: Turn my rough notes into a structured business report
description: Organizes messy notes, bullets, and findings into a clear business report with an executive summary, sections, and next steps.
content:
Turn my notes into a well-structured report.

**Notes:** [PASTE - bullets, fragments, numbers, quotes, half-sentences are fine]
**Report purpose:** [e.g. "monthly update to leadership", "findings from our pilot", "incident summary"]
**Audience:** [WHO WILL READ IT]
**Length:** [e.g. "2 pages", "under 800 words"]
**Template or headings to follow, if any:** [OPTIONAL]

Do this:
1. Work out the main message my notes support and put it in a short executive summary (3-5 sentences) at the top.
2. Group the notes into logical sections with clear headings (for example: background, what we found, what it means, recommendations, next steps).
3. Write in full, plain sentences. Use tables for comparisons or numbers, bullets only for lists of 3+ items.
4. End with next steps: action, owner, date.

Then return:
- The report.
- **Gaps:** points where my notes are thin, contradictory, or missing data, marked in the text as [ADD: ...].
- **Cut list:** anything from my notes you left out and why.

Rules:
- Use only the facts, numbers, and names in my notes. Do not invent figures, quotes, or results.
- Keep my meaning; if a note is ambiguous, ask in a [CONFIRM: ...] marker rather than guess.

title: Turn my scattered thoughts into a clear business argument
description: Shapes rough ideas into a structured argument with a clear claim, reasons, evidence, and answers to likely objections.
content:
Help me turn my scattered thoughts into a clear, logical business argument.

**My thoughts:** [PASTE NOTES, BULLETS, OR A BRAIN DUMP]
**What I want the reader to agree to or do:** [e.g. "fund a pilot", "change our pricing", "hire another analyst"]
**Who I need to convince:** [ROLE, and what they care about - cost, risk, growth, customers]
**Evidence I have:** [DATA, EXAMPLES, CUSTOMER FEEDBACK, BENCHMARKS - or "none yet"]
**Format I'll use:** [email / one-page memo / talking points / slide]

Steps:
1. State my main claim in one sentence. If my notes support more than one claim, show the options and recommend one.
2. Find the 2 to 4 strongest reasons that support it, grouped so they don't overlap.
3. Attach evidence to each reason from what I gave. Where a reason has no evidence, mark it [NEEDS EVIDENCE] and suggest what would prove it.
4. Identify the strongest counterarguments and how to answer each honestly.
5. Spot weak links: assumptions, logical leaps, or points that undercut the case.

Return:
1. **The argument outline** - claim, reasons, evidence, counterarguments with responses, and the ask.
2. **A draft** in the format I chose, leading with the claim and ending with a specific ask.
3. **Weak spots** - what a skeptical reader would challenge first.

Don't invent data or examples. I decide whether the case is strong enough to make.
variables: PASTE NOTES, BULLETS, OR A BRAIN DUMP
DATA, EXAMPLES, CUSTOMER FEEDBACK, BENCHMARKS - or "none yet"
email / one-page memo / talking points / slide

title: Write a babysitter info sheet with emergency details
description: A one-page guide for sitters with routines, house rules, allergies, and step-by-step emergency instructions.
content:
Write a clear, one-page information sheet for our babysitter or caregiver.

**Kids:** [names, ages]
**Routines:** [meals, naps, bedtime steps, screen rules]
**Allergies, medical conditions, medications:** [DETAILS, including where medicines are kept and how to use them]
**House rules and things to avoid:** [e.g. "no snacks after 7", "back door sticks", "dog not allowed upstairs"]
**Contacts:** [parents' numbers, backup adult, neighbor, pediatrician]
**Home address and nearest cross street:** [ADDRESS]
**Practical info:** [Wi-Fi, where the first-aid kit, flashlight, and fire extinguisher are]

Organize it into:
1. At-a-glance box: address, parent numbers, emergency number for my country, allergies in bold.
2. Each child: routine, comfort tips, what calms them down.
3. Food and bedtime schedule in a short table.
4. House rules (sitter-friendly, not a long list).
5. "If something goes wrong": step-by-step for an allergic reaction, an injury, a child who won't settle, a lost child, and a fire. Always: call emergency services first for anything serious, then call me.
6. A blank notes section for the sitter to tell me how the evening went.

Use short lines and headings so it's readable in a hurry. Use [ADD] wherever I haven't given details; never make up medical instructions.
variables: meals, naps, bedtime steps, screen rules
parents' numbers, backup adult, neighbor, pediatrician

title: Write a basis of design narrative for an engineering project
description: A clear basis of design document that records design criteria, assumptions, codes, and system choices for client and team review.
content:
Help me write a basis of design (BOD) narrative for an engineering project.

**Project:** [type, size, location, occupancy or use]
**Discipline(s):** [e.g. "mechanical and plumbing", "structural", "civil and stormwater", "electrical"]
**Owner's project requirements:** [PASTE or summarize - performance goals, budget, sustainability targets, maintenance preferences]
**Design criteria:** [e.g. design temperatures, loads, occupancy, rainfall event, soil bearing values from the geotechnical report, redundancy requirements]
**Codes, standards, and guidelines:** [list with editions, as adopted by the jurisdiction]
**Systems selected and alternatives considered:** [WHAT and WHY]
**Assumptions and open items:** [LIST]
**Audience:** [owner, commissioning agent, permitting authority, internal team]

Write the BOD with these sections:
1. Project overview and purpose of this document.
2. Design criteria, in a table with values, units, and source (owner, code, report, or engineering judgment).
3. Codes and standards list with editions.
4. System descriptions: what each system is, how it works, and why it was chosen over alternatives, in plain language.
5. Assumptions, with who must confirm each and by when.
6. Interfaces with other disciplines.
7. Open items and decisions needed from the owner.
8. Revision history.

Keep the writing plain enough for a non-engineer owner to follow. Use only values I provide - mark anything missing [ENGINEER TO PROVIDE] and never fill in design values, loads, or code requirements from memory. Final content must be reviewed by the engineer of record.
variables: type, size, location, occupancy or use
list with editions, as adopted by the jurisdiction

title: Write a clear how-to guide or user manual
description: Produces step-by-step instructions people can actually follow, with prerequisites, troubleshooting, and warnings.
content:
Write a how-to guide that a first-time user can follow without help.

**What it explains:** [PRODUCT / PROCESS / TASK]
**Who will use it:** [AUDIENCE and their skill level]
**Format:** [one-page quick start / full manual / help-center article]
**Source material:** [PASTE notes, existing docs, feature list, or steps as I know them]

Structure:
1. What this guide helps you do (one sentence) and what you need before starting.
2. Numbered steps — one action per step, in the order the user does them, with the expected result after key steps.
3. Tips and warnings placed exactly where they matter.
4. Troubleshooting: common problems → likely cause → fix.
5. FAQ (only questions a real user would ask).

Rules:
- Plain language; define any term the reader might not know.
- Use only the information I've given. Where a step is unclear or missing, insert [CONFIRM: …] instead of guessing.
variables: one-page quick start / full manual / help-center article

title: Write a complaint that gets a problem fixed
description: A firm, factual complaint or dispute letter to a company, landlord, or service provider that asks for a specific remedy.
content:
Help me write a complaint that gets results.

**To:** [COMPANY / LANDLORD / SERVICE — and the department if known]
**What happened (with dates):** [FACTS IN ORDER]
**What I've already tried:** [calls, emails, reference numbers]
**Impact on me:** [cost, time, inconvenience]
**What I want:** [refund / replacement / repair / compensation / apology — be specific]
**Evidence I have:** [receipts, photos, emails]
**Channel:** [email / letter / web form / social media]

Write a complaint that:
- Opens with the issue and the exact remedy I'm requesting.
- Lays out a clear, factual timeline. No insults, no exaggeration.
- References my evidence and any order/account numbers.
- Sets a reasonable deadline for a response and states the next step if it isn't resolved (e.g. escalation, chargeback, regulator or ombudsman).
- Stays under 300 words.

Then give me a 2-sentence version for a phone call or chat, and tell me which consumer-protection body usually handles this kind of issue in [COUNTRY] so I can check it myself (I'll verify — this isn't legal advice).
variables: COMPANY / LANDLORD / SERVICE — and the department if known
email / letter / web form / social media

title: Write a concise executive summary for an audit report
description: Condenses a full audit report into a one-page summary with an overall opinion, key messages, and management commitments.
content:
Help me write the executive summary for an internal audit report.

**Audit area and objectives:** [WHAT we reviewed and why]
**Scope and period:** [IN and OUT of scope]
**Findings:** [PASTE titles, ratings, and short descriptions]
**Positive observations:** [what is working well]
**Management action plans:** [owner roles and dates]
**Overall rating scale:** [PASTE definitions, e.g. Satisfactory / Needs Improvement / Unsatisfactory]
**Readers:** [e.g. CFO, audit committee, business unit head]

Write:
1. **Overall opinion** - the rating and one or two sentences justifying it against the scale definitions.
2. **Why it matters** - the business impact in plain terms, 2-3 sentences.
3. **Key findings** - the most important 3-5 as one-sentence bullets, highest risk first, each linking to the business consequence.
4. **What is working well** - 1-3 genuine positives, specific not generic.
5. **Management's commitments** - headline actions and target dates.
6. **Themes** - any pattern across findings (e.g. ownership, manual processes, system limitations).

Rules:
- One page maximum (about 350 words).
- No audit jargon without explanation; write for a busy executive.
- The opinion must be consistent with the findings and the rating scale - flag if it is not.
- Use only the facts I gave you; mark gaps [ADD].
variables: PASTE titles, ratings, and short descriptions
e.g. CFO, audit committee, business unit head

title: Write a correction or clarification for a published story
description: A clear, proportionate correction notice, the fixed copy, and an internal note on how the error happened.
content:
Help me correct an error in a story we already published.

**Original published text:** [PASTE THE WRONG PASSAGE, headline, or caption]
**What is actually correct, and how we know:** [THE CORRECT FACT and its source]
**Where it appeared:** [web, print, newsletter, social posts, syndication partners]
**Who raised it:** [reader, subject, internal - and any complaint wording]
**Our corrections policy:** [PASTE OR SUMMARIZE, e.g. "note at the foot of the article, dated"]

First decide: is this a correction (a factual error), a clarification (accurate but misleading or unclear), or an editor's note (a larger problem with sourcing or fairness)? Explain your choice.

Then write:
1. The corrected passage for the article.
2. The correction notice: state what was wrong and what is right, briefly and plainly. Do not repeat a damaging false claim in detail, do not bury the fix, and do not over-apologize or blame the reader.
3. Versions for each place it ran (print corrections column, a reply or update for social posts, a note to syndication partners).
4. A short reply to the person who raised it.
5. An internal note: how the error got through, and one change to the editing process that would catch it next time.

If the error involves an allegation about a person or a legal risk, flag it for our lawyer before publishing the correction. Use only the facts I give you; mark gaps [CONFIRM].
variables: PASTE THE WRONG PASSAGE, headline, or caption
THE CORRECT FACT and its source
web, print, newsletter, social posts, syndication partners
reader, subject, internal - and any complaint wording

title: Write a course catalog description that gets people to enroll
description: Learner-focused catalog copy, a short promo blurb, and enrollment message that sell the value of a training course.
content:
Write the catalog listing and promotional copy for my training course.

**Course title (current):** [TITLE]
**Who it is for:** [ROLES, LEVEL, PREREQUISITES]
**Objectives:** [LIST]
**Format, length, and schedule:** [DETAILS]
**What learners will be able to do afterward:** [JOB OUTCOMES]
**Why people might not enroll:** [e.g. "too busy", "think they know it", "past courses were boring"]
**Where it will appear:** [LMS catalog, intranet, email, Slack/Teams]

Writing rules:
- Lead with the learner's problem or payoff, not the topic or the course history.
- Use "you". Describe outcomes as things people do on the job.
- Be specific about time commitment and format so people can plan.
- No hype words ("transformational", "unlock your potential"). Do not promise outcomes the course cannot guarantee (e.g. promotions).
- Make the "who this is not for" clear to reduce wrong-fit enrollments.

Return:
1. Three title options that say what learners will be able to do.
2. A catalog description (100-150 words) with: hook, what you will be able to do (3-5 bullets), format and time, who it is for, prerequisites.
3. A 40-word promo blurb.
4. A short Slack/Teams announcement.
5. 5 keywords or tags so it shows up in LMS search.

title: Write a heartfelt message for any occasion
description: Birthday, thank-you, congratulations, condolence, or get-well messages that sound personal, not generic.
content:
Help me write a personal message.

**Occasion:** [birthday / thank-you / congratulations / condolence / get well / farewell / apology]
**To:** [NAME and relationship — e.g. "my aunt", "a colleague I barely know", "my best friend"]
**Where it goes:** [card / text / email / speech / social post]
**Details that make it personal:** [shared memories, what they did, inside jokes, what I appreciate about them]
**Tone:** [warm / funny / formal / simple]
**Length:** [one line / short paragraph / longer]

Write 3 versions with different approaches (e.g. sincere, light, short). Each must use at least one of my specific details — no greeting-card clichés. For condolence messages, keep it simple and sincere: no silver linings, no "everything happens for a reason".
variables: card / text / email / speech / social post

title: Write a lay summary of my research for the public or funders
description: Explains my study's findings accurately in plain language for funders, press offices, or patients, without overstating results.
content:
Write a plain-language (lay) summary of my research.

**Paper abstract or findings:** [PASTE]
**Audience:** [e.g. "funder's public website", "university press office", "patients and caregivers", "policymakers"]
**Length and format required:** [e.g. "150 words", "blog post of 600 words", "3 bullet points"]
**Why it matters in everyday terms:** [YOUR VIEW]
**What it does NOT show:** [limits people might misread, e.g. "a mouse study", "correlation only", "small pilot"]

Rules:
- Reading level around grade 8; define or replace every technical term.
- Answer in order: what was the question, what did we do, what did we find, why does it matter, what happens next.
- Use concrete comparisons for numbers (e.g. "about 1 in 5 people") and keep them accurate.
- Match certainty to the evidence: no "cure", "proves", or "breakthrough". Name the study type (e.g. animal, observational, early-stage).
- If this involves health, add that people should not change treatment based on the study and should talk to their clinician.

Return the summary, a one-sentence version for social media, a suggested headline that is accurate rather than sensational, and a list of any phrases a journalist might over-interpret.
variables: e.g. "150 words", "blog post of 600 words", "3 bullet points"

title: Write a methods section another researcher could replicate
description: Turns my notes into a complete methods section another researcher could replicate, with gaps flagged.
content:
Write the methods section of my paper from my notes.

**Field and target journal style:** [e.g. "psychology, APA 7", "biomedical", "computer science"]
**Study design:** [DETAILS]
**Participants, samples, or data sources:** [recruitment, inclusion/exclusion, dates, setting]
**Materials, instruments, or equipment:** [names, versions, validation, settings]
**Procedure:** [step by step]
**Analysis:** [software and versions, models, tests, handling of missing data and outliers]
**Ethics approval and preregistration:** [IDs or "none"]
**Relevant reporting guideline:** [e.g. CONSORT, STROBE, ARRIVE, or "not sure"]

Rules:
- Write so another researcher could repeat the study: who, what, when, where, how, and how many.
- Use subsections in the field's standard order. Past tense, precise quantities and units.
- Separate planned from exploratory analyses.
- Do not fill gaps with plausible details. Any missing information (version numbers, exact settings, dates, exclusion counts) becomes [ADD: what is needed].
- Do not invent citations for instruments or methods; mark them [CITE].

Return the methods section, then a replication checklist listing every [ADD] and [CITE] and which reporting-guideline items are not yet covered.
variables: e.g. CONSORT, STROBE, ARRIVE, or "not sure"

title: Write a news analysis article that connects the dots
description: An analysis piece that explains a current story by linking it to history, data, and similar events, with every claim sourced.
content:
Help me write a news analysis article on a current story.

**The story:** [WHAT HAPPENED, with links or pasted reporting]
**My sources:** [articles, reports, research papers, data, past coverage I want to draw on]
**Angle or question:** [e.g. "why this keeps happening", "what this means for small lenders"]
**Publication and readers:** [WHERE IT WILL RUN, who reads it]
**Length:** [e.g. "1,200 words"]

Write an analysis, not a news report:
1. **Lede** that states the story and why it matters now, in 2-3 sentences.
2. **Nut graf:** the central argument or insight the piece will support.
3. **Context:** connections to past events, earlier policy, research, or similar cases elsewhere that most coverage misses. Use only connections my sources support.
4. **Evidence:** data and quotes from the sources, each attributed in the text.
5. **Other views:** the strongest counterargument or alternative explanation, treated fairly.
6. **What to watch next:** concrete signals or dates that will show where this is heading.
7. **SEO package:** headline options, a meta description, and a few search phrases to work in naturally.

Rules: separate fact from interpretation clearly ("the data shows" vs. "this suggests"). Never invent facts, quotes, statistics, or sources; if a claim needs support I have not provided, mark it [SOURCE NEEDED]. Avoid sensationalism; the insight should come from the connections, not from dramatic wording. End with a list of every source used so I can fact-check before publishing.
variables: WHAT HAPPENED, with links or pasted reporting
WHERE IT WILL RUN, who reads it

title: Write a nonfiction book proposal for agents and editors
description: A complete nonfiction proposal: overview, author platform, comparable titles, marketing plan, chapter summaries, and sample chapter guidance.
content:
Help me write a nonfiction book proposal to send to literary agents or editors.

**Working title and one-line premise:** [DETAILS]
**What the book argues or teaches:** [THE BIG IDEA, and the reader's payoff]
**Who it is for:** [THE READER, and what shelf it sits on - e.g. business, memoir, popular science]
**Why me:** [credentials, lived experience, access, research]
**My platform:** [newsletter subscribers, social following, speaking, media appearances, organizations - real numbers only]
**Comparable titles I know of:** [TITLES, AUTHORS, YEARS]
**Chapter ideas:** [ROUGH LIST]
**Expected length and delivery time:** [WORD COUNT, months to finish]

Draft these sections:
1. Overview: a hook, the big idea, why now, and what the reader gains (2-3 pages' worth).
2. Target audience: who buys this and how big that readership is.
3. Author bio focused on why I am the person to write it.
4. Platform and marketing plan: specific things I will do, not wishes.
5. Comparable titles: 4-6 recent books, each with how mine is similar and different. Prefer books from the last five years and avoid blockbusters as comps.
6. Chapter-by-chapter outline: a paragraph per chapter showing the arc.
7. Book specs: length, illustrations, delivery date.

Then tell me which section is weakest and which chapter would make the strongest sample chapter.

Do not invent comparable titles, sales figures, or platform numbers. Suggest comps only as [VERIFY - CHECK PUBLICATION DETAILS], and mark gaps [ADD].
variables: THE BIG IDEA, and the reader's payoff

title: Write a one-page specific aims page for a grant
description: Drafts a tight specific aims page that sells the problem, gap, hypothesis, aims, and payoff on a single page.
content:
Help me write a specific aims page (or one-page project summary) for a research grant.

**Funder and mechanism:** [e.g. "NIH R01", "NIH K award", "foundation pilot grant"]
**Problem and its significance:** [burden, cost, scale, with sources]
**What is known and the critical gap:** [DETAILS]
**My central hypothesis or objective:** [DETAILS]
**Preliminary data:** [KEY FINDINGS, or "none"]
**Planned aims:** [2-3 aims with approach for each]
**Team and environment strengths:** [DETAILS]
**Expected outcomes and impact:** [DETAILS]

Structure (must fit on one page, roughly 500 words):
1. Opening hook: the problem and why it matters now.
2. The gap: what is unknown and why it blocks progress.
3. Long-term goal, objective of this proposal, central hypothesis, and rationale (preliminary data).
4. Aims: each with a bold, active title, a short approach, and the expected outcome. Aims should be related but not dependent on each other succeeding.
5. Payoff: expected outcomes, innovation, and impact.

After drafting, review it as a busy study-section reviewer would: is the hypothesis testable, are aims independent, is the scope feasible for the budget and time, and is anything vague? Give 5 specific fixes. Mark statistics without a source I provided as [CITE].
variables: e.g. "NIH R01", "NIH K award", "foundation pilot grant"

title: Write a paper or conference abstract within the word limit
description: A tight, structured abstract that states the problem, method, key result with numbers, and implication without exceeding the limit.
content:
Write an abstract for my research.

**Type:** [journal article / conference submission / thesis / poster]
**Word limit and required structure:** [e.g. "250 words, Background/Methods/Results/Conclusions" or "unstructured"]
**Research question or aim:** [DETAILS]
**Design, data, and methods:** [sample, setting, approach, key analyses]
**Main results, with numbers:** [effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, or key qualitative findings]
**Implication:** [why it matters and for whom]
**Draft or full text (optional):** [PASTE]

Rules:
- Stay under the word limit; report the final word count.
- One sentence of background at most, then the gap.
- Include the main quantitative result with its uncertainty, not just "significant".
- Conclusions must follow from the results; no causal language for an observational design.
- No citations, undefined abbreviations, or claims not in the paper.
- For a conference abstract with incomplete results, describe what will be presented and mark expected results [PENDING].

Return two versions (one plain, one emphasizing the most novel finding), each with its word count, plus 5 keywords and a one-sentence lay summary.
variables: journal article / conference submission / thesis / poster
why it matters and for whom

title: Write a patient experience report from visits and surveys
description: Turns visit notes, patient and staff feedback, and survey data into a structured report with findings and recommendations.
content:
Help me draft a patient experience report from site visits and feedback I collected.

**Services visited:** [e.g. "two primary care clinics and a nursing home", "hospital outpatient clinic"]
**Purpose of the visits:** [WHY, and any statutory or organizational program they were part of - e.g. a patient advocacy site-visit program or quality review]
**Methods:** [observation, patient questionnaires, staff questionnaires, interviews; dates; number of responses]
**Data and notes:** [PASTE SURVEY RESULTS, QUOTES, OBSERVATIONS]
**Audience:** [provider, funders or payers, board, public]
**Length:** [e.g. "about 20 pages"]

Structure:
1. Summary: the 5 most important findings and top recommendations.
2. Introduction: the program, purpose, and the services involved.
3. Methodology: how visits ran, who we spoke to, sample sizes, and limitations (e.g. small samples, who was not reached).
4. Findings by theme (e.g. access and waiting, dignity and respect, communication, environment, staffing, food and hydration, involvement in care), each with data, representative anonymized quotes, and observations.
5. What is working well, so good practice is recognized.
6. Recommendations: specific, numbered, each linked to a finding, with a suggested owner and a space for the provider's response.
7. Appendices: questionnaires and full results.

Also suggest the charts to include (chart type, data, and title for each).

Rules:
- Use only the data I provide; mark gaps [ADD DATA]. Do not inflate percentages from small samples; report counts alongside them.
- Remove anything that could identify a patient, resident, or staff member.
- Keep the tone factual and constructive. Flag any safeguarding concern in my notes for immediate escalation through the proper channel rather than waiting for the report.
variables: provider, funders or payers, board, public

title: Write a player scouting report from my match notes
description: Turns your match notes into a structured, position-aware scouting report with precise language and a clear recommendation.
content:
Help me write a player scouting report from my notes.

**Sport and level:** [e.g. "soccer, second division", "college basketball"]
**Player:** [NAME or anonymized ID, age, position(s), foot/hand, current club or team]
**Matches or footage watched:** [DATES, OPPONENTS, minutes observed]
**My raw notes:** [PASTE]
**What my club needs:** [ROLE, playing style, system - e.g. "ball-playing center-back for a high line"]
**Report format or grading scale we use:** [e.g. "1-10 per attribute", "A-D", or "none"]

Write the report with these sections, using my grading scale where I gave one:
1. Profile summary (3 sentences): who the player is and the headline judgment.
2. Physical: speed, acceleration, strength, endurance, agility, and the position-specific physical demands of my sport.
3. Technical: the core skills for this sport and position (e.g. first touch and weaker foot in soccer; shooting, handle, and footwork in basketball), each rated with evidence.
4. Tactical: positioning, movement off the ball, pressing and defensive work, decision-making, versatility.
5. Mental: work rate, composure under pressure, leadership, response to mistakes.
6. Weaknesses and risks: specific, with the situations where they showed up.
7. Fit for our system and role, and the player's likely ceiling.
8. Recommendation: Sign / Monitor / Reject, with the next step (more live viewings, data check, background references).

Rules:
- Every claim ties to something observed; mark single-match observations as such. Never invent statistics, transfer values, or injury history; use [ADD DATA] where needed.
- Use precise, varied scouting vocabulary appropriate to the position, not generic praise.
- Flag where the sample is too small to judge.
- Keep personal or medical details factual and within what my organization permits.

title: Write a point-by-point response to peer reviewers
description: Turns reviewer comments into a courteous, organized response letter with a tracked plan for every revision.
content:
Help me write a point-by-point response to the reviewers of my manuscript.

**Journal and decision:** [e.g. "major revision, resubmit within 60 days"]
**Reviewer and editor comments:** [PASTE all comments, labeled by reviewer]
**Changes I have made or plan to make:** [NOTES per comment, with page/line numbers if known]
**Comments I disagree with, and why:** [YOUR REASONING and any evidence]
**Word or page limits that constrain changes:** [DETAILS or "none"]

Steps:
1. Split every comment into separate, numbered points (R1.1, R1.2, R2.1...). Do not merge or skip any, including minor ones.
2. Classify each: required change / reasonable request / misunderstanding / out of scope / disagreement.
3. For each point, draft a response that thanks briefly (once, not every time), states exactly what changed, and quotes the revised text with its location. Mark anything I have not done yet as [TO DO].
4. For disagreements, respond respectfully with reasoning and evidence, and offer a partial concession where possible (e.g. a new limitation sentence).
5. Flag where two reviewers ask for conflicting changes and suggest how to reconcile them for the editor.

Return:
- A short cover note to the editor summarizing the main changes.
- The response letter: Comment (quoted) | Response | Change made and location.
- A revision checklist of every [TO DO], ordered by effort.

Never invent analyses, results, or citations I have not provided; mark them [ADD] instead.
variables: PASTE all comments, labeled by reviewer
NOTES per comment, with page/line numbers if known

title: Write a proposal to start a club or program
description: A persuasive proposal for a new club, contest, or program at a school or organization, with goals, logistics, budget, and roles.
content:
Help me write a proposal to start a new club or program.

**The idea:** [e.g. "a debate and public speaking club", "a history contest", "a coding club"]
**Organization:** [school, community center, nonprofit, workplace]
**Who decides and who reads this:** [principal, board, colleagues who would help run it]
**Participants:** [ages or groups, expected numbers]
**Why now:** [the need, interest, or gap - with any evidence]
**Resources I need:** [space, time slots, budget, volunteers, outside experts]
**Who will help run it:** [names or roles]

Structure the proposal:
1. **Summary:** the idea and the ask in 3-4 sentences.
2. **Purpose and goals:** what participants gain, with 2-3 measurable goals.
3. **How it will work:** format, schedule, session outline, and for a contest: eligibility, rules, judging criteria, and prizes.
4. **Roles:** who does what, including what I'm asking colleagues to commit.
5. **Resources and budget:** a simple table with costs and possible funding sources; mark unknowns [ADD COST].
6. **Risks and how we'll handle them:** low turnout, scheduling conflicts, supervision and safeguarding for minors.
7. **Pilot plan and next steps:** start small, review after [PERIOD], and what I need approved by when.

Keep it to about 2 pages, warm but concrete. Also give me a 1-minute pitch I can use when presenting it in a meeting.
variables: principal, board, colleagues who would help run it
the need, interest, or gap - with any evidence
space, time slots, budget, volunteers, outside experts

title: Write a public notice residents will actually understand
description: A legally complete public notice for a hearing, rate change, or service change, plus a plain-language version for web and social channels.
content:
Write a public notice for my agency.

**Type of notice:** [e.g. "public hearing", "proposed fee or rate change", "road closure", "service change", "comment period"]
**What is happening and why:** [DETAILS]
**Who is affected and where:** [areas, addresses, groups]
**Key dates:** [hearing date and time, comment deadline, effective date]
**How people can take part:** [in person, online, phone, written comments, address]
**Legal requirements I know of:** [e.g. "must run in newspaper of record 10 days before", "required elements list"; or "unsure"]
**Languages needed:** [LANGUAGES]
**Accommodation contact:** [ADA / disability accommodation and interpretation request contact]

Give me:
1. **The formal notice** with every required element I listed, in the order a legal notice normally follows: title, authority, description, time and place, how to comment, where documents can be viewed, accommodation statement, contact.
2. **A plain-language version** (under 150 words, about 6th to 8th grade reading level) that leads with what changes for residents and what they can do about it.
3. **A social post** (under 280 characters) and a **text alert** (under 160 characters).
4. A checklist of required elements, marking any I have not supplied as [ADD].

Rules: dates, times, and locations in bold; no jargon or unexplained acronyms; never invent legal citations, deadlines, or fees. Remind me to confirm publication and posting requirements with our clerk or counsel.
variables: hearing date and time, comment deadline, effective date
in person, online, phone, written comments, address

title: Write a quarterly portfolio review letter to a wealth client
description: A plain-English client letter on performance, market context, portfolio changes, and next steps, with required disclosures flagged.
content:
Write a quarterly review letter to a client whose portfolio I manage.

**Client context:** [goals, time horizon, risk profile, any life changes this quarter - no names]
**Performance:** [PASTE portfolio return for quarter, year-to-date, and since inception, net of fees, plus the agreed benchmark returns]
**Allocation:** [current vs. target by asset class]
**Changes made this quarter and why:** [trades, rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting]
**Market context I want to mention:** [2-3 points I believe matter for this client]
**Upcoming items:** [RMDs, contributions, meeting date, documents needed]
**Tone:** [warm and plain / more detailed for an experienced investor]

Structure:
1. Opening: one sentence on how the portfolio did relative to the client's plan, not just the market.
2. Performance summary in a small table (portfolio vs. benchmark, net of fees), with one paragraph explaining the main contributors and detractors.
3. What we changed and why, linked to their goals.
4. Market context in plain language - no predictions stated as fact.
5. Where they stand against their goals and whether anything should change.
6. Action items for them, with dates in bold.

Rules:
- Use only the figures I give; mark any gap [CONFIRM]. Never fabricate returns or benchmark data.
- No promises or guarantees of future results; no cherry-picked periods.
- Keep it under 500 words.
- List the disclosures my firm likely needs (past performance, net-of-fee basis, benchmark description) as [CONFIRM with compliance].
variables: current vs. target by asset class
RMDs, contributions, meeting date, documents needed
warm and plain / more detailed for an experienced investor

title: Write a sole-source justification that passes approval
description: A clear, defensible case for buying from one supplier without competitive bidding, with the evidence approvers and auditors look for.
content:
Help me write a sole-source (or single-source) justification for a purchase.

**What we're buying and estimated value:** [ITEM OR SERVICE, TOTAL CONTRACT VALUE, DURATION]
**Proposed supplier:** [NAME]
**Why only this supplier:** [e.g. "proprietary technology", "compatibility with installed equipment", "only certified source", "urgent need", "follow-on to existing work"]
**Evidence:** [MARKET RESEARCH DONE, OTHER SUPPLIERS CONTACTED AND WHY THEY DON'T QUALIFY, TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS]
**Price reasonableness:** [HOW I KNOW THE PRICE IS FAIR - past prices, price lists, benchmarks, negotiated discount]
**Our policy or regulation:** [PASTE THE ALLOWED REASONS OR THRESHOLD FROM OUR PROCUREMENT POLICY]
**Approvers:** [WHO SIGNS]

Requirements:
- Tie the justification to the specific allowed reason in my policy; don't use a reason my policy doesn't list.
- Show that alternatives were genuinely considered, with facts, not assertions like "no one else can do it".
- Separate sole source (only one exists) from single source (we prefer one among several); be honest about which applies.
- If urgency is the reason, explain why it wasn't foreseeable, since self-made urgency usually fails review.
- Include the price reasonableness basis and any plan to compete it next time.
- Use only facts I provide; mark gaps [ADD EVIDENCE].

Return:
1. The justification memo with headings: Requirement, Proposed supplier, Justification, Market research, Price reasonableness, Risks, Future competition plan, Approval.
2. A list of weak points an auditor might challenge, with how to strengthen each.
variables: ITEM OR SERVICE, TOTAL CONTRACT VALUE, DURATION

title: Write a staff report recommending action to a council or board
description: A council or board staff report with background, analysis, fiscal impact, options, and a recommended motion elected officials can act on.
content:
Write a staff report for an upcoming council, commission, or board meeting.

**Governing body and meeting date:** [e.g. "City Council, regular meeting"]
**Item type:** [action item / consent item / discussion only / public hearing]
**What we are asking them to do:** [e.g. "approve a contract", "adopt an ordinance", "accept a grant"]
**Background and history:** [prior actions, dates, why this is before them now]
**Analysis and facts:** [KEY DATA, findings, legal requirements]
**Fiscal impact:** [cost, funding source, budgeted or not, ongoing vs. one-time]
**Alternatives considered:** [OPTIONS]
**Public input received:** [SUMMARY, if any]
**Related plans or policies:** [e.g. "general plan", "strategic plan goal 3"]

Structure the report as:
1. Title and recommended action, written as a motion the body can adopt word for word.
2. Summary (under 120 words) for officials who read only this part.
3. Background.
4. Discussion and analysis.
5. Fiscal impact, including the account or fund if I gave one.
6. Alternatives, each with its consequence.
7. Environmental, legal, or equity considerations I named.
8. Attachments list.

Rules:
- Neutral, factual tone. Staff reports inform; they do not lobby. Present alternatives fairly.
- Plain language a resident reading the public packet can follow. Define acronyms on first use.
- Do not invent figures, vote history, or legal requirements; mark gaps [ADD] or [CONFIRM].
- After the report, list 5 questions officials are likely to ask with short suggested answers.
variables: action item / consent item / discussion only / public hearing
prior actions, dates, why this is before them now
cost, funding source, budgeted or not, ongoing vs. one-time

title: Write a station work instruction operators will actually follow
description: A one-page work instruction with numbered steps, key points, the reason behind each, and quality and safety checks at the station.
content:
Write a work instruction for a production station.

**Station and operation:** [e.g. "Line 2, Op 40: final torque and label"]
**The steps as done today:** [ROUGH notes, an existing SOP, or a description from the best operator]
**Tools, fixtures, and materials:** [LIST]
**Quality requirements:** [torque values, dimensions, visual standards, checks the operator must do]
**Safety hazards and PPE:** [pinch points, sharp edges, chemicals, required PPE]
**Takt or target cycle time:** [SECONDS, if known]
**Operator context:** [experience level, languages, literacy, whether it will be shown on a screen or printed]

Write it in the standard work / Job Instruction format:
- A header: station, part numbers, revision, date, approver [ADD].
- Required PPE and safety warnings at the top, with icons described in brackets, e.g. [ICON: safety glasses].
- Major steps numbered, each under 10 words and starting with a verb.
- For each step: key points (anything that makes or breaks quality, safety, or ease) and the reason for each key point.
- Quality checks marked clearly as CHECK, with the accept/reject criteria.
- What to do if something is wrong: stop, who to call, how to tag suspect parts.
- Placeholders for photos, e.g. [PHOTO: correct connector orientation].

Rules: one page if possible, plain words, no jargon an operator wouldn't use, no step that hides two actions. Do not invent specifications; mark gaps [CONFIRM WITH ENGINEERING]. After the instruction, list the steps I should verify by watching an operator do the job.
variables: e.g. "Line 2, Op 40: final torque and label"
pinch points, sharp edges, chemicals, required PPE

title: Write a strong first draft from my brief
description: Turns your goal, audience, and key points into a clear, usable first draft.
content:
Act as an expert business writer who prioritizes clarity, usefulness, and strong structure.

**Context**
I need to create content for [AUDIENCE] to achieve [OBJECTIVE].

**Task**
Write a first draft that is clear, specific, practical, and easy to scan. Lead with the most useful idea. Avoid filler, generic statements, unsupported claims, and unnecessary jargon.

**Format**
Return:
- Title
- Draft
- One-sentence core message
- Suggested CTA, if relevant

**Objective:** [PASTE]

title: Write a well-argued essay
description: Plans and writes an essay with a clear thesis, evidence, and counterarguments.
content:
Help me write an essay.

**Topic or question:** [TOPIC]
**Type:** [argumentative / analytical / opinion / reflective / academic]
**Audience and level:** [e.g. "university course", "general readers of a newspaper"]
**Length:** [WORD COUNT]
**My view or angle (if I have one):** [POSITION]
**Sources or material I must use:** [PASTE OR "none"]

Process:
1. Propose 2–3 possible thesis statements and recommend one.
2. Give an outline: introduction, 3–5 body sections each with its main point and supporting evidence, the strongest counterargument and a rebuttal, conclusion.
3. Write the full essay from the outline.

Rules:
- Every claim needs support: evidence, an example, or reasoning. Mark anything that needs a citation as [CITATION NEEDED] — never invent sources or statistics.
- Clear topic sentences and transitions; no filler.
- Match the requested level and length.

If this is for a graded assignment, follow my course's rules on AI use.
variables: e.g. "university course", "general readers of a newspaper"

title: Write an account handover document for the next account owner
description: A complete handover of a customer account so the next owner knows the history, people, risks, and open commitments.
content:
Help me write a handover document for a customer account I'm passing to a colleague.

**Account basics:** [COMPANY, PRODUCTS, CONTRACT VALUE, START DATE, RENEWAL DATE, KEY CONTRACT TERMS]
**My notes, CRM history, or brain dump:** [PASTE]
